NOTIFICATIONS 


No. 1221M.2A-35/60.—2Ilst February 1962.—In 
exercise of the power conferred by the proviso to 
article 309 of the Constitution of India, the Governor 
is pleased hereby to make the following rule regula- 
ting the recruitment to the posts of Special Officers 
under the Local Self-Government and Panchayats 
Department, in the West Bengal General Service, 
uamely :— 


RULE 


The method of recruitment and the qualifications 
for direct recruitment to the gazetted posts of Special 
Officers, Grade I, in the pay scale of Rs. 325—30— 
475—35—1,000 (E.B. after 8th and 16th stages) and 
of Special Officers, Grade I], in the pay scale of 
Rs. 275—15—350—20—650 (E.B. after 8th and 16th 
Stages) in the West Bengal General Service, for 
appointment #4 Government as Administrators and 
Executive Officers of municipalities, shall be 
as detailed below: — 


_ (1) Method of recruitment to both the posts of 
Special Officer, Grade I, and Special Officer, 
Grade II: ; ; 

(i) By transfer from the West Bengal Civil Service 
(Executive) or the West Bengal Junior Civil 
Service; or রর 

(ii) by transfer from other State Services in con- 
sultation with the Public Service Commis- 
sion, West Bengal; or 

(iii) shy selection (direct recruitment). 


(2) Qualifications for direct recruitment to the post 
of Special Officer,, Grade I: 

(i) A degree of a recognised university; 

(ii) Five years’ experience in a responsible position 
in a Government Office or a statutory body 
or a commercial concern of repute. 

Age: Not more than 45 years, relaxable for a 

well-qualified and experienced candidate. 
(3) Qualifications for direct recruitment to the post 
of Special Officer, Grade 11: 

(i) A degree of a recognised university; 

(ii) three years’ experience in a responsible posi- 
tion in a Government office or a statutory 
body or a commercial concern of repute. 


Age: Not more than 35 years, relaxable for a 
well-qualified and experienced candidate. 


By order of the Governor, 
J. C. TALUKDAR, Jt. Secy.

No. 5321. — 8th February 1962. — Whereas 
Messrs. Shalimar Chemical Works Private Limited, 
in the district of 24-Parganas, not being licensees, 
are engaging in the business of supplying energy to 
Messrs. Shalimar Tools and Allied Products at their 
factory premises in Shalimar Park, Narendrapur, in 
the district of 24-Parganas (hereinafter referred to as 
the said area); 


And whereas the Fartabad Union Board ٭ز‎ the 
local authority constituted for the said area; 


And whereas the said area does not form part of 
any cantonment, aerodrome, fortress, arsenal, dock- 
yard or camp or of any building or place in the occu- 
pation of the Government for,defence purposes; , 

And whereas the said area is not includéd within 
the area of supply of any licensee; 


Now, therefore, in eexrcise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 28 of the Indian Elec- 
tricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), the Governor is 
রী after consulting the West Bengal State 

lectricity Board and with the consent of the local 
uuthority concerned, namely, the Fartabad Union 
Board, to give the said Messrs. Shalimar Chemical 
Works Private Limited (hereinafteg referred to as the 
sanction-holders) sanction to engage in the business 
of supply energy within the said area, subject to the 
following conditions, namely :— 


(1) that the provisions of section 11, section 17, 
section 18, sub-sections (1) and (4) of sec- 
tion 21, section 24, section 26 of the Indian 
Electricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), and the 
provisions of the Indian Electricity Rules 
1956, shall apply as if the sanction-holders 
were licensees; 


(2) that the rates per unit for the supply of energy 
shall not exceed the bulk supply rate at 
which Messrs. Shalimar Chemical Works 
Private Limited are purchasing power from 
the West Bengal State Electricity Board; 


(3) that the sanction hereby granted shall cease 
to be operative as soon as the West Bengal 
State Electricity Board shall be in a posi- 
tion to supply energy to the said area; 


(4) that the sanction-holders shall, on _ being 
called upon by the West Bengal State 
Electricity Board to do so, be bound to 
make over the undertakings forthwith to the 
said Board and the sanction-holders shall 
be entitled to receive from the said Board 
reasonable compensation therefor based on 
fair market price, as may be agreed upon 
between the sanction-holders and the said 
Board, and in case of any dispute, the same 
shall be referred to arbitration in accord- 
ance with the provisions of the Arbitration 
Act, 1940 (X of 1940); 


(5) that the sanctfon hereby given shall be liable 
to be rescinded or revoked in 0859 the 
sanction-holders fail to supply energy 
efficiently and satisfactorily or fail to com- 
ply with any of the terms and conditions

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 
ORDERS 


(hereinafter referred to as the Union) filed the 
written statement on 22nd August 1961 duly signed 
and verified by Shrimati Gayatri Das Gupta described 
as the Secretary of the Union. 


The case of the Union is that Shri Harendra 
Chakraborty who happened to be the Assistant 
Secretary of the Union was a permanent worker of 
this Company since 1952 and that the Company 
issued orders transferring him to the Bombay 
Factory on Ist November 1960, even though there 
was no such condition of service that a workman 
could be transferred from one State to another, and 
that there was sufficient work at Jadavpur Factory. 
Shri Chakraborty then wrote a letter to the Company 
on 5th November 1960 to consider amongst other 
mattérs his difficulties to go to Bombay and request- 
ed the Manager to withdraw the order of transfer. 
At the same time the Union took up the matter at 
the instance of Shri Chakraborty and wrote to the 
Labour Commissioner on 7th November 1960 solici- 
ting intervention with respect to the matter of 
transfer wherein amongst other points it was alleged 
that the order of transfer had been issued with mala 
hde intention of weakening and crushing the Union 
of which Shri Chakraborty was the Assistant Secre- 
tary, Shri N. C. Kundu, the Assistant Labour Com- 
missioner, who dealt with the dispute, as raised, at 
once intervened and asked the parties to maintain 
Status quo pending conciliation. The said officer 
ulso called the parties at a joint conference fixed on 
10101) November 1960. The Company did not attend 
the conference and in violation of the directions to 
maintain status quo refused employment ٠ 
Shri Chakraborty from 1100 November 1960. 
Shri Chakraborty then wrote to the Company on 
1111) November 1960 requesting the management 
again to reconsider his case and allow him to resume 
his duties forthwith. The development of the matter 
was also brought to the notice of the Assistant 
Labour Commissioner by the Union in the letter, 
dated 12th November 1960. The Company there- 
after wrote to Shri Chakraborty on 16th November 
1960 with reference to his letter, dated 5th Novem- 
ber 1960, asking him to join at Bomba Factory 
within 48 hours. On receipt of that letter 
Shri Chakraborty again wrote to the Manager of 
the Company praying for withdrawal of the order 
of transfer and permitting him to resume his duties 
at Jadavpur. At the same time the Union also 
wrote to Shri Kundu, Assistant Labour Commis- 
sioner, protesting against the action of the employer. 
The Company by their letter, dated 7th December 
1960, informed the Assistant Labour Commissioner 
that the worker in question did not comply with 
the order of transfer and that he had accepted 
employment elsewhere and, therefore, the workman 
would stand dismissed. Shri Chakraborty informed 
the Manager, in writing, on 13th December 1960 that 
he had not accepted any employment elsewhere. In 
spite of that the Manager by the letter, dated 15th 
December 1960, dismissed him from service without 
giving him any hearing. It § contended by the 
Union that the entire action of the management was 
illegal, unjustified and mala fide.

(hereinafter referred to as the Company) filed the

Commissioner started the conciliation proceedings 
at once and wrote to the Company to maintain 
status quo pending conciliation enclosing ulong with 
the Union’s letter, dated 7th November 1960, and 
further asked the employer to meet at a joint con- 
ference at his office on 10th November 1960 [vide 
Ext. 1(H)]. Shri Ghosh, the Manager of the Com- 
pany, in his deposition stated that Shri Kundu, the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner, did not direct the 
employer to maintain status quo. But the evidence 
clearly reveals that the said Manager received the 
memo. Ext. 1(H), addressed by the Assistant Labour 
Commissioner and, 25 a matter of fact, he gave 
reply to the same on 9th November 1960, justifying 
the action [vide Ext. A(5)]. In spite of having receiv- 
ed the letter from the Conciliation Officer to main- 
tain status quo the management refused employ- 
ment to Shri Chakraborty since 11th November 1960, 
and thus violated his direction. It however trans- 
pires from the evidence that Shri Chakraborty work- 
ed in this factory till 10th November 1960. 1015 
also significant to note that the management inform- 
ed Shri Chakraborty in reply to his letter, dated 5th 
November 1960, on 16th November 1960 that they 
have duly received the letter from the Labour Com- 
missioner [vide Ext. 1(a)]. By that letter the manage- 
ment also informed Shri Chakraborty that if he 
failed to join at Bombay Factory within 48 hours, 
disciplinary action under the Standing Orders of the 
Company would be taken against him. There is no 
Satisfactory explanation forthcoming from _ the 
management as to why the registered letter sent by 
Shri Chakraborty on 5th November 1960 had not 
been duly received when delivered by the postal 
eat and, as such, a reply had been given at such 
ate stage. There is also nothing to explain why in 
spite of the definite direction from the Conciliation 
Officer to maintain status quo, the Company thought 
it রি to refuse employment to Shri Chakraborty 
and thereby cause a termination of service with effect 
from llth November 1960. Be that as it 19) 
Shri Chakraborty again wrote to the Company on 
18th November 1960 on receipt of the letter, dated 
16th November 1960, from the Company, requestin 

the management to take a sympathetic view an 

withdraw the order of transfer and permit him ta 
join his duties [vide Ext. A(2)]. At the same time 
the Union wrote to the Conciliation Officer on 19th 
November 1960 pointing out that the Company had 
violated the direction to maintain status quo and 
refused employment to Shri Chakraborty from 110 
November 1960 [vide Ext. l(m)]. It may be noted 
that the Conciliation Officer in the meantime again 
called a joint conference between the parties by his 
letter, dated the 12th November 1960, and the date 
of joint conference was fixed on 25th November 
1960 [vide Ext. 1(i)], in response to the letter from 
the Union, dated 12th November 1960 [vide Ext. 1(n)]. 
It appears from the evidence that the management 
did not attend the joint conference called by - the 
Conciliation Officer to be held on 25th November 
1960. But at the same time on 22nd November 1960 
the Company wrote to the Conciliation Officer that 
in view of the fact that the Union was not recog- 
nised by them, they were unwilling to sit at a joint 
conference with the Union and would like to discuss 
the matter Separately with the Conciliation Officer 
and that the transfer of Shri Chakraborty was fullv 
justified for the same reason as mentioned in the 
previous letter, Ext. A(5) (vide Ext. A(6)]. Then on 
7th December 1960 the Company wrote to the Con- 
ciliation Officer that they were reliably informed 


individual . 


written statement on 4th November 1961. It is con- 
tended by the Company that this is an 
dispute and, therefore, the Tribunal has no jurisdic- 
tion to entertain the same. Regarding the merits of 
the case it is contended that the Company after con- 
sultation and agreement with the particular Trade 
Union as recognised by them transferred এ large 
number of workmen to Bombay Section 95 per 
Standing Orders and further that the transfer of 
Shri Chakraborty was by way of promotion. 
Besides, it is contended that upon receipt of the 
letter from the Assistant Labour Commissioner the 
management expressed their views to the said officer 
in writing on 9th November 1960 but that they 
never sat in joint conference with the representatives 
of the Union before the Assistant Labour Commis- 
sioner. Further it is alleged that the workmen by 
accepting employment elsewhere had abandoned his 
services under this Company and thereafter the order 
of dismissal had been passed. 


At the time of hearing from the side of the Union 
the dismissed workman, Shri Harendra Chakraborty, 
has been examined. On the other hand, the Com- 
pany examined Shiri S. R. Ghosh, Manager of the 
Jadavpur Factory of the Company. Besides, a large 
volume of documents including the correspondence 
that passed between Shri Chakraborty ৪00 the 
management and those between the management and 
the Union with the Assistant Labour Commissioner, 
Shri N. C. Kundu, are proved and marked as 
exhibits. I shall refer to the evidence, oral and 
documentary, as necessary in course of my adjudi- 
cation. It is very necessary to go through the con-

The Government of West Bengal by its Labour 
Department order No. 1847-I.R./IR/4L-22/61, dated 


17th April 1961, referred to this Tribunal an 
industrial dispute between the Joint Steamer 
Companies (Messrs. I.G.N.R. Co. Ltd. and R. S. N. 
Co. Ltd.), 4 Fairlie Place, Calcutta-1 (hereafter 


referred to as the Companies), and their workmen 
represented by Inland Steam Navigation Workers’ 
Union, 16/17 College Street (Room No. 55), 
Calcutta-12 (hereafter referred to as the Union), for 
adjudication under section 10 of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act. 


The only issue referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication in this case runs as follows: 


Working hours for the workmen employed in the 
Crew Registration and Payment Office. 


AWARD 


The workmen's case in their written statement is 
as follows: The Indian General Navigation and Rail- 
way Company Ltd. and the River Steam Navigation 
Company Ltd., popularly known as Joint Steamer 
Companies, carry on transport business in different 
parts of India, having their Head Office at 2 and 
4 Fairlie Place, Calcutta. The Companies have 
different establishments in different places of India 
and West Bengal. The lead Office of these 
Companies has several departments including Joint 
Labour and Welfare Department, Joint Marine 
Department, Joint Engineering Department, Joint 
Claims Department and Joint Traffic Audit Denart- 
ment. The Companies have several Ghat Offices 
also at Jagannath Ghat, Armenian Ghat, etc. The 
services of the employees at Ghat Offices and Head 
Office Departments are inter-transferable and these 
employees are divided into two categories, namelv, 
clerical and non-clerical or subordinate staff. The 
Department of Crew Registration and Payment 


8 annas in excess of his normal wages per day. But 
in 1959 when Bansi went on leave Bansidhar was 
ordered to work in his place and not Sukhan, the 
reason for prefering Bansidhar to Sukhan being that 
Sukhan did 1701 know how to repair the machines 
in the event of a break-down. It further appears 
that since the middle of 1۱961 the stentor machines. 
installed in the factory, were dismantled and they 
were replaced by new German Famatex machines 
which require more দ্যা workmen and Sukhan 
has been working as helper to these qualified work- 
men operating these new machines. 


It is at once obvious that by having officiated for 
some days during 1957 and 1958 Sukhan has not 
earned the right of working in place of Bansi when- 
ever Bansi goes on leave or when he is having his 
weekly off days. It appears that in the past, two 
other men, Daragoai and Sadagar, used to work in his 
place and then from 1959 Bansidhar has_ been 
entrusted with this work in the absenge of Bansi. As 
none of these workmen have acquired a right to work 
in place of Bansi in his absence it cannot be said to 
be a condition of the service of any of these work- 
men that whenever Bansi goes on leave he must 
be allowed to officiate in his place. The question to 
whom an officiating appointment should go is entirelv 
a matter of discretion with the management. The 
Standing Orders of the Company do not seem to 
provide for such a case and there is nothing therein 
to suggest the existence of a right in any workman 
who occasionally acts for another to act for him 
whenever he is absent. Consequently, section 33(2), 
Industrial Disputes Act, has no _ application at 
all to such a case and there 15 no 
question of any contravention of 15 pro- 
visions. Thus the first condition of the maintain- 
ability of an application under section 33A, namely, 
that there has been a contravention of the provisions 
of the section 33 does not exist and the whole 
application therefore, of Sukhan under section 33A 
must be held to be not maintainable at all. My 
award, therefore, is that as_ section 33(2) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act does not apply to the facts 
of the case, Sukhan’s application under section 33A 
is not maintainable.

arbitrate also. If the workers are, unreasonably 
sweated or over-worked and if they are made to 
work more than what 1s desirable. the workers can 
certainly agitate for reduction of working hours and 
thus for betterment of their service conditions. 
Conspiracy approach of old days towards such 
labour agitation or concerted labour activity 1s not 
any longer possible or permissible. The workers’ 
right or privilege of taking recourse to concerted 
labour activity for betterment of their service 
conditions, such as reduction of working hours and 
Increase In wages cannot be any longer curtailed or 
suppressed simply by saying that it falls within the 
rurview of the Management function and forms the 
subject matter of an individual contract That 
zribunal can interfere and do interfere in such cases 
15 amply demonstrated by innumerable decisions of 
tTnbunals, High Courts and the Supreme Court 
Even the Supreme Court decision in a case between 
these very Companies and their workmen (Ghat 
employecs) is a sharp pointer in this respect (a copy 
of the judgment has also been filed by the Companies 
and 15 on record) Whatever be the older conception 
of law on this point, the old doctrine of laissez faire 
no longer holds good or rules the day 11) the present 
sct-up of changing saciety and the labour manage- 
ment relationship Unrestricted freedom of action 
of the Management at times militates against the 
yust interest of the workers Hence, I am unable 
to accept the preliminary objection raised on behalf 
of the Companies. 


Office (hereafter referred to as C.R.P.O.) 1s being 
controlled and guided by the Joint Welfare and 
Labour Department, Joint Traffic Audit Department, 
jomt Clams Department and Joint Marine and 
Engineering Department. But the working hours of 
C.R PO. are different from that of the Head Office. 
1116 working hours at the Head Office are from 
10 am to 5 pm. from Monday to Friday with half 
dn hour’s recess in the middle and from 10 a.m. to

concerned requested the Management for introduction

to agree. This policy of the Management 1s discri- 
minatory and unfair, and hence this reference. 


The Companies, on the other hand, inter alia, 
allege in their written statement as follows: Although 
these two Companies have been operating in mutual 
collaboration since about 1890, they have always 
been and still are two separate and distinct entities, 
and each one of them maintains 115 own separate 
accounts, and their assets also are distinct. 
Although the carnings derived from the transport 
business ure pooled together and divided equally 
between the two Companies, a large portion of their 
expenditure 1s not shared equally, with the result 
thet the financial position of each of the two 
Companies 1s not same and similar. Prior to 1955, 
the ratings working on all the Companies’ vessels 
were contract labour—the system being that the 
Deck ratings were employed by Masters and 
Serangs, and the Engine Room ratings were employed 
by Drivers; and the ratings were discharged also by 
their respective employers During 1955, the 
Companies mutually agreed with the Bengal 
Mariners’ Union representing the ratings that the 
Said system of contract employment would ا‎ 
discontinued, and all ratings would become direct 
employces of the Companies In pursuance of this

rating personnel, and this department 15 working 
accordingly since then The Companies deny that 
the CRP.O is a part of or 1s controlled by the

Statement. The Joint Marine Department and the 
Joint Engincering Department apart from their 
various functions of technical nature administer the 


ranking personnel, namely, Masters, Scrangs and

C.RPO administers the rating personnel. Thus 


the status of the C.R P.O. 1s rather same as that of the 
Ghat Offices. The C.R P.O. works independently of

10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with half an hour's recess in the

Joint Claims Department or Joint Marine and 
Engineering Department. As the names of 01959 
departments suggest, the nature of their primary job 
or work 15 quite different from that of the C.R.P.O.. 
and they are separate and independent  establish-

written statement, it will be perfectly clear that this 
office was set up in 1955 only for the first time for 
dealing with the rating personnel independently of 
the other departments. But simply because 0115 
Office is under the general control. of the Head Office, 
it cannot be said that it is a part and parcel of the 
Head Office itself. It is contended that the staff of 
this office is transferable to Head Office and vice 
versa. But 0.۲۰۷۷۰ 1—Mr. Roberio-—swears that the 
Head Office employees are not transferable 00 
C.R.P.O. or other such offices. In fact, when the 
Service conditions, pay-scales and privileges of the 
Head Office employees are different from those of 
the C.R.P.O. employees, the question of transfer 
from one to the other does not arise. P.W. 2—Shri 
Debendra Nath Deasi—tries to say that he actually 
worked for some months at the Head Office and then 
was transferred to this department. But the fact is 
that he, along with some other employces, were 
previously workers of different Ration Shops only and 
these Ration Shops were abolished sometime in 1955. 
After this abolition, they were likely to be thrown 
out of employment. So, on an agreement with some 
Union, the Companies agreed to absorb these Ration 
Shop workers in other departments without 
discharging them outright. Thus these are really 
not cases of transfer. One may be temporarily 
allowed to work in some section of the Head Office. 
So, this does not prove that this department stands 
on the same footing with the Head Office. It is 
next contended that the Labour and Welfare Depart- 
ment deals with passports, visa, etc., of the rating 
personnel and does necessary work in that con- 
nection; and this department also attends to a part 
of this passport job on behalf of that department, 
and thus this department is a limb or branch of the 
other. But the fact is that passports are mainly 
dealt with by the Labour and Welfare Department 
ot the Head Office. The C.R.P.O. is required to do 
very little in that connection. Masters and Serangs 
of different vessels collect the passports of the crews 
and hand over the same to the C.R.P.O. and the 
C.R.P.O. simply issue receipts in printed forms for 
the passports received. These passports are there- 
after sent to the Labour and Welfare Department 
which 0065 everything needful ا‎ this connection. 
This department 06110 in close touch with the crews, 
simply collects the passports for transmission and 
thus serves as conduit pipe only for these passports. 
Simply because reccipts are issued by this office on 
behalf of the Passport Section of the Labour and 
Welfare Department. it cannot be said that the 
C.R.P.O. is also a part and parcel of that department. 
I have already said that determination of job-content 
is a Management function. So, merely because this 
department has been assigned the duty of collection 
of passports of the crews, it cannot, as of right, claim 
Same service conditions with the Labour and 
Welfare Department. Existence of an independent 
Controlline Officer for this department also shows 
that this department is not really under the other 


department. The Labour and Welfare Department 
advises the Management in respect of labour 
problems of all departments and looks after the 
welfare of the personnel of all the departments of 


t 


So, I pass on the merit of the issue. The C.R.P.O. 
employees now work for seven hours a day between 
9-30 am. and 5 p.m. with half an hour's recess in 
the middle. It is nobody’s case. that this period of 
work or working hour really transgresses any 
statutory provisions. The workmen’s contention is 
that in fixing these working hours for them, the 
Management has made invidious discrimination 
between this department and other Head Office 
departments which control and guide this depart- 
ment. The Head Office Department works for six 
and half hours only between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. It 
is urged that this C.R.P.O. being only a limb of the 
Head Office Department, this unfair discrimination 1s 
creating a strong dissatisfaction in the minds of the 
workers. The contention of the Management on the 
contrary is that this C.R.P.O. is really an independent 
establishment or department, and is neither a branch 
nor a limb of the Head Office Departments. The 
nature of work and the service condition of this 
department, it is alleged, are different from those of 
the Head Office, and the employees of this depart- 
ment cannot be placed at par in all respects with 
the employees of the Head Office. There are other 
similar establishments at different ghats, and thus 
away from the Head Office; and any preferential 
treatment of this department may again create a 
discontent in those departments. Moreover, the 
nature and exigencies of work entrusted 00 this 
department do not permit such change in working 
hours as claimed or desired by the present workmen. 
Both parties have adduced evidences. I have care- 
fully considered the evidences on record and argu- 
ments of both sides on this point, and I may at once 
observe that I have no sufficient reason for reduction 
in the working hours for Monday to Friday for these 
workmen. As regards Saturday, the Management is 
also eager to bring these employees at par with the 
Ghat employees of the Companies [vide paragraph 
11(e) of the written statement of the Companies] and 
J shall consider this Saturday matter before I 
conclude. The workmen's contention is that no real 
harm will be done to the Companies if C.R.P.O. is 
allowed to function from 10 a.m. and work for six 
and half hours only per diem. But I may point out 
that the methods of operation of the office and the 
plant and also the job-content are really Manage- 
ment function, and no Tribunal should normally 
interfere with these internal arrangements, unless 
there be a case of grave injustice likely to seriously 
jolt or jeopardise the labour-management relation- 
ship. At present, the workers of this department arc 
not working for more than 42 hours a weck, even 
if they are made to work full time on Saturdays. 
Forty-two-hour week cannot be said to be an 
unreasonable one. The Management ts agreeable to 
reduce the working hours of Saturdays by further 
two hours or so. So, forty-hour work a week will 
be quite a reasonable condition even apart from 
other considerations. So, from this standpoint, the 
present workmen have no case. The simple argu- 
ment of the warkmen in support of their contention 
is that the Head Office of the Companies works for 
35 hours only a week, and so they should also work 
not more than 36 hours. But I do not find any 
sufficient reason to bring them at par with the Head 
Office Departments where conditions of service are 


undoubtedly different. I find no substance in the 
contention that this department of C.R.P.O. is 
nothing but a branch of Joint Labour and Welfare 
Department, or Joint Traffic’ Audit Department or

in Ghat offices. They prefer their existing arrange-

and spread-over will continue for all week days 
except Saturday. On Saturday the Ghat offices work 
from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. without recess in accordance 
with a Supreme Court decision. If any worker of 
Ghat Establishment is detained beyond 3 p.m. for

recess. If any workman of this department 15 
detained beyond 2-30 p.m. for half an hour or more 
up to 5 p.m. he will be paid one-fourth day’s wages 
in addition to his normal wages.

The next contention of the workmen of C.R.P.O. 
is that their.day’s work actually commences from 
10-30/11 a.m. and that they usually have no work 
to do before the ratings come to office. Admittedly, 
the gate meant for the crews opens at 10 a.m. It is 
accordingly urged that the Companies will not be 
prejudicially affected if the C.R.P.O. commences 
day's work at 10 a.m. But this contention makes 
no impression on me. This office is required to deal 
with and make payments to at least 500/700 crews 
every day, and in busy periods this office is required 
to make payments of Rs. 50,000/60,000 a day to 
the crews alone. So, one can easily imagine that 
ا‎ papers and records are to be checked and 
prepared and kept ready in advance before these 
huge payments to the crews are actually made and 
before they enter the office for receiving payments. 
It is admitted by P.W Shri Sambhunath 
Mukherjee also that they are to keep money ready 
in advance before crews come for receiving payments. 
It is also conceded that the amounts due to different 
crews are to be ascertained and calculated in advance 
before payment. This office admittedly calculates 
and prepares records in advance as to what payments 
are to be made in respect of different items to any 
one of the crews (vide deposition of Shri 
Mukherjee ۶۷۷ 1). So, it is idle to argue that 
these workmen have to sit idle for half an hour after 
9-30 am. They have enough work to do before the 
ratings do actually come. It is admitted that they 
are often required to work overtime also and for 
that they earn overtime wages too. From the 
deposition of O.P.W. 2 Mr. Morris D. Braellan, an 
Assistant in the C.R.P.O., it will be clear that over- 
time work is a regular feature in this office now and 
for the last two months overtime work is being done 
every day. So, the normal duty hour cannot be 
curtailed as desired لی‎ td for facilitating the 
earning of overtime wages by the workmen. To me 
it appears that the necessity for overtime work 
should normally be reduced to the minimum for 
obvious reasons. Thus considering all the circum- 
stances, I think, the Management has every justifica- 
tion for commencing the work of this office at 
9-30 am. Undue delay in disposing of the rating 
personnel may mean delay in quick turn round of 
the vessels. The evidence is that these Steamer 
Companies have rival competitors in the field--both 
on land and water—-and any unreasonable and 
unecosomjc move involving delay in turn round may 
directly injure the interest of the employer and 
indircetly of the employecs also. Any _ serious 
detriment to the interest of the employer § may 
ultimately recoil on the head of the employees also. 
Our motto should always be to work reasonably hard 
and earn more in the interest of all concerned. Thus 
considéring all the facts and circumstances, ] find 
that the working hours of this C.R.P.O. cannot he 
made like that of the Head Office. Of course, the 
Management also has no objection to give the 
employecs of this office same facilities as enjoyed 
by Ghat employees, ctc., who stand more or less on 
the same footing. The Ghat employees work on 
Monday to Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. with one 
hour's recess in the middle. I have been definitely 
told on behalf of the workmen of the C.R.P.O. that 
they do not like to work from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. as

FINDINGS 


The Union has examined two witnesses in support 
of its case. They have said that some workmen 
including Shri Sew went to the house of the 
proprietor of the Company on 5th July 1957 to 
demand payment of their wages. On the following 
day the proprietor paid wages to all the workmen 
except Shri Sew whom he discharged on that day. 
They have denied that any charge-shcet was issued 
to him on 6th June 1957 or that he was dismissed 
on 13th June 1957. The Company has not adduced 
any evidence in support of its case. So the case of 
the Union stands proved. Hence I hold that the 
discharge of Shri Sew alias Shewnath Bhar is 
unjustified. So I order that he shall be reinstated 
and paid wages for the period of his forced unemploy- 
ment. The above order shall be carried out within 
a month of the publication of this award in the 
“Calcutta Gazette”. 


It appears from the evidence adduced on behalf 
of the Union that there have been changes in the 
name of the Company which is carrying on business 
at the site and with the machineries of Messrs. 
Amritasar Industrial Works, Ranigunj. It is on 
evidence of the Union that Shri Keshar Singh is the 
proprietor of all the companies in the names of 
which the business is being run. Shri Keshar Singh 
who appeared before me on 15th December 1961 has 
admitted in his petition that he is the proprietor of 
Messrs. Amritasar Industrial Works. So I order 
that the above award will be binding on Shri Keshar 
Singh, the proprietor of Messrs. Amritasar Industrial 
Works, Ranigunj.

By order No. 4434-L.R./IR/1L1L-538/58, dated 
Calcutta. the 16th October 1958, Government of 
West Bengal, Labour Department, referred an 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Amritasar 
Industrial Works and their workmen represented by 
thé Amritasar Industrial Workers’ Union to the 
Second Labour Court for adjudication regarding the 
issue mentioned in the order of reference. 


Issue 


1. Whether the discharge of Shri Sew alias Shew- 
nath Bhar is justified? Fo what relief is he entitled? 


After several adjournments the case was fixed for 
nearing on 2156 November 1961. On that day two 
witnesses on behalf of the Union were examined and 
cross-examined, and on the prayer of the Company 
the 0956 was adjourned to 15th December 1961 for 
further evidence and arguments. On that day none 
appeared for the Company and no evidence was 
adduced on its behalf. The President of the Union 
who appeared for the Union argued the case of the 
Union. There was none to argue the case on behalf 
of the Company. The hearing was concluded and 
the award was reserved. Later that day Shri P. K. 
Nandi, Advocate, with Shri Keshar Singh, Proprietor, 
appeared for the Company and filed a petition praying 
for re-opening of the case and fixing a date for 
hearing, on the ground stated in the petition. 
Accordingly the case was adjourned to 29th 
December 1961 for fixing a date of hearing. On that 
date none appeared for the Company to press the 
prayer for fixing a date of hearing. Accordingly | 
ordered that the hearing of the case would be deemed 
to have been concluded on 15th December 1961. 


The case of the Union, as stated in its written 
Statement, is as follows: 


Shri Sew alias Shewnath Bhar, the workman 
mentioned in the issue of the order of reference, 
was a permanent workman of Messrs. Amritasar 
Industrial Works (hereinafter referred to as the 
Company), Ranigunj. He was summarily discharged 
on 5th July 1957 without any charge-sheet or enquiry 
on a false charge of entering the bungalow of the 
Proprietor of the Company. The fact was that the 
Proprietor having not come for the whole day, the 
workers went to see him at his house for their 
wages. The proprietor instead of paying their wages 
abused them and drove them away. As_ the 
discharge of Shri Sew is unjustified, the Union prays 
for his reinstatement and payment to him compensa- 
tion for the period of forced unemployment. 


The case of the Company, as stated in its written 
Statement, is as follows: 


Shri Sew was discharged not on a charge of 
entering the bungalow of the proprietor on 5th July 
1957, as alleged in the written statement of the 
Union. He had been given several charge-sheets on 
different occasions. On 215٦ May 1957 he was given 
a charge-sheet for stealing a bag of coal from the 
factory, suspended and _ was later let off with a 
warning. He was given another charge-sheet on 
6th June 1957 for inducing all the coolies to suspend 
their work and not to.use salt in the preparation of 
acid cakes, so that the quality of the product might 
be worse. He was asked to give a reply to the 
Charge-sheet by 9th June 1957. On his failure to 
give any explanation to the charge-shect, he was 
dismissed on 13th June 1957. He was also asked to 
collect his dues from the office. He collected all his

AWARD 


The above dispute over the issue given in the 
schedule to the order of reference and reproduced 
below was first referred for adjudication to the First 
Labour Court by the Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, order No. 2050-1.R./IR/4L-34/ 
59, dated the 13th May 1959, and the same dispute 
was subsequently referred for adjudication to this 
Tribunal by the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
Department, order No. 4083-I.R./IR /4L-34/59, dated 
the 2nd August 1960, in supersession of the said 
previous order of reference after the abolition of the 
said Court. 


The issue referred for adjudication stands thus:— 


Issue 


Fixation of the principle and quantum of bonus 
payable in 1958. 


According to the order of reference, the dispute is 
between eight owners of Passenger Transport 
Services plying on routes Nos. 52 and 58, Howrah, 
as mentioned in annexure I to the order of reference 
and their workmen represented by Howrah Jila Bus 


Karmi Parishad, 150 Mahendra Bhattacharjee Road, 
Howrah. 


After service of notices of the present reference 
issued by this Tribunal, the parties appeared. The 
Union filed its written statement and thereafter the 
employers concerned, except Nos. 4 and 6 of 
annexure I to the order of reference, adopted the 
written statements already filed by them before the 
First Labour Court and there was no appearance on 
hehalf of the said employers Nos. 4 and 6. The case 
was first fixed for hearing on 3rd November 1961. 
On that date, none of the parties appeared and no 
step was taken on hehalf of any of them. The 
Tribunal suo moto adjourned the case to 23rd 
December 1961 in order to give the parties another 
chance to appear and have an adjudication on the 
issue. In the meantime, on 19th December 1961 
there was an application for adjournment for one of 


[Part I 


urged that Shri Pathak was afforded all reasonable 
Opportunities to defend himself, and 1709 rules of 
natural justice were actually violated. In fact, even 
before the charge-sheet was issued a preliminary 
enquiry was held by the said Senior Mill Labour 
Officer in presence of Shri Pathak and the charge- 
sheet was issued after the case was prima facie 
established against him.’ It is strongly urged that 
the decision of the Management was not influenced 
by any extraneous consideration or by any spirit of 
victimisation. The previous service record of Shri 
Pathak was also bad, and the Management rightly 
decided to dismiss him, as the offence committed 
by him was rather grave. 


Other facts will appear from the body of the 
award that follows: 
DECISIONS 


The only issue referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication is whether the dismissal of Shri 
Dudnath Pathak, a Jamadar, was justified. He has 
been dismissed on the ground of a misconduct under 
rule 14(c)(ix) of the standing orders, i.e., for neglect 
of work. The charge framed against him was for 
“neglect of duty because he was found to be absent 
during duty period from 2-30 p.m. to 45۔5‎ p.m. 
without permission of the Management.” It is urged 
on behalf of the workman that mere absence from 
duty without permission cannot amount to neglect 
of work within the meaning of the rule 14(c)(ix) of 
the standing orders, and so on the charge levelled, 
no offence of “neglect of work” can be concluded. 
In fact, this was also one of the grounds taken in 
the written explanation submitted be the workman 
(vide Ext. D). But I must observe that geometrical 
precision in the language of a charge framed by a 
Management against its employee cannot be always 
expected. In judging the same, we must look more 
to the substance than to the mere form or 


formal expressions. If the language of the 
charge 02 sufficiently clear and if there 
be no confusion or _ difficulty in under- 


standing the real significance of the charge, it cannot 
be said that the workman was prejudiced in his 
defence. In this case, in the heading of the charge 
framed it was clearly mentioned that the charge 
was for neglect of duty, as the workman remained 
absent from duty between certain duty hours with- 
out permission. Shri Pathak was a member of the 
Watch and Ward Staff. His duty hours were from 
2 p.m. to 6 p.m. The charge is that he remained 
at his duty post up to 2-30 p.m. and then he took 
french leave and slipped away without permission. 
Ile came back to his post again at 5-45 p.m. evidently 
to show as if he was there from the beginning to 
the end of his duty period. Thus apart from the 
dishonest motive, if any, if the charge be otherwise 
true, he certainly neglected his work or dutv. The 
learned representative for the workman thinks that 
the charge as framed might at best be placed under 
rule 14(c)(v) and not 14(c){ix) of the standing orders. 
But J am unable to accept this contention. 
Rule 14(cXv) contemplates total absence from duty 
without leave, tut not neglect of dutv by 
surreptitiously withdrawing from it after joining it 
formally. The charge is that Shri Pathak purported 
to take over the charge of his duty and also to make 
over the charge at the close of duty hour and yct 
he did not actually do the duty entrusted to him. 
So, I find nothing wrong in the charge itself, and the 
41817015881] cannot be held to be bad on this ground.

The Government of West Bengal by its Labour 
Department order No. 830-I.R./1IR/7L-33/60, dated 
215 February 1961, and subsequent corrigendum 
No. 39-1.R./IR /7L-29(A)/61 dated 4th January 1962, 
referred to this Tribunal 21) industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Titaghur Jute Factory Co., Ltd. 
No. 2 Mill, Titaghur, 24-Parganas (hereafter referred 
to as the Company), and their workmen represented 
by Titaghur Jute Factory (Nos. 1 & 2) Workers’ 
Union, P.O. Khardah, district 24-Parganas (hereafter 
referred to as the Union), for adjudication under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


The only issue referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication in this case is this: 
Whether the dismissal of Shri Dudnath Pathak its 
justified? To what relief, if any, is he 
entitled? 


AWARD 


Briefly stated, the case of the workman concerned 
—Shri Dudnath Pathak—in his written statement 15 
as follows: At the relevant time, Shri Pathak was 
working as Second Jamadar of the Company. On 
28th March 1960 a charge-sheet was issued against 
him on false and malicious allegations. He gave a 
reply to the charge on 30th March 1960. Thereafter 
the Management held a perfunctory enquiry without 
affording him proper opportunity to defend himself. 
The enquirv was neither fair nor in accordance with 
the rules of natural justice. The Enquiring Officer, 
however, fund him. guilty, and on his recom- 
mendations the Management dismissed Shri Pathak. 
Shri Pathak’s allegation is that the Enquiring Officer 
-—Shri K. K. Mukherjee-—had grudge against him 
from before. Moreover, the Management also 
became displeased with him, simply because he 
pressed his just claim before the Management for his 
appointment as Head Jamadar. Thus it is alleged 
that this charge-shect was motivated by other 
reasons, and not for any actual offence committed 
by him. Hence, this reference. 


The Company’s case, on the other hand, in its 
written statement is this: It is urged by the 
Company that a proper and impartial enquirv was 
held against Shri Pathak, and the Enquiring Officer 
had neither bias nor grudge against him. It is also 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH I, 1962 639 


ParT I] 


০০১১৯ 


The evidence of the Management is that the post 
of the Head Jamadar was abolished for economic 
reasons after the retirement of the permanent 
incumbent of that post, and so there was no 
occasion for appointment of Shri Pathak (the then 
second Jamadar) as the Head Jamadar. This was a 
matter exclusively within the discretionary juris- 
diction of the Management, and so I do not think 
that the disputed charge was motivated for any 
claim of Shri Pathak. Evidence is that Shri Pathak 
was never appointed as Head Jamadar even tempo- 
টা and he was not ever asked to do the duties 
of the erstwhile Head Jamadar. So, this allegation 
is too vague and airy to lead to any definite adverse 
conclusion. It is next urged that Shri Pathak in 
course of his round duties found Durwan Shri 
Purushuttam absent from his duty post, for the 
latter had gone out for taking opium liquor. It is 
alleged that Shri Pathak having threatened Shri 
Purushuttam to be reported against, the latter held 
gut a threat to the former. The Management held 
an informal preliminary enquiry in this respect also 
and found no material to proceed against Shri 
Purushuttam. I fail to see how the misconduct, if 
any, of Shri Purushuttam can be a reason for this 
charge-sheet against Shri Pathak. It is absurd to 
suggest that Shri Purushuttam was big and powerful 
enough to influence not only Shri Mukherjee but also 
the Manager in issuing a false charge-sheet against 
Shri Pathak. ] am afraid these are all wild and 
frivolous allegations only in an attempt to camouflage 
the offence committed by him. So, after carefully 
considering all the facts and circumstances on record, 
] am unable to accept the contention that the pro- 
ceedings before the domestic Tribunal were vitiated 
by anv bias of the Enquiring Officer or the mala 
fides of the Management. Shri Pathak also 
examined a few witnesses before the domestic 
Tribunal in support of his defence case. But the 
Enquiring Officer could not accept his contention 
or believe his defence witnesses. There were 
materials before the domestic Tribunal to support 
the conclusion drawn by the Enquiring Officer. It 
has not been accepted that Shri Pathak as Jamadar 
had any supervisory duties outside the mill premises 
and that he اہ‎ attended his normal duties on 
that day. Even Shri Baram Deo Durwan referred to 
bv Shri Pathak himself does not support the conten- 
tion of Shri Pathak. Shri Mukherjee in giving his 
finding after the enquiry has discussed his reasons and 
the evidences at length and the same cannot be said 
to be perverse or the conclusion drawn baseless. 
The law is, I am not to consider if a different 
conclusion might be drawn on the evidences recorded 
at the enquiry. My duty is to see if the conclusion 
drawn by the Enquiring Officer or the Management 
is supnorted by the materials. If the conclusion 15 
possible, it cannot be called perverse anv longer. 
Shri Pathak’s witnesses were no doubt disbelieved. 
But there were many witnesses, on the other side 
to give a different version. Even before me, the 
same history has been repeated, and 1 have no reason 
to conclude that the Enquiring Officer was perverse 
in his finding and that the charge was baseless. 
Even the revly of Shri Pathak to the charge-shect 
was drafted by a lawyer, and so at all relevant times 
Shri Pathak had presumably proper leagl advice too 
to guide him. Shri Pathak has no sufficient evidence 
to establish that all the Durwans except a few on 
his side entered into a conspiracy with the Manage- 


ment for bringing a baseless charge against him. 


کت 


After the charge-sheet was issued, Shri Pathak 
filed his written explanation. It may be mentioned 
in this connection that the charge was not framed 
in hot haste and all on a sudden. On receipt of a 
coinplaint against Shri Pathak, a preliminary enquiry 
was held in presence of Shri Pathak who was given 
full opportunity to explain the circumstances 
alleged against him. The Management issued a 
charge-shcet only after being satisfied as to a prima 
fucie case after the preliminary enquiry. ظ‎ final 
enquiry was held after Shri Pathak filed his written 
reply to the charge-sheet issued. This enquiry was 
held with due notice to Shri Pathak and he was 
called upon to be present at the enquiry with all his 
witnesses (vide Ext. E). The final enquiry was held 
by Shri Kumud Kanta Mukherjee, the Senior Mill 
Labour Officer, and the entire proceedings of the 
enquiry before the domestic Tribunal were recorded 
by Shri Mukherjee in his own handwriting. Shri 
Pathak and his witnesses were present at the enquiry 
and they were examined also at length. The 
Management also examined its own witnesses. The 
Secretary of the Works Committee, evidently a 
representative of the workmen, was admittedly 
present all through. The Junior Labour Officer 2150 
attended the proceedings. From the deposition of 
Shri Mukherjee read with the recorded proceedings 
] am satisfied that Shri Pathak was given a patient 
hearing and allowed all opportunities to defend him- 
self. I am unable to believe the worker's allegation 
that the statements recorded were not read over and 
explained to the witnesses within his hearing. The 
evidence is there to show the contrary, and I believe 
it. Shri Pathak admittedly affixed his signature to 
the statements. So, I find nothing wrong with the 
rroccedings before the domestic Tribunal, and the 
finding cannot be challenged on that ground also. 
Even if the recorded statements had not been read 
over, that alone would not vitiate the porceedings 
unless it is clear that there was absence of bona 
fides on the part of the Enquiring Officer. It Is 
urged on behalf of the workman that the enquiry 
was not impartial, as Shri Mukherjee had a grudge 
against him for he had refused to depose falselv 
in Shri Mukherjee’s favour in a criminal case brought 
against certain persons. Shri Mukherjee has been 
examined heforé me and he swears that he never 
requested Shri Pathak to depose falsely in his favour 
in any criminal case. The alleged criminal case was 
filed at best 9110 years back. and it ts difficult for 
me to believe that this 01810 or ١۲٦۹۷۱۲۷ was 
influenced by or had anvthing to do with that 
criminal case of a decade back or that the charge 
was motivated by any previous grudge. Shri Pathak 
was charge-sheeted more than once previously also, 
and he was punished also as a result. The complaint 
on the last occasion came from the Sccuritv Officer 
and not Shri Mukherjee, and a preliminary cnquiry 
was held on the instruction of the Manager. After 
the result of the preliminary enquiry was reported 
to the Manager, he directed issuc of the charge-shcet. 
1 am unable to believe that Shri Mukherjee had any 
bias against Shri Pathak. Shri Pathak. of course, 
cites other causes also for this alleged false charge- 
sheet. But. none of his contentions makes anv 
impression on me. His contentin is that ۴ 
repeatedly pressed his claim for being appointed 
Head Jamadar and assigned the quarter of that Head 


Jamadar after the old Head Jamadar had retired, 
and hence the Management got annoyed with him. 
But this allegation makes no impression on me. 


{Part I 


ہے' 

also in support of their respective contentions. But 
1 am not required to come to এ) independent 
decision on the merit of the issue, as the decision 
of the Management or the validity of the domestic 
enquiry has not been dislodged in accordance with 
the principles laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court in the case of Indian Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. 
and their workmen (A.LR. 1958 S.C. 130). How- 
ever, this much can be said in brief that no suflicient 
material has been placed before me also for coming 
to a conclusion that it is a fit case for the Tribunal 
to interfere. There is sufficient evidence before me 
also to support the Management conclusion and 
decision. So, without further discussion, ] find that 
this Tribunal has no reason to interfere. The work- 
man is, therefore, not entitled to any relief in this 

case. 


This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me.

্ 
The witnesses (except Ram Sankar) who supported 
Shri Pathak bear surname “Pathak”, and the 
یت ایت‎ case is that these witnesses are related 
to Shri Dudnath Pathak, and hence their evidence 
was not acceptable. Shri Ram Sankar’s statement 
before me 15 alsc at variance with what he had 
stated before the domestic Tribunal. So, it cannot 
be said that the Enquiriny Officer was manifestly 
wrong in disbelieving these defence witnesses. Nor 
do J think that this Tribunal has any sufficient reason 
to interfere on the ground of severity of punish- 
ment. The service record of Shri Dudnath Pathak 
and previous depatrmental charge-sheets agianst 
him are on record. So, considered in the light of 
his previous service record and other circumstances, 
it cannot be said that Shri Pathak did not really 
merit dismissal, and that the punishment’ was 
unusually severe and harsh to raise a presumption 
of victimisation in his favour. 


Lastly, it is argued that the departmental enquiry 
did not come to any finding that Shri Pathak had 
no duty outside the mill premises, and this point 
was not considered even though Shri Pathak pleaded 
that he had gone out in discharge of his duties 
only. But I may point out that Shri Pathak pleaded 
nothing like this in his reply. Rather, he pleaded 
therein that he had met different Durwans inside 
the mill premises several times during the relevant 
period and that he was on duty all along accord- 
ingly. He raised such a_ plea at the time of 
preliminary enquiry no doubt, and referred to 
Baramdeo Durwan_  in_ that connection. But 
Baramdeo failed to support him’ even & the 
preliminary او‎ No such plea was however 
taken in reply to the charge-shect. At the time of 
final enquiry, he relies on his statement in reply 
and not on the statement at the preliminary enquiry. 
He gives rather an evasive statement at the final 
enquiry that he is bound to go outside the mill 
premises to see the Company’s mill premises. He 
does not say that he had gone out actually during 
the relevant period in discharge of his duties only. 
His statement is rather argumentative, and 6ا‎ 
allegation is that if his duties were not both inside 
and outside the mill premises, how he could he 
charge-sheeted for loss of Company's 00101১০1015 
outside the mill compound? Evidently, Shri Pathak 
referred to the charge-sheet, dated 16th March 1960 
(vide Ext. (ا‎ But in that case, the charge was for 
negicct of duty under quite a_ different circum- 
stance. He was presumably off duty at the time 
and took no action to prevent loss or damage to 
Company’s properties at the instance of some mis- 
creants, even though he was informed about it 
by the round Durwan. So, that does not prove 
that he had normal duties outside the mill premises. 
That was an extraordinary occasion and that duty 
also was extraordinary on account of his very whole- 
time employment by the Company and not on the 
ground of normally assigned regular duties. So, I 
do not think that the action of the Management can 
be challenged on that ground. There 15 positive 
evidence before me to show that as a Jamadar Shri 
Pathak had no normal duty outside the mill premises. 
He could go out only on express direction or with 
previous permission of the authority. There are 
Line Durwans and Zamin Durwans for outside 
duties. Thus I am unable to accept the argument 
and hold that the Enquiring Officer was wron7 in 
finding Shri Pathak guilty of neglect of work or duty. 

Both the parties have adduced evidence before me

periods. The contention of the workmen concerned 
is that they were punished without any proper

in this connection, | may at once refer to the charge-

on 19th April 1960 at 10 am. From Exts. B to B-2

and Harka Bahadur submitted their explanations in

It is also peculiar that these three 0 submitted

is the case in respect of the other four persons. 
They also submitted their explanations in identical 
language and the Management also dealt with them 
in a similar manner. Be that as it may, the real 
point at issue is whether there was at all any enquiry 
or whether there was any proper enquiry in respect 
of all or any one of the workmen concerned. The 
Management files Exts. L-series read with Ext. O to

charge-sheeted persons on two different dates. But 
the Management fails to produce any other paper in

the Management seeks to convince me that proper

was fair and impartial also. In this connection, J

no enquiry about the charge on 20th April 1960.

already present there from before. He alleges that 
ও few minutes after his arrival at the place of enquiry,

Office and informed the workmen including Ran

As against this, the Company’s case in its written 
Statement, in short, is this: At the relevant time, 
there were 1,362 workers including clerical and 
medical staff on the roll of the Company. There is 
another Union functioning in this garden, and this 
is known as “Duars Cha Bagan Mazdoor Sangha” 
affiliated to I.N.T.U.C. The Company believes that 
this Union really represents the majority of the 
workers of this garden. The Company denies any 
knowledge of the workers under reference being 
active members of their Union. It is also denied 
that payment of monthly wages to the workers of 
this garden is made within 8th of every month or that 
the Paharia workers are always given payment on 
the first day of payment and before the Adibasi 
workers. The workers are usually paid within 10th 
day of each month, and there were many occasions 
on which the Adibasi workers were actually paid 
before the Nepali workers. At the relevant time, 
the practice obtaining in the garden was that when 
the Wage Register was completed by the garden 
Accounts Department and payment was ready, the 
Line Chowkidar used to be instructed to inform the 
Section workers in the morning that payment would 
be made on that day. In accordance with 0115 
garden practice, the garden Chowkidar informed the 
Adibasi workers that their wages would be paid on 
the 8th April 1960. The Pahari workers were well 
aware that they would not be paid their wages on 
the 8th April 1960 and yet they deliberately came 
in a body to the office on that day at about 
5-30 p.m. to intimidate the Management, so that 
their wages might be paid on that day, and the 
charge-sheeted workers took leading part 11) 
instigating the riotous conduct. Mr. McLeod, the 
then Manager, explained to the Pahari workers that 
it would not be possible to pay them on that very 
date because the relevant Pay Book, etc., were not 
ready by that time and assured them that they 
would be paid on the following day. In spite of 
this, the charge-sheeted workers’ incited and 
instigated other employees to surround the Manager 
and the Assistant Managers and abused them in filthy 
language and actually kept them confined for about 
54 hours. As the crowd became restless and their 
attitude threatening, the Management had 00 
summon the Police. The Managerial staff were 
allowed to leave office at about 10-30 p.m. after the 
intervention of the Police Officer. Consequently, the 
Management was compelled to charge-sheet the 
workers under reference together with four others 
and after proper enquiry the Management 0০০৮ 
action against them 25 mentioned in the issue 
referred to above. There was 180 violation of the 
principle of natural justice and the Management was 
not actuated by any mala fides or spirit of 
victimisation.

DECISIONS 


From the issue framed in this case, it will appear 
that out of seven دسا‎ charge-sheeted, three ٤۴ 
dismissed and the rest suspended for different 


{Part 1 


648 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 1, 1962 


৯ ১০০৭০ 


Normally, this is not likely or possible. So, it is 
clear that the Management wanted them to have a 


Statement prepared in advance with an ulterior 
motive. The matter does not stand there only. 
From the so-called recorded proceedings (Ext. L- 


Series) it appears, as if the written statements of 
Mr. Mcleod, Mr. Anand, Mr. Baird 014 seven 
members of the staff referred to above (Ext. O) were 
actually read out, translated and confirmed as correct 
at the domestic enquiry in the very presence of the 
charge-sheeted persons. But peculiarly enough, none 
of the witnesses examined before this Tribunal has 
the courage to say that Mr. Mcleod also prepared a 
statement in advance and that it was also read out 
at the enquiry. Thus if these proceedings be taken 
as correct, Mr. Mcleod not only figured as a 
complainant, but also as a witness before himself and 
as a judge at the enquiry and ultimately he decided to 
punish all the seven charge-shected persons. But 
the funniest part of the story is that the written down 
Statement of neither Mr. Mcleod nor of Mr. Baird 
are forthcoming. The statement of Mr. Anand, also 
finds no place in the enquiry proceedings produced 
before me. The Management simply pleads _ its 
ignorance about the whereabouts of the previously 
written statements of all the high officials except 
that of the poor clerks employed by the Company. 
Proceedings have been drawn up to show as if all 
the persons who made statements in writing were 
examined before the domestic tribunal afresh to get 
their statements confirmed. But unfortunately, all 
the witnesses swear that they were simply present 
at the enquiry and were not asked anything by 
anybody. I may observe that non-production of the 
Statements of Mr. Mcleod, Mr. Baird and Mr. Anand 
may not be without significance. These statements 
may be purposely withheld or suppressed, and for 
reasons not disclosed by the Management before this 
Tribunal. In any case, I have great suspicion about the 
bona fides of non-production of these statements. ۵ػ٥‎ 
Company’s case is that these statements in writing 
were not only read over and explained to the charge- 
sheeted persons, but these workmen were also given 
opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses cxamined 
on behalf of the Company, and yet the opportunity 
Offererd to them was not availed of by any one ot 
them. In this connection, I may refer to the cross- 
examination of O.P.W. 3, Mr. D. Baird. He says 
that he cannot say what was the date of enquiry. 
He, however, adds that the enquiry was held at 
about 9/10 a.m. But he admits that he went to the 
place of enquiry at about 10-30 a.m. and remained 
there for about five minutes only. From_ the 
deposition of O.P.W. 4, Mr. O. P. Anand, it will be 
clear that the charge-shceted persons were called 
before the Manager one by one and Mr. Mcleod 
read out the statements already prepared (if he read 
out at all) to the individual charge-shected persons 
and asked them to cross-examine the witnesses 
examined by the Company. So, if it be a fact that 
enquiry was held in respect of different charge- 
sheeted persons one after another, Mr. Baird cannot 
possibly remain present at the enquiry to be crass- 
examined by all the charge-sheeted workmen, 
because he was admittedly there for not more than 
five minutes. I also fail to understand whether there 
was at all any scope for cross-examining Mr. Baird 
when he had been to the place of enquiry at 
10-30 a.m., the enquiry having been held at 9/10 a.m. 
Mr. Anand tries to say that nobody made any oral 
statement before the سکس‎ Officer on the date

Mr. Mcleod, the then Manager of the Tea Garden, 
purported to hold the enquiry. But Mr. Mcleod is

this Tribunal and they try to allege that in fact

sheeted persons referred to above. So, it is 
incumbent on me to scrutinise the materials on 
record and see how far the Management’s allegation 
of holding proper enquiries holds good. From 
Ext. A-series it will at once be clear that the charge- 
sheets were actually issued by the Manager himself 
and the recital of the charges will make it further 
clear that the Manager himself was the de facto 
complainant, the allegation being that the workers 
adopted threatening attitude, insulted and abused 
the Manager personally and also decided not to 
allow the Manager to leave the factory compound. 
But in spite of this position, the Manager himself 
figured as the Enquiring Officer at the domestic 
enquiry. Thus, he was not only the complainant 
but the judge also of the enquiry. He was not only 
personally aggrieved, but vitally interested also in 
the consequences of the enquiry. Most of the 
witnesses on the Company’s side pleaded ignorance 
as to whether the Manager himself prepared any 
written statement in advance and whether it was read 
over at the time of the so-called enquiry. But even 
a plain reading of Exts. L-series---the so-called 
enquiry proceedings—will show that the Manager's 
personal opinion contributed a good deal towards 
his decision in the matter. He _ referred to his 
so-called personal knowledge whenever convenient 
and came to a finding against the charge-sheeted 
workmen. Thus it goes without saying that 
Mr. Mcleod unfortunately placed himself as a judge 
in his own case. It is the accepted principle of 
natural law that one should not be a judge in his 
own case or cause. Though this rule can some- 
times be relaxed in departmental enquiries held on 
behalf of the Management, the rule should not 
actually be relaxed under all circumstances. In a 
case where the offence, if any, ۷88 committed 
personally against a particular person, he should not, 
in all fairness, hold the enquiry, because for obvious 
reasons he is likely to be strongly biased against the 
charge-sheeted persons and so his decision cannot 
always be impartial. So, in this particular case, 
I cannot approve of the action of Mr. Mcleod in 
holding the enquiry, if any, against the charge- 
sheeted persons. Nevertheless, I may point out that 
no witness on behalf of the Management was actually 
examined at the time of enquiry and in presence of 
the charge-sheeted persons. It is admitted by the 
Management that certain employees of the garden 
were aSked to prepare written statements in respect 
of the incident long before the date of enquiry, and 
some time after the alleged occurrence. Exhibit O

seven different employees of the garden. This 
exhibit purports to show as if all these seven 
signatories witnessed the entire incident as recorded 
and their version was identical in all respects.

doubt if there was any enquiry; and if there was any 
enquiry at all, it can hardly be said to be a proper 
one. So, the action of the Management in respect 
of these charge-sheeted persons cannot be justified 
simply with reference to the so-called domestic 
enquiry made by the Management. 


Nevertheless, the punishment inflicted by the 
Management cannot be straightway set aside, 
simply because there was no enquiry or no proper 
enquiry. In this connection, | may refer to a 
decision of the Supreme Court in the case of 
Punjab National Bank Ltd. vs. All-India Punjab 
National Bank Employees’ Federation and another 
reported in A.I.R. 1960 (S.C.) 160 where there 
Lordships observed as follows: 


“If no enquiry has, in fact, been held by the 
employer, the issue about the merits of the 
impugned order of dismissal is at large before 
the Tribunal, and on the evidence adduced before 
it the Tribunal has to decide for itself whether 
the misconduct alleged is proved, and if ‘yes’, 
what would be the proper order to make. In 
such a case, the point about the exercise of 
managerial functions does not arise at all.” 


Thus it is clear that where there was no domestic 
enquiry in the true sense of the term, it is incumbent 
on the Tribunal itself to look into the merits of the 
case on the evidences adduced before it by the 
parties. Of course, it is needless to add that where 
the Tribunal has to rely on evidences before it, both 
parties must have sufficient opportunity to adduce 
proper evidence on the merits of the case. In the 
present case, both the parties have no doubt adduced 
evidence in support of their respective contentions 
and also on the merits of the case. So, I shall

only when the Management gave them an assurance 
that payment of their wages would be made on the 
following morning. It is also sufficiently established 
that several clerks had to work overtime till 11 p.m. 
at night to make the books and other relevant papers 
ready for promised payment on the following 
morning. It is also in evidence that on account of 
obstruction and interference of a section of Nepali 


workers, Mr. Anand had to suspend payment to 
Adibasi_ workers also for some time. Of course, 
Mr. Anand could complete payment to Adibasi 


workers later, after the workers had made _ the 
Manager a target of their attack. So, in the face of 
all these facts and circumstances, I am unable to 
accept the contention of the workers that they had 
no mala fides or intention to break discipline. In 
paragraph 9(h) of the written statement filed by the 
workers, the workmen themselves admit that they 
had some reasons for getting agitated. But I have 
already shown that in fact the workers had no reason 
whatsoever to go to the office to make demand for 
immediate payment or to get agitated also in that 
connection. The Management in its discretion and 
‘without violating any previous undertaking wanted 
to make payment to Nepali workers in the afternoon 
of 9th April 1960. But the workers were not to 
listen to the Management or vacate the office 
compound. They not only squatted inside and out- 
side ‘the office compound, but kept the Manager and 
the members of the staff confined also till 10-30 p.m. 
I think, this act by itself constitutes a gross 
indiscipline. Because of this conduct of the work- 
men, Police had to be sent for and actually some 
Police Officers came to the garden that evening. 
The Police, of course, took no action against the 


workers, and the treason thereof is not very far to

AWARD 


The workmen represented by Shri Gopal Tin 
Factory Workers’ Union (hereinafter referred to as 
the Union) filed the written statement on 30th May 
1961, through Shri Sudhir Kumar Ghosh, the 
President of the Union. The dispute is concerning 
the dismissal of two workmen. The caSe as made 
out by the Union in the written statement is to the 
effect that Shri Jitendra Nath Mukherjee and Shri 
Santi Banerjee were recruited as Shoulderman and 
Machineman (Ball Press) respectively by the Company 
in the latter part of the year 1959 and that they 
along with other workmen organised the Trade 
Union in order to ameleorate the conditions of 
service of the workmen. A charter of demands was 
submitted by the:Union. The management paid 
bonus in part, two weeks before the Pujas of 1960 
to all workmen except these two workmen. Then 
on 19th September 1960 the management all on a 
sudden terminated the service of Shri Santi Banerjee 
without assigning any reason whatsoever. Again 
on 3rd October 1960 the services of Shri Jitendra 
Nath Mukherjee were terminated. For such 
unjustified action of the employer the Union took 
up the cause of the workmen, thus penalised before 
the Labour Directorate. All attempts for amicable 
settlement however failed, and as such the dispute 
was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. The 
Union alleges that the action of the management in 
dismissing these two workmen had been wholly mala 
fide, opposed to the principles of natural justice and 
arosc out of unfair labour practice. 


Messrs. Shri Gopal Tin Factory (P.) Ltd. (hercin- 
after referred to as the Company) filed the written 
statement on 4th July 1961. It is contended by the 
Company that these two workmen had never 10001) 
dismissed as alleged and that their termination of 
service took place under different circumstances so 
much so that Shri Mukherjee was a casual and 
temporary worker recruited,in February 1960 and 
that he was served with a simple notice of termina- 
tion of service. As he was recruited as a temporary 
worker to carry out some surplus work and there 
was no need in retaining him in service the manage 
ment discharged him. 


As for the other workman, Shri Banerjee, it is 
stated that he was recruited as a casual worker and 
that he worked as a helper till 17th September 1960, 
and that he himself abondoned the service as he did 
not turn up for work since 19th September i960 
without giving any information whatsoever to the 
Company which resulted in an automatic termination 
of his services. It is contended by the Company 
that both these workmen were daily-rated workers 
who were paid on the basis of “no work, no pay.” 
Besides, it is contended that the Company had never

Undoubtedly, the management of a concern has 
the power to direct its own internal administration 
according to certain rules and conditions of service 
applicable to workman. But at the same timc the 
power is not unlimited: afd when a dispute arises on 
the question as to whether the termination of service 
is justified or not, the Industrial Tribunal has got 
to examine how the termination took place and 1 
it be found that the action of the management had 
been mala fide or that it was prompted by a spirit

the worker is entitled to get appropriate relief. In 
the instant case, the employer terminated the service

evidence. The fact 07190 076 Wage Register had been

surplus work. Evidently, unless there be some

contained in the letter of 


termination 01 service

within a limited time. ‘here is no evidence adduced

work was in hand at the time Shri Mukherjec 
was recruited and whether the recruitment was at all 
connected with the execution of such temporary 
additional work likely to 1951 for a limited period. 
‘the question whether Shri Mukherjee was a

Shri Shanti Banerjee 

There is no controversy on the point that Shri 
Banerjee was recruited aS a helper in the Ball Press 
Department of this establishment. 10 appears from 
the Attendance Reyister that he was recruited on 
1801) April 1960. 1170 said Register also shows that

and also tor a few days in early part of September 
1959, The evidence of Shri Banerjee that he was 
ugain taken in service in December 1959 یز‎ 
apparently not correct. Shri Banerjee admitted that 
he worked in September 1959 and then he was 
discharged. 1 take it that he worked for about two 
months in 1959 and then was discharged and that he 
was recruited afresh on 18th April 1960. He admits 
his signature in the Wage Register, Ext. C, wherein 
he is described as a temporary worker (vide Wage 
Register showing payment for the week ending 30th 
April 1960). The Wage Register turther indicates 
that he received payment up to the weck ending on 
17th September 1960. But all through in the Wage 
Register his name was shown as a temporary worker. 
The evidence of Shri Banerjee is to the effect that 
he demanded that he should be made permanent 
and that he should be paid bonus. At the same time 
he stated in the cross-examination that temporary 
workmen are not paid bonus. Naturally, therefore, 
his demand for bonus was unjustified. The question 
however arises for consideration as to how the 
termination of service 01 this workman took place. 
According to the version of the employer, Shri 
Banerjee attended ofhce up to the 17th September 
1960 which was a Saturday and he failed to turn up on 
the 19th September onward. In the Attendance 
Register I find that he was marked absent on the 
19th, 20th and 2150 September. The employer's 
version is that when a temporary unskilled worker 
fails to turn up, they do not wait for an indefinite 
period for a workman to report to duty and make 
their own arrangement to carry on their work. From 
the facts and circumstances of the case ] am inclined 
to hold that Shri Banerjee when refused bonus, 
considered it not worthwhile to continue his servicc 
under this employer, at a small wage of Rs. 1-9 per 
day and that he himself abandoned the © services. 
Obviously, therefore, the termination of service of 
this workman did not proceed from any initiative 
taken by the employer. In the circumstances the 
termination of service of Shri Banerjee was not, in 
fact, in the nature of dismissal or even discharge of 
the workman, proceeding from the employer. In 
this view 1 do not find any reason to interfere with 
the termination of service of Shri Santi Banerjee.

an understanding that he would be retained only for
