after six months of service he was made permanent. 
O.P.W. | Shri Saha stated im the examination in 
chief that permanent workers are paid bonus. by 
perinanent workers he means to say that only those 
workers who work [or 240 days in a year are to be 
treated as permanent. This oral statement of Shri 
Saha is not proved by any evidence. Rather the 
facts indicate that workers are treated aS permanent 
after six months of service and that all permanent 
workers are admittedly paid bonus. In the fact of 
these circumstances it cannot be explained why 
bonus had not been paid to Shri Mukherjee. Of 
course, I am not concerned in this case to find out 
and determine any question relating to a claim ol 
bonus in favour of Shri Mukherjee. But at the 
same time when it is admitted that bonus had been 
paid to permanent workers on the eve of Pujas, 
the fact that Shri Mukherjee had demanded bonus 
43 permanent worker and that he stood dismissed all 
on a sudden after that can reasonably be taken as 
circumstantial evidence to indicate what was the 
real reason behind the dismissal. 


It is true that the onus is upon the Union to 
establish the allegation as to victimisation. In this 
case | find from Ext. G that a charter of demands 
had been submitted by this Union on 13th April 
1960 and that an amicable tripartite settlement had 
been made on 30th March 196]. The learned 
lawyer for the Company urged that the relation 
between the employer and the workmen had been 
cordial and the Company never thought of being 
harsh against workers who were prominently 
connected with the Union. The tripartite  settle- 
ment leads support to the Company's version. Upon 
consideration of the facts and circumstances | hold 
that there is no case of victimisation established in 
the instant case. But it is proved beyond doubt 
that the employer dismissed this workman just 
because of the fact that a legitimate demand for 
participation of bonus had been put forward, and 
that in dispensing with his services the employer 
proceeded mala fide when a case to support the 
action was made out to the extent that the work- 
11811] concerned was purely a temporary hand 
recruited for additional work undertaken 0/ the 
concern. I therefore find that the Union has been 
able to establish a case of unfair labour practice on 
the part of employer. Besides, | hold that the 
management proceeded mala fide in terminating the 
services of Shri Mukherjee. So the normal relief us 
lo reinstatement must follow. 1 therefore direct that 
Shri Mukherjee be reinstaged. by the Company in the 
sume post he was occupying at the time of his 
dismissal and that he be paid the same wages as he 
was then getting. Considering the facts and 
circamstances of the case, I think it would be unwise 
to direct the employcr to pay Shri Mukherjec the 
wages for the period of his unemployment from the 
date of dismissal till his reinstatement. His service 
during the period would be counted as leave without 
pay.

CALCUTTA POLICE NOTIFICATION 


Dated Calcutta, the 15th February 1962. 


Whereas I am satisfied that the western portions 
of Bentinck Street from the frontage of Income-tax 
Office up to the crossing of Waterloo Street, from the 
entrance of Orient Cinema up to the crossing of 
Mangoe Lane and the eastern portions of Bentinck 
Street from Ganesh Chandra Avenue up to the cross- 
ing of Princep Street, from Sooterkin Street up to the 
crossing of Meredith Street should be made “No 
Parking Zones” in the interest of public convenience 
and safety, I. the undersigned. by virtue of powers 
vested in me under sections 74 and 75 of the Indian 
Motor Vehicles Act (Act IV of 1939) read with Gov- 
ernment of West Bengal. Home (Transport) Depart- 
ment Order No. 2383/WT, dated the 9th April 
1957, order that the portions of the road aforesaid 
be declared as “No Parking Zones”. 


U. MUKHARJI, 
Commissioner of Police, Calcutta.

of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (11 of 1948), the Governor proposes to 
make in the West Bengal Minimum Wages Rules, 1951, as subsequently 
amended, (hereinafter referred to as the said rules), is hereby published as 
required by sub-section (1) of the said section for the information of persons 
likely to he affected thereby. 


The draft will be taken into consideration on the Ist June 1962 and 
uny objection or suggestion with respect thereto which may be received by 
the undersigned before that date will be considered.

Extracts from the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, and the Rules made 
thereunder. 


Whom. the Act affects 


The Act applies to persons engaged on scheduled employments on speci- 
fied class of work in respect of which minimum wages ae been fixed. 
No employee can give up by contract or agreement his rights in so far as 
it purports to reduce the minimum rates of wages fixed under the Act. 


Definition of wages 


‘*Wages’’ means the remuneration payable to an employed person on 
the fulfilment of his contract of employnfent. It include house-rent allow- 
unce, but exclude— 


(i) the value of any house-accommodation, supply of light, water, 
medical attendance; 


(11) any other amenity or any service excluded by general or special 
order of the appropriate Government; 


(111) any contribution paid by the employer to any Pension Fund or 
Provident Fund or under any Scheme of social insurance; 


(iv) any travelling allowance or the value of any travelling concession ; 


(v) any sum paid to the person employed to defray special expenses 
entitled on him by the nature of his employment; 


(vi) any gratuity payable on discharge. 


The minimum rate of wages may consist of— 


(i) a basic rate of wages and specitl allowance called the cost of 
living allowance, 


(11) a basic rate of wages with or without a cost of living allowance 
and the cash value of any concessions, like supply of essential 
commodities at concession rates, 


(111) an all-inclusive rate comprising of basic wages, cost of living 
ullowance and cash value of concession, if ۰ 


The minimum wages payable to employees of scheduled employment noti- 
tied under section 5 read with section + or as revised from time to time 
under the aforesaid sections may be— 

(a) a minimum time rate 

(b) a» minimum piece rate 

(c) a guaranteed time rate 

an over-time rate;‏ (ا) 
diftering with (a) different scheduled omploymenta, (b) different classes ot‏ 


work, (c) different localities, (d) different wage-periods and (e) different age 
yroups. 


Computation and conditions of payment 


The employer shall pay to every employee engaged in scheduled employ- 
ment under him wages at a rate not less than the minimum rate of wages 


fixed for that 01888 of employee.

employed. 


The wages of a person discharged shull be paid not later than the second 
working day after his discharge.

that period. 


Where an employee does two or more classes of work to each of which 
a different minimum rate of wages is applicable, the employer shall pay to 
such employee in respect of the time respectively occupied in each such 
eluss of work wages at not less than the minimum rate in force in respect 
of each such 112১৭. 


Where an employee is employed on piece work for which minimum time 
rate and not a mininnum piece rate has been fixed, the employer shall pay 
to such employee wages at not less than the minimum time rute.

Maimtenance of Registers and Records 


_ Every emplover shall maintain a reyister of wages specifving the follow-

Inspections 


An Inspector can enter into any premises and can exercise powers of 
inspection (including examination of documents and taking of evidence) as 
he may deem necessary for carrying out the purposes of the Act, 


Clams and Complaints 


A complaint under section 22(a) relating to payment of leas than the 
Ininimum rates of wages or less than the smount due to an emploved person 
under the provisions of the Act can be made to the Court only after an 
application in respect of the facts constituting the offence has heen presented 
under section 20 and has been granted wholly or in part, and the appropriate 
Government or an Officer authorised by it in this behalf has sanctioned the 
making of the complaint.

A complaint under section 22(b) or 22-A regarding contravention of the 
provisions relating to hours of work and weekly day of rest or other niiscel- 
laneous offences, etc, can be made to the Court by of with the sanction of 
an Inspector. The time limit for making such complaints is one month 
from the date of grant of sanction by the Inspector, in the case of offences 
falling under section 22(b) and six months from the date on which the 
offence is alleged to have heen committed, in the cuse ot offences falling 
under section 22-۸۰. 


Action by the Authority 


The Authority may direct the payment of the amount by which the 
minimum wages payuble exceed the amount actually paid together with the 
payment of compensation not exceeding ten times the amount of such 
excess. The Authority may direct payment of compensation in cases where 
the excess is paid before the disposal of the application. 


If a malicious or vaxacious complaint is made, the Authority may 
1mpose a penalty not exceeding Rs. 50 on the applicant and order that 
it be paid to the employer. 


Every direction of the Authority shall be final. 


Penaltars for Offences under the Act 


Any employer who contravenes any provision of the Act or of any rule 
or order made thereunder shall, if no other penalty is provided for such 
contravention by the Act, be punishable with fine which may extend to 
five hundred rupees. If the person committing any offence under the Act 
is a Company, every person wha at the time the offence was committed, was 
in charge of, and was responsible to, the Company for the conduct of the 
business of the Company us well as the Company shull be deemed to be 
guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished 
accordingly : 


Provided that nothing contained in the Act shall render uny such person 
liable to any punishment provided in the Act if he proves that the offence 
was سن‎ lg without his knowledge or that he exercised 011 due diligence 
to prevent the commission of such offence. 


Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) of section 22C 
where an offence under the Act has been committed hy a company and it 13 
proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance 
of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, 
secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretury 
or other officer of the company shall also be deemed to be guilty of that 
offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. 


Explanation 


(a) ‘company’? means any body corporate and includes a firm or other 
association of individuals, and 


(hb) ‘‘director’’ in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm.

Note I1.—An assistant. who is holding substan- 
tively a post in the lower division, will, 
when promoted to officiate in the upper 
division draw an initial pay of not less 
than Rs. 170 (i.e., the 3rd stage in the

Stage in the scale). 


Note I1—In the case of a person who is 
already holding the post of .an upper 
division assistant on the date from which 
this amendment comes _ into force, his 
initial pay in the scale as now revised 
(viz., Rs. 150—10—370—15—400) shall be 
fixed at the stage next above the pay he 
was drawing immediately before that 
date, subject to the condition that his 
initial pay shall be fixed at not less than 
Rs. 190 if he is holding the post in a sub- 
stantive capacity; otherwise, it shall be 
fixed at not less than Rs. 170.

Assistant’ in Note II will also include 
Chamber Clerk, Accounts Clerk, 


Reference Clerk and Drawing Clerk 
mentioned above.”

Sessions of the year 1962 of the High Court at

will be held at the Court House on Monday, the

Government Promissory Notes originally standing 
in the name of State Bank of India, by whom they 
were never endorsed to any other person having 
being lost, notice is hereby given that payment of 
the said notes and the interest thereupon have been 
stopped at the Public Debt Office, Reserve Bank of 
India, Calcutta, and that application is about to be 
made for the issue of duplicates in favour of the 
registered proprietors. The public are cautioned

OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT MAGISTRATE. 
COOCH BEHAR 


ORDER 
Dated, Cooch Behar, the 23rd February 1962 


Whereas I am of opinion that for maintaining 
supplies essential to the life of the community, it is 
necessary to prevent unlawful trade and smuggling to 
any Hat or market or place of sale situated within 
five miles in the district of Cooch Behar from Indo- 
Pakistan border; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred 
by section 20 of the West Bengal Security Act, 1950 
(Act XIX of 1950), as delegated to me _ under 
section 38 of the said Act by the State Government 
in their notification No. 2170-P/30-9/50, dated the 
110 April 1950, I hereby order that all movement of 
any commodity, article or thing excepting such as 
exempted or may be exempted by me in writing in 
the manner specified in the said order, in Hats or 
markets or any other place of sale lying within a belt 
of five miles in the district of Cooch Behar from the 
Indo-Pakistan border be prohibited after dusk. 


The above order shall remain in force for a period 
of three months from the Ist March 1962. Any 
person contravening this order shall be punishable 
according to the provisions of law. 


Given under my hand and seal of the Court, this 
twenty-third day of February 1962. 


J. K. LAHIRI, 
District Magistrate.

ary 1962. Both parties’ representatives appeared, but

AWARD 


After service of notice on the parties, both the 
parties entered appearance before this Tribunal and 
filed their respective written statements in respect of 
the matter in dispute. After Completion, of 
tadbir by the parties, 12th February 1962 was fixed 
for hearing of the case. On that day, however, both 
the parties filed a joint petition of compromise 
settling their dispute amicably out of Court. I have 
gone through the petition of compromise and find 
that the terms are lawful and fair and reasonable. 
So, the petition of compromise is .recorded, and the 
award is passed in terms of compromise. ‘The 
petition of compromise will form part of the award 
and be marked as Annexure “A” to the award. 
Thanks are due to the parties for settling their 
dispute amicably. 


This is my award.

These workmen were dismissed on the ground that 
they were found guilty of 11150017400 in the sl.ape 
of their having suddenly gone on a strike on the

having incited other workmen to stop their work 
with the result that there was a complete stoppage 
of work for sometime and there was little wofk 
throughout the shift. Charge-sheets were submitted 
against these four workmen and they also submitted 
their explanations. Then according to the Company, 
there was an enquiry and as a result of the enquiry 
they were found to be guilty of the charge. Accord- 
ing to the applicants they did not incite other work- 
men, but there was a stoppage of work as a result 
of Bakridani, another workman being aNowed to 
work although that was a day when she was enjoy- 
ing her annual leave. It is further the case of the 
workmen that there was really no enquiry at all. 


On behalf of the workmen the four workmen were 
examined, namely, Kiron, two Sundaris, and Sricharan 
and on behalf of the management Shri R. K. Goel, 
Labour Officer who held the enquiry, Ramdas Prulal 
who was at the time employed as the Officer-in-Charge 
of the High Speed Winding in the “A’ shitt, Bakri- 
dani, a workman over whom there was this trouble 
and Ramprotap Singh, the Time-Keeper in-charge of 
the “A” shift at the time. 


The evidence on both sides indicates that troubles 
started on the 19th October 1958 shortly after the 
“A” shift began at about 5-30 a.m. According to 
the workmen Bakridani who was enjoying her 
annual leave was allowed to work and that is what 
admittedly led to the incident. Then according to 
the Company, a number of workmen came into the 
main alley shouting and signalling with their hands 
to others to stop work. Sricharan is alleged to have 
been amongst the workmen who took the lead in 
the matter and who came into the main alley shout- 
ing at their co-workers to stop their machines and 
Signalling with their hands to do so. Kiron, Sundari, 
ticket number 96 and Sundari, ticket number 64, 
along with others are also alleged to have come to 
the main alley and then to have proceeded to other 
machines which were still running and 00 have 
forced the workmen of these machines to stop work- 
ing. The workmen of course deny this. The work- 
men further deny that there was any enquiry. On 
the dates when the inquiry is said to have been held 
admittedly both the Sundaries and Sricharan were 
present although they say that there was really no 
enquiry. Kiron was, however, admittedly not pre- 
sent, both according to herself and according to the 
witness for the Company. 


The first question therefore for consideration in 
this case is whether there was an enquiry at all and 
the next question is whether if there was an enquiry, 
on the evidence adduced during the enquiry, the 
charges against the workmen could be said to have 
been made out. 


On the first point the cases of two Sundaris and 
Sricharan must be treated separately from that of 
Kiron because admittedly Kiron was not present 
during the enquiry. Sundari, ticket No. 64, says in 
her examination-in-chief itself as follows: “There 
was an enquiry into the charge-shect. I was present 
at the enquiry. At the enquiry I was told that ] 
would be called fater and thereafter no letter reach-

the termination of my Service.” Of course, she ار‎

AWARD 


These four applications under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act by (1) Sundari, ticket No. 64, 
in case No. 151/59, (2) Sricharan, ticket No. 149, in 
case No. 152/59, (3) Sundari, ticket No. 96, in case 
No. 153/59 and (4) Kiron, ticket No. 102, in case 
No. 154/59, all belonging to the “A” shift of the 
High Speed Winding Department were consolidated 
at the ‘instance of the parties, because the charge- 
sheets against all of them arose from the same inci- 
dent and they were dismissed as a result of the 
same enquiry. 

hey were dismissed with effect from 4th Decem- 
ber 1958 (vide ‘Exts. 4, 4,, and 4,). The applications 
under section 33A were filed on the 2nd of Decem- 
ber 1959. The Company filed its applications under 
section 33(2)(b) on the 6th February 1960 and tend- 


হও one month’s wages at about the same time. 
vidently, therefore. the applications under the 
proviso to section 33(2)(b) were made and one 


month’s wages under that proviso were tendered more 
than a year after the date of dismissal of these 
workmen. Evidently, these cannot be construed as a 
substantial compliance with the requirements of the 
proviso and it must accordingly be held that there 
was a contravention by the Company of the ۴٠ 
ments of the proviso to section 33(2)(b). The first 
condition therefore for the maintainability of the 
applications under section 33A is fulfilled and the 
applications must accordingly be held to be main- 
tairtable.

Admittedly, the whole incident of the 19th Octo- 
ber 1958 arose from what the workmen considered 
the managements’ unwarranted permission to Bakri- 
dani to work while she was still enjoying her annuai 
leave. The management has led evidence to show 
that Bakridani was not actually enjoying her annual 
leave on that date as her photo book Ext, N shows 
that she actually had no leave in 1958 at all. It 
appears from this exhibit that she had leave from 
2oth August 1957 to 8th September 1957 and there- 
atter she had leave from 6th March 1961 to 20th 
March 1961. On behalf ‘of the workmen this exhi- 
bit has been challenged on the ground first that it 
should have been in the custody of Bakridani her- 
self and secondly that it does not bear anybody’s 
Signature. There is no column in the book for any- 
body’s signature. It appears that it is a book pres 
cribed under rule 87 of the rules under the Factories 
Act. There is nothing in rule 87 to suggest that the 
entries in the leave book must be signed by anyone. 
Of course, the rule provides that the leave book 
shall be the property of the worker and the Manager 
or his agent shall not demand it except to make 
entries of the dates of holidays or interruptions in 
service and shall not apt it for more than a week 
at a time. The question how the management came 
to be in possession of the leave book so as to enable 
it to produce it before the Tribunal was not put to 
any of the witnesses. Consequently, it is impossi- 
ble for the Tribunal to say how the management 
was in possession of the book. It is just possible 
that Bakridani was cited as a witness by the manage- 
ment and the management got hold of the leave 
book from her in order to ensure its production 
before the Tribunal. Whether that is so or not, the 
fact remains that the leave book does show 081 
Bakridani was not on leave at all in 1958 so that the 
question of her being on leave on the 19th October 
1958 was obviously raised by someone among the 
workmen with a mischievous purpose. The trouble 
therefore that occurred on the 19th October 1958 ور‎ 
entirely due to this incorrect impression in the mind 
of some of the workmen. Even if it could be assum- 
ed for the sake of argument that Bakridani was 
enjoying her leave on the 19th October 1958 there 
would be no justification at all for the workmen 
behaving in the manner in which they did behave 
and I have no hesitation in saving that the behaviour 
of the workmen was wholly unjustified, when there 
was no basis at all for the information that Bakri- 
dani was enjoying her annual leave.

Orders shall come into operation on the expiry of 
30 days from the date of publication of the award 
exactly like the rest of the award of which it forms 
apart. In this view the Standing Orders on which 
the management relies are the Standing Orders 
governing the cases of these four workmen. On

I have already said that there has been a contra- 
vention, in each of these four cases, of the require- 
ments of the proviso to section 33(2)(b) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. I have also come-to the 
conclusion that on the materials the management 
was justified in finding all the four workmen guilt 
of the misconduct with which they were charged. 
The question now is what the Tribunal’s award 
should be in such a case. The Supreme Court has 
laid down the law on this matter clearly in the case 
of Equitable Coal Ltd. and Algu Singh and another, 
1958, I, L.L.J. 793. That was a case in which the 
Supreme Court had to consider the scope and effect 
of the provisions of sections 22 and 23 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act of 1950. 
These sections raise the same question as sections 
33 and 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act. Conse- 
quently, the law as laid down there will govern the 
cases under sections 33(2)(b) and 33A also. ‘Their 
Lordships observe as follows: “In an enquiry held 
under section 23, two questions fall to be consider- 
ed. Is the fact of contravention by the employer 


of the provisions of section 22 proved? If yes, is 
the order passed by the employer against the 
employee justified on the merits? If both these 


questions are answered in favour of the employee, 
the Appellate Tribunal would no doubt be entitled 
to pass an appropriate order in favour of the 
employee. If the first point is answered in favour 
of the employee, but on the second point the finding 
is that, on the merits, the order passed by the 
employer against the employee is justified, then the 
breach of section 22 proved against the employer 
may ordinarily be regarded as a technical breach 
and it may not, unless there are compelling facts in 
favour of the employee, justify any substantial order 
of compensation in favour of the employee. It is 
unnecessary to add that, if the first issue is answer- 
ed against the employee, nothing further can 

done under section 23.” In this case the Supreme 
Court has also considered whether the Tribunal 
would be justified in passing an order of compensa- 
tion in favour of the workmen if in spite of contra- 
vention of the requirements of the section § the 
management was justified in holding that the work- 
men concerned were guilty of misconduct and if 
that finding justifies the order of dismissal. In the 
light of that decision it must be held that in this case 
also in spite of contravention of the provisions of 
section 33, the workmen are not entitled to anything 
in the shape of compensation for their dismissal, for 
the dismissal is by no means wrongful although 
there was a technical contravention of the require- 
ments of the proviso to section 33(2)(b). On behalf 
of the workmen reliance was placed on the decision 
of the Supreme Court in the case of Sasa Musa 
Sugar Works (Private) Ltd., and Shobrati Khan and 
others 1959, TI, L.L.J.° 388 and the case between 
Hotel Imperial, New Delhi, and others and Hotel 
Workers’ Union in the same volume of the Labour 
Law Journal at page 544. In the first case the

Regarding issue No. 12 the Tribunal says in para-

(Standing Orders) Act provides for certification of 
Standing Orders on receipt of the draft under sec- 
tion 3. Evidently, therefore, it is only where the 
employer submits a draft set of Standing Orders that 
it is open to the Certifying Officer to certify them. 
There is no provision for certification of Standing 
Orders which form part of a Tribunal’s award, 
because the Tribunal frames the Standing Orders 
after giving the parties an opportunity of suggesting 
their own draft Standing Orders and after hearing 
them. It would be perfectly useless for a Tribunal 
to go through the procedure of letting the parties 
have an opportunity of submitting their draft stand- 
ing orders, then of giving them a hearing on their 
draft, and finally framing Standing Orders of its own. 
if the whole process has to be gone through afresh 
before the Certifying Officer. As a matter of fact, 
section 5 itself provides an answer to the question 
whether it was intended that the Certifying Officer 
Should again sit in judgment over the Tribunal’s 
award in the matter. The very use of the clause 
“on receipt of the draft under section 3” with which 
Section 5 opens shows that it is only when draft 
Standing orders are submitted by the employers that 
the Certifying Officer is entitled to certify them. The 
Standing Orders in a Tribunal’s award cannot by 
any means be construed as a mere draft. Conse- 
quently, there is no question of certification of such 
Standing Orders. The question now arises what is 
the meaning of paragraph | of the Standing Orders 
which says that these orders shall come in force as 
indicated in the manner in the Industrial Employ- 
ment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. I think the only 
reasonable meaning that can be attached 00 this 
paragraph of the Standing Orders is that the Stand- 
ing Orders should come into force as_ stated in 
section 7 which of course is not applicable in terms 
to the Standing Orders forming part of an award 
because where there is no certification by a Certify- 
ing Officer there is no question of anv appeal from 
the order of the Certifying Officer. The date of 
operation of a set of Standing Orders forming part 
of a Tribunal’s award must be the same as that 01 
an award under section 17A of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act In other words section 7 o! the Indus- 
trial Employment (Standing Orders) Act in its «ppli- 
cation to the Standing Orders forming part of a 
Tribunal’s award has to be read in the light of sec- 
tion 17A of the Industrial Disputes Act, and subject 
to such modifications as this may require. The 
obvious implication, therefore, of paragraph 1 of the 
Standing Orders in this case is that these Standing

FINDINGS 


] first take up the preliminary objection raised by 
the two Companies. Both the Companies say that 
Messrs. Nava Rastra Oil Mills (P.) Ltd. closed their 
business on Ist June 1958 and a few months later 
leased their machineries and the premises to 
Messrs. Lal Chand Sohanlal. The deed of lease 
(Ext. 3) shows that the lease was for a 
period of one year and five months up to ٤۴ 
March 1960. None of the Companies has adduced 
any evidence on the point as to whether Messrs. 191 
Chand Sohanlal continued to hold over after the 
Puy of the lease or whether Messrs. Nava Rastra 
Oil Mills (P.) Ltd. started their business again. Even 
if it be held that Messrs. Nava Rastra Oil Mills (P.) 
Ltd. closed their business finally on Ist June 1958, 
there is no evidence to the effect that the dispute 
which has led to the present order of reference arose 
after lst June 1958. The fact that the date of the 
order of reference is only a month after Ist June 
1958 raises a presumption that the dispute was raised 
before Ist June 1958. It has been held by the 
Supreme Court in the case of Pipraich Sugar Mills 
Ltd. reported at page 95 of A.I.R. 1957 (S.C.) that 
the power of the State to make a reference must be 
determined with reference not to the date on which 
it is made but to the date on which the right which 
is the subject matter of the dispute arises, and that 
the machinery provided for in the matter would be 
available for working out the right which accrucd 
prior to the dissolution of the business. Again, it 
has been held by the Bombav High Court in the case 
of New Guiarat Cotton Mills Ltd. reported at page 
111 of A.I.R., 1957 (Bombay) that if a successor 
decides to run the same business which was carried 
on by the predecessor, the employees of the old 
concern are entitled to submit a dispute before the 
Industrial Tribunal regarding their rights and 
obligations in the business of the old concern, and 
those rights and obligations must be regarded as 
continuing and enforceable against the new manage- 
ment and not affected by the substitution of the new 
management for the old. This is exactly the situation 
in the present dispute. So ] hold that the order of 
reference is perfectly valid and the order adding 
Messrs. Lal Chand Sohanlal as a party is free from 
any legal defect. 


As to the objection of Messrs. Lal Chand Sohanlal 
that the Union mentioned in the order of reference is 
not a Union of the workmen concerned, that Com- 
panv has not adduced anv evidence in surnort of this 
objection. As the order of reference raises a 
presumption that the Union mentioned in the order

AWARD 


This is an application by Shri Jnanendra Nath Das 
under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
complaining against the termination of his services 
by a notice, dated 11th August 1961, with effect from 
1705 August 1961 and praying for reinstatement. His 
case is that he was employed as a clerk at a monthly 
salary of Rs. 60 with effect from 27th July 1960, that 
at the time of his appointment he was not given any 
letter of appointment, that he is an active member 
of the Union and his father who is also an employee 
of the Company has incurred the displeasure of the 
Company by the assistance he rendered to the Secre- 
tary of the Union in the matter of inspection of the 
account books of the Company under the orders of 
the Tribunal and that was why the applicant was 
victimised by the termination of his services. He has 
also stated that the Company has kept his father in 
service but because he assisted the Secretarv of the 
Union he has not been allowed to do any work but 
only to record his attendance and to sit idle through 
the whole day. The case of the Company, on the

This is an application under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act filed by one Raghunath 
Beura alleging that the employers, Messrs. Master 
Stores, arbitrarily dismissed him from service with 
effect from the 9th November 1960 without getting 
approval of such action from the Tribunal under 
section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


The employers, Opposite Party, filed a written 
objection in which it is contended that the work- 
man concerned was employed on probation on 9th 
May 1960, and as his work was not found satisfac- 
tory he was not confirmed. 


After several adjournments the case was fixed for 
hearing on 7th February 1962 and 017 that date 
neither the workman nor the lawyer representing 
the workman appeared before the Tribunal to pro- 
ceed with the case. Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate, repre- 
senting the employers, was present. I therefore take

no fixed hour of attendance also in the factory. His

right. It is also in evidence that Shri Das used to

Shri Das is not a workman within the meaning of

The issue referred to this Tribunal for adjudica- 
tion is this: 


1. Whether the dismissal of Shri Ramesh 
Chandra Das is justified? To what relief, 
if any, is he entitled? 


Both the partics have filed written statements 
stating their respective cases in the matter in issue. 
The case of the workmen concerned is that he was 
a permanent employee of the concern and yet his 
services were suddenly terminated with effect from 
the 2nd of June 1961 without any notice, charge- 
sheet or enquiry. It is alleged that this wrongful act 
of the management was motivated by a spirit of vic- 
timisation alone because of the trade union activities 
of the workman concerned. 


The Company on the other hand, inter 2118, 
alleges that Shri Das was never a workman of the 
Company and as such no industrial dispute can be 
raised in this connection. It is alleged that Shri Das 
was only a consultant and used to come to the Com- 

any’s factory only intermittently. The Company, 
it is urged, had absolutely no control over Shri Das, 
who was in fact a free-lance advisor to several Com- 
panies including this Company on technical matters, 
and tHe present Company having felt that Shri Das’s 
advice was no longer required, informed him to that 
effect and he also stopped advising the Company as 
from the Ist January 7۰ 


Thus from what I have stated above, it will be 
clear that the real point at issue is whether there is 
at all any industrial dispute within the meaning of 
the law. If Shri Das is not a workman within the 
meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act as alleged, a 
reference in respect of such a person will no doubt 
be invalid and this Tribunal will have no jurisdiction 
to adjudicate in the matter and the other workman 
of the concern not being interested in the employ- 
ment or non-employment of such a person no indus- 
trial dispute can be raised also. 


The essential condition of a person being a work- 
man within the terms of the definition in section 2(s) 
is that he should be employed to do the work in the 
industry, that there should be, in other words, an 
employment of him by the employer and thus there 
should be the relationship of employer and employee 
or master and servant. The prima facie test for the 
determination of the relationship between master 
and servant is the existence of the right of the 
master to supervise and control the work done by 
the servant not only in the matter of directing what 
work the servant is to do, but also the manner in 
which he shall do his work. The nature or extent 
of control which is requisite to establish the rela- 
tionship must necessarily vary from business to 
business. In the present case the Company runs a 
power.loom factory of ten looms only, engaging 18/ 
19 workers in all. The positive evidence of one of 
the directors of the Company is that Shri Das was a 
mechanic and used to do job-work only for this 
Company and he would correct machineries as_and 
when required. Further evidence is that the Com- 
pany had no control over his duty hours and he had

entitled?

No. 876Fos.—6th February 1962.- Whereas the 
Governor thinks that in the case of the forest lands 
situate within the district of West Dinajpur and 
described in the schedule below, the enquiry and 
record referred to in the first paragraph of sub- 
section (3) of section 29 of the Indian Forest Act, 
1927 (XVI of 1927), will occupy such length of time 
as in the mean time to endanger the rights of 
Government; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 29 of 
the Indian Forest Act, 1927 (XVI of 1927), the 
Governor is pleased, pending such enquiry and record 
to declare, with effect from the date of the publi- 
cation of this noftfication in the “Calcutta Gazette”, 
such forest lands, to be protected forests.

No. 2190G.—3rd March 1962.—In exercise of the 
powers conferred upon me by clause (2) of Article 
229 of the Constitution of India and with the 
approval of the Governor conveyed in the Guvern- 
ment of West Bengal, Law (Judicial) Department, 
letter No. 1255]./J-2R-48/61, dated the 2151 Feb- 
ruary 1962, I do hereby make the following Rule: — 


“Where the Chief Justice is satisfied that the 
operation of any rule regulating the conditions 
of service of Officers and servants of the High 
Court causes undue hardship in any particular 
case, he may by order dispense with or relax 
the requirement of that rule to such extent 
and subject to such conditions as may be 
considered necessary for dealing with the case 
in a just and equitable manner”. 


H. K. BOSE, Chief Justice.

1. Gratuity Scheme. 


The Burn's Employecs’ Union represents the 
case of the clerks, sub-staff, sarkars, checkers of the 
Burn and Company at its Howrah unit renowned as 
the Howrah Iron Works. All other Unions repre- 
sent the labours or workmen of this particular unit 
of the Company. Hereinafter the Burn & Company 
will be described as the Company whereas the 
Unions will be described by their respective names 
whenever necessary. Each of the said Unions has 
filed a separate written statement in which it has 
described the facts and circumstances and laid its 
claim towards the framing of the gratuity scheme. 


In the written statement of the Burn’s Employees’ 
Union the following case has been made out. The 
Company is a highly prosperous engineering con- 
cern empleying about 8,000 workmen in all, the 
number of the clerks. sub-staff, sarkars and chéckers 
being about 1,100. The employees were suffering 
from various difficulties and inconveniences and 
had serious grievance for a long time. Their repre- 
sentations to the Management for redressing proved 
futile. This Union was formed in 1946 for ameliorat- 
ing the conditions of the employees. The Com- 
pany has only one type of retiral benefit in 
the form of Provident Fund Scheme introduced for 
the clerks in 1926 and for the sub-staff and others 
in 1946. On account of low wages given to them 
and growing needs for maintenance of their family, 
they often take loan from friends and relations with or 
without interest and also from the Burn’s Employees’ 
Co-qperative Credit Society with interest and in 
extreme cases from their own Provident Fund. 
The employees are thus unable to save any money 
to fall back upon after retirement and the family 
is at ruin when death occurs to the workmen. The 
matter was agitated in the past. By the award of 
late G. Palit, passed in 1960, the rate of Provident 
Fund Contribution was increased to 10 per cent. 
of the basic pay but the claim for gratuity scheme 
was disallowed. Again in the award of the First 
Industrial Tribunal of West Bengal, published in 
July 1953, the claim for gratuity scheme was 
rejected. The Union preferred an appeal against 
that award and the Learned Labour Appellate Tri- 
bunal by its judgment, dated 29th April 1955, up- 
held the decision of the Tribunal and rejected the 
claim for gratuity scheme. Scveral very material 
points were not considered by the Learned Tribunal 
and the Labour Appellate Tribunal. On 4th Nov- 
ember 1959 the Union gave notice to the Company, 
terminating the award and claiming one month's 
pay for each year of service as gratuity. The Union 
has summarised its reasons in support of the claim 
for gratuity, thu:s 


(a) The workmen were always in debt and 
Provident Fund money was insufficient to 
fall back upon. after retirement, _parti- 
cularly when unemployments of the sons 
and dependants are very common;

That claim was rejected by the then Learned Tribu-

Still holds good and also operates as 165 judicata. 
The argument advanced by Shri D. L. Sengupta on

Mr. Jinwalla, in course of his argument, referred me 
to the provisions of sections 18 and 19(6) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act and his contention was that 
notice of termination should have also been given 
to other employees than those represented by the 
Emplovees’ Union. This contention carries no sub- 
stance. Under section 18(3)(a) of the Act the award 
is binding on all parties to the industrial dispute; 
and under clause (d) of sub-clause (3) of this section 
the award binds all persons who were employed in 
the establishment or part of the establishment, as 
the case might be, to which the dispute related on 
the date of the dispute. In the present case, the 
persons to whom the dispute in question actually 
related were the particular categories of emplovees 
whom the Employees’ Union now represents. So it 
cannot be said that the workers other than those 
renresented bv this particular Union were bound by 
the award is question. Section 19(6) of the Act pro- 
vides that the award shall continue to be binding 
on the parties until a period of two months has 
clarsed from the date on which notice was given bv 
any party bound by the award to the other party 
or parties tntimating its intention to terminate the 
award. The Employees’ Union was no doubt a party 
in the award in question and bound dy it. This 
Union gave notice of termination only to the other 
partv, namelv, the Company, Mr. Jinwalla referred 
to the word “parties” occurring in sub-clause (6) of 
Section 19 as stated above and contended that the 
Flurality of the term jndicates that notice of termi- 
nation should have also been given to other parties. 
nomelv, the cmnlovees represented by the three 
other Unions. This is not a sound ar valid conten- 
tion at all. What is required by section 19(6) of the 
Act is that notice should be given by any party 


question of gratuity should be determined on an 
industrywise basis and not on a unit basis partt- 
cularly when the conditions of service of the 
different categories of the workmen employed in the 
Engineering Industry in West Bengal have been 
Standardised by the Omnibus Engineering Tribunals; 
otherwise, the industrial peace and the quality of 
competitive condition should be adversely affected. 
The Government of India has set up a Technical 
Committee to examine the question of the enhance- 
ment in the rate of provident fund contribution. 
Pending such assessment, the present adjudication 
Should not proceed. The First Engineering Tri- 
bunal in 1948 awarded some sort of gratuity under 
certain conditions. Those provisions were itmple- 
mented by the Company for the hourly-paid work- 
men but did not affect the monthly-paid employees 
of the Company as they had been in enjoyment of 
prvoident fund benefits since 1918. The provident 
fund scheme, meant for the hourly-paid workmen, 
was first introduced by the Company in 1946. . The 
question of gratuity was not referred for adjudica- 
tion either to the Second Omnibus Engineering Tri- 
bunal in 1950 or to the Third Omnibus Engineering 
Tribunal in 1953, the Government made a reference 
to the First Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, for 
adjudicating the question of gratuity at the instance 
of Burn’s power Union, who claimed to repre- 
sent the monthly-paid clerical, technical and sub- 
Ordinate staff and hourly-paid sarkars and checkers. 
That Tribunal rejected the issue for additional 
benefit of gratuity by its award, dated the 24th July 
1953. The Union’s appeal against that award was 
rejected by the Learned Labour Appellate Tribunal. 
The Company has not attained sufficient financial 
prosperity or stability to undertake an additional 
long-term financial burden of the nature of gratuity. 
Any additional payments/benefits by one unit 
would affect its competitive strength. The existing 
terms of employment and other fringe benefits are 
adequate and generous. For the hourly-paid work- 
men the Company has an “Attendance Bonus” 
scheme whereby they, on an average, annually earn 
about 75 per cent. of their monthly basic salarly. In 
addition under ‘“Purashkar” scheme (Production 
Bonus) they, on an average, annually earn 7/8 
months’ basic salary. For the monthly-paid staff 
and subordinate staff there is also an_ Incentive 
Scheme in force. Instead of solving industrial peacc, 
this spasmodic reference/adjudication will create 
more labour complications. The provident fund 
schemes in operation are generous and will go a 
far way towards old age pension. The award of the 
First Industrial Tribunal, confirmed by the decision 
of the Labour Appellate Tribunal in rejecting the 
employees’ claim to gratuity or nension, is based on 
sound reasonings which still hold good and operates 
as “res judicata”. There has been 110 material 
change of circumstances since the last award to 
justify a re-examination or introduction of a scheme 
for gratuity. The grounds urged by the different 
Unions in support of their claim for gratuity are 
not sustainable on merits also. The Comrany is not 
in a position to bear a long-term financial 
burden which a_ scheme of _ gratuity will 
envisage for the reasons mentioned above. 
In view of these facts and circumstances the claim 
of the Unions for introduction of the gratuity scheme 
should not be allowed.

Gujrath Engineering Company’s case that so far as 
other concerns are concerned, gratuity scheme may 
also be introduced there later if there is demand by 
the workmen and if the financial position justifies it. 
So it is no use saying that other similar concerns had

In the above views, therefore, the objection of the 
Company regarding the point of termination of the 
previous award in question is rejected. Other rele- 
vant points may be considered and discussed in due 
course. 


Another objection of importance as adumbrated 
by Mr. Jinwalla on behalf of the Company is that 
the matter concerning a gratuity scheme should be 
considered on industrywise basis, not on the basis 
of a unit alone like the Howrah Iron Works of the 
Company. It is undisputed that the Company has 
Several units including the Howrah Iron Works at 
Howrah and the Raniganj Works at  Raniganj. 
Mr. Jinwalla tries to draw analogy to the framing 
of grades and wage scale according to industrywise 
basis. As to the reason for his contention, Mr. 
Jinwalla says that the effect of the standardization 
fixed in the First Engineering Award would be 
nullified if only one unit here and one there 19 
Selected to be festened with the burden and as such 
it is quite wrong to differ from the norms fixed by 
the older award to make a new scheme for a parti- 
cular unit. He has referred to two cases reported 
in 1960 (2) L.L.J. 21 at page 30-32 (Bharat Khand 
Textile Manufacturing Company Ltd.) and 11 7.۶. 
372 (Mill Owners’ Association, Bombay) in support 
of his contentions. In the last named case under 
reference the Bombay Industrial Court held that a 
gratuity scheme, if awarded, should be on industry- 
wise basis after taking into consideration the capa- 
city of the Industry as a whole and not of the indivi- 
dual units or groups. In 1960 (2) L.LJ. 21, the 
Industrial Court adopted Industrywise basis in 
deciding the question of ay scheme. The 
Hon’ble Supreme Court approved of that. But I do 
not think this case would go to help the cause of 
the Company. Even the Hon'ble Supreme Court held 
in the above case that it would no doubt, be open 
to the Industrial Court to deal with the dispute unit- 
wise, Just 85 it was open to the Industrial Court to 
deal with it on an industrywise basis, and that 
there were several factors in favour of adopting the 
latter approach. It is clear, therefore, that the con- 
sideration of the question on industrywise basis is 
not the only way of approach to decide above the 
question of gratuity scheme, and that in view of 
particular or special facts and circumstances of each 
casc, the matter may be decided on unitwise basis 
or on industrywise basis, as the case may be. In 
support of the Union’s contention that unitwise con- 
sideration is applicable in suitable cases, reference 
has been made to the cases reported in 1961 (1) 
L.L.J. 513 (case of Garment Cleaning Works) and 
1961 (2) L.L.J. 180 (case of French Motor Car Com- 
nany Ltd.). In the first case it has been observed 
hy’ the Hon’ble Supreme Court that it is one thing 
to hold that the gratuity scheme can, in a proper 
case, be framed on industry-cum-region basis, and 
another thing to say that industry-cum-region basis 


bound by the Award to the other party or parties 
which also must be bound by the same award. Here, 
the other party bound by the award in question, was 
the Company itself, none else. So it was not at all 
necessary for the Employees’ Union to give notice 
of termination to the other workers represented by 
the three other Unions as they were not parties to 
the award in question. To give notice of termina- 
tion to persons who are not parties to or bound by 
the award in question will bear no sense. So there 
is nothing wrong or defective in the giving of ter- 
mination notice by the Employees’ Union alone to 
the Company. So this objection on behalf of the 
Company falls through. 


In this connection I may also make mention of 
Shri D. L. Sen Gupta’s contentions made on behalf 
of the Employees’ Union. His argument is that the 
earlier award may be interfered with if it appears 
that there have been changes of circumstances since 
then and that, even without change of circumstances, 
the previous award may be interfered with if there 
was any fundamental error in the award itself. 
Reference has been made to the cases reported in 
1957 (1) L.L.J. 226 at page 231 (the case of the Burn 
& Company) and 1961 (2) L.L.J. 660 (the case of 
Gujrath Engineering Company). The gist of the deci- 
sion in the former case under reference is that for 
change in circumstances and fundamental error, the 
award in question may be interfered with. The 
principle enunciated in the other case under refer- 
ence is that the fact that in similar other concern 
there is no gratuitv scheme must be held to be 
immaterial in adjudicating on the demand for intro- 
duction of gratuity scheme, that the proper way to 
look at the problem is that if a gratuity scheme can 
be introduced in a concern taking into account its 
financial position. it should not be refused simply 
because no gratuity scheme is in force in similar 
other concerns. The previous award of the Tribu- 
nal was passed by Shri N. C. Banerjee, who simply 
rejected the claim for gratuity without stating any 
specific reason. In the judgment of the Learned 
Appellate Tribunal, the following reasons were 
Stated in rejecting the claim for gratuity: 


(a) sufficient retiring benefit in the shape of pro- 
vident fund contribution: 


(b) under the Engineering Award or the Mercan- 
tile Award, there is no provision for double 
retiring benefit; 


(c) the introduction of gratuity scheme will entail 
heavy financial burden on the Company and 
will adversely affect its position on the com- 
petitive market; and 


(d) in the sister concerns there is no such provi- 
sion. 


It is to be noted that in that judgment the Company's 
financial position does not appear to have been con- 
sidered in the least. The rejection of the claim was 
.based on sufficiency of provident funds and 101- 
existence of $uch a scheme in sister concerns. These 
views ,are clearly against the fundamental principles 
enunciated in the cases referred to above. The 
Hon'ble Supreme Court held that double retiring 
benefit in the shape of gratuity in addition to provi- 
dent fund may be given if the financial position of 
the Companv properly and really justifies it. It has 
been found to be immaterial whether similar other 
concerns granted or did not grant such a scheme. 
The Hon’ble Supreme Court has observed in the

It is an admitted fact that the Company's contri- 
bution to the employees’ contributory provident fund 
is at the rate of 10 per cent. of the basic pays or 
6} per cent. of the basic pays and dearness allowance

that no additional liability in the shape of gratuity 
need be fastened on the Company, which would 
then be put hard financially. In conderation of the 
evidence adduced, I am unable to say that the wages 
earned by the employees are very substantial. It 
cannot be said that they get even fair wages, not to 
speak of living wages. In this connection the Com- 
pany relies on certain charts filed by it, viz., Exts. D, 
E, F, G and H. Exhibit D shows the maximum and

April 1961. Exhibit E shows average salary per

and subordinate staff for 1960-61. Exhibit F is the 
Statement showing maximum and minimum earnings 
of the hourly-paid workmen in April 1961. Exhibit 
G is the chart of average monthly wages of these 
workmen in 1960-61. Output of Puraskar units is 
shown in Ext. H in regard to the years 1956-57 up 
tn November 1961. In Ext. D dearness allowance, 
Company’s contribution to provident fund and to 
State Insurance Fund as well as canteen subsidy and 
medical benefit have been included. These items are 
also included in Exts. E, F and G, besides incentive 
allowance being included in Ext. D, attendance and 
Puraskar allowances being included in Ext. F. Con- 
tributions to provident fund and Employees’ State 
Insurance Fund are legal obligations. Canteen sub- 
sidy and medical benefits are also legal obligations 
of the Company under the Factories Act. Puraskar 
allowances and attendance allqgwances are not روح‎ 
able to all the employees. inasmuch as those who 
produce more and those who have regular attendance 
are entitled to get such allowances. The workers 
include both skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled per- 
sons. The average shown in the Company’s charts 
would undoubtedly show somewhat high figures as 
the skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled have been

is the only basis on which gratuity scheme can be 
framed, and that in fact in a large majority of cases, 
‘gratuity schemes are drafted on the basis of the 
units and it has never been sugyested or held that 
such schemes were not permissible. In reference to 
the French Motor Car Company’s case as_ cited 
above, it may be said that a gratuity scheme existed 
for the Bombay branch of the Company whereas a 
fresh scheme for gratuity was introduced in the 
Calcutta branch. In that connection it was held that 
the introduction of the scheme in the Calcutta 
branch of the Company would not adversely affect 
the Company's finances. Mr. Jinwalla has argued 
with reference to the case in 1961 (2) L.L.J. 660, 
which was cited on behalf of the Union and partly 
discussed above, that mere financial condition is not 
enough if other sister industries have 00 such 
schemes and that the decision in the case under 
reference does not militate against the proposition 
about industrywise basis. 1] am unable to accept this 
contention particularly when, as seen above, the 
industrywise basis is not the only way of considera- 
tion of the point at issue inasmuch as every case 
would depend on special circumstances and _ facts 
bearing on the same. But the point has been made 
clear by the Hon’ble Supreme Court by holding that 
if a gratuity scheme can be introduced in a concern 
taking into account its financial position, then it 
Should not be refused simply because no gratuity 
scheme is in force in similar other coricerns. In fact 
it is not correct to say that no sister concerns have 
formulated any scheme for gratuity. From the 
evidence of P.W. 1, Shri Bamapada Mukherjee, as 
well as the documents filed in that connection, it 
appears that there are gratuity schemes in the Indian 
Iron and Steel Company and the Indian Standard 
Wagon Company. I am not so much concerned with 
the actual reasons for which the schemes were intro- 
duced by those Companies. Anyway, such schemes 
were framed on compromise after a strike and the 
fact remains that such gratuity schemes are in 
existence in those Companies which are sister con- 
cerns undoubtedly being of the same group (including 
the Burn & Co.) under the self-some Managing 
Agents. It goes without saying, therefore, that 
gratuity schemes do exist in similar concerns. What 
is more 15 that the present Company itself has a 
gratuity scheme for its Raniganj unit. So, whatever 
the reason for introduction of that scheme for the 
Raniganj Works, the Company cannot now success- 
fully contend that the consideration of the gratuity 
scheme for purpose of the Howrah Iron Works must 
be on industrywise basis when it has a scheme tor 
gratuity for another unit of its own. As to the 
reasons for that scheme at Raniganj, the same may 
be discussed later on in some other connection. 


In consideration of the above, I find this parti- 
cular objection of the Company to be absolutely 
untenable. A gratuity scheme may be introduced 
on basis of unitwise consideration if the circum- 
Stances as well as the financial position of the Com- 
pany permit.

and there is a substantial provision for provident 
fund to which the Company itself makes ےج‎ ৮০1৬

the schemes for payment of Puraskar allowance,

Company itself granted gratuities at Raniganj at 
higher rates than the said maximum 11) several 
cascs. The Employees’ Union has put in“a list 
(Ext. 2) to show grants of such higher rates to ‘as 
Many as fvurteen persons, eight of them getting the 
higher facilities before Shri. Palit’s Award and six 
getting the same subsequent to that award. Thus, 
there must be a very good reason for not fixing any 
limit for maximum wages payable as gratuities. So 
I accept this proposition as being 16750119710 .nd 
fair. In my view, however, no gratuity should be 
paid to a person unless he completes 10 years ot 
services; nor should gratuity be paid to a person who 
is dismissed for misconduct or misdemeanour. It is 
said for the Unions that in case of termination of 
services for misconduct, gratuity may be given if the 
misconduct does not involve any financial loss to the 
Company. Of course, there are some cases in which 
this proposition was accepted but even in Exts. V 
and V/1, to which the Unions have referred such a 
benefit to a dismissed person was denied. I also 
think it quite proper that in case of dismissal! or 
discharge for misconduct, no gratuity should be paid. 


In the result, I frame the gratuity scheme in this | 


case as follows: 


(1) On the death of an emplovee or worker while in 
service, or on his becoming physically or mentally 
incapacitated for further service, or on retirement or 
resignation of an employee or worker, or on termina- 
tion of service of an employee or worker by th* 
Company cxcept for misconduct, gratuity shall be 
paki at the rate of half a month’s basic wages for each 
completed vear of service, to be paid to the employce 
or the worker concerned or his heirs or nominees, as 
the case may be. There should be no limit for 
maximum in respect of longer duration of service. 


(2) There shalt be no gratuity payable to a person 
rendering service helow 10 years. 


(3) Basic wages for the purposes of the present 
scheme shall be the average of hasic wages 3۲۶۴ 
to a worker or employee during the 12 months 
immediately preceding death. disability, retirement. 
resignation. or termination of service otherwise than 
for misconduct, as the case may be. 


(4) For the purposes of recKoning 
service, break not exceeding six months 
condoned. 


(5) No gratuity shall be paid to a person dismissed 
or discharged for misconduct or misdemeanour. 
(6) This scheme shall have retrospective effect from 


the date of the present reference. In giving this 
effect, ex-gratia payments, if any, shall be adjusted.

suggests, is a big book shop selling books and at the 
same time it is a publishing institution. The 
Company’s document Ext. H (notice displayed in the 
shop under the provisions of Bengal Shops and 
Establishment Act 1940) shows that the Company 
carries on publishing and book-selling business. Two 
other documents Exts. M and M/1 which are letters 
issued by the Chief Inspector, Shops and Establish- 
ment, Government of West Bengal, one to the 
Assistant Secretary of the Union and the other to the 
Manager of the Press, will show that the Oxford 
University Press is a book shop. Shri S. R. Das 
Sharma who is an employee of the Press and the 
Vice-President of the Union 1095 stated on oath 
before the Authority under the Payment of Wages 
Act that selling of books is a principal work of the 
Oxford University Press. He further deposed in 
that case that the sale proceeds of books constitute 
the revenue of the Company (vide Ext. F). There- 
fore it is abundantly clear that the Company is not 
a Press but the concern carries on book-selling and 
publishing business.

Issue No. 3: Overtime 


One of the points of dispute specified by the Guv- 
ernment in the order of reference is overtime. ۴٣ 
is not working hours and overtime. The Union 
claims that working hours should also be fixed as 
incidental to the overtime or by way of consequential 
relief. This Tribunal has been called upon to fix tie 
overtime allowances and there is nothing specified in 
the order of reference as to the fixation of the work- 
ing hours. Unless and untill that point is specificd 
in the order of reference by the Government. this 
Tribunal, in my opinion, will have no jurisdiction 
to go into the question of working hours and fixing 
the same without being called upon by the Govern- 
ment to fix the hours of work. and as such that point 
being outside the scope of reference this Tribunal 
is ousted of jurisdiction to fix the working hours. 


The Union's case is that overtime is being paid 
at the rate of 1/160th plus 1/4th of the basic wage 
for any work done after 5-30 p.m. which amount 
is considered inadequate by the Union. The Company 
admits the payment at the above rate but some 
attempt was made to describe the overtime payment 
as an incentive allowance. In this respect the Com- 
pany, of course, has failed miserably. Some of the 
Company's witnesses have admitted overtime pav- 
ment and maintenance of overtime registers (Exts. X 
series). These registers have been clearly described 
as overtime registers in which overtime paymnts have 
been recorded. Therefore, it is proved beyond doubt 
that the Company has been paying overtime at the 
rate of &/16011) plus 25 per cent. for any work done 
after 5-30 p.m. The basis of this calculation, accuid- 
ing to P. W. 2 Shri Gangadhar Sen. is the monthly 
basic wage divided by the total number of working 
hours in a month which is 160. So. the existing over- 
time rate is ]}th of the basic wage for any work 
done beyond 5-30 p.m. The Union is dissatisfied with 
this rate. The Union claims that it should be at the 
rate of basic salary divided by 160 plus half. I have 
already found from the document Ext. H that the 
Company claims to be a shop under the West Bengal 
Shops and Establishment Act, and similarly it has 
been recognised by the Government (vide Exts. A, 
۔(۱/ھ‎ The Union has also admitted the fact in 
its letter, dated 27th August 1959, addressed to the 
Manager of the Oxford University Press (vide Ext. 
E/1). Therefore, I find that the Company is liable 
to pay for the overtime work at the rate of one and 
one-half times the ordinary rate of wages payable to 
the workmen as provided in section 13 of the Benyal 
Shops and Establishment Act, 1940. The overtime 
wages be paid accordingly.

The Company’s case as made out in its written 
statement is briefly this: 

The Company's Jute Mill was divided into two 
sneds each of which being treated as a‘complete unit 
in itself with its own separate complement of staff— 
one was called the Old Mill and the other the New 
Mill. This Old Mill was closed in 1957 82170 the 
employees thereunder were given option of retrench- 
ment or new appointment in the New Mill, if and 
when available. Many of the workmen accepted 
retrenchment, but others indicated their willingness 
to accept new employment in the New Mill, and 
some remained silent. Shri ]ندم‎ Paul was working 
as a jute ledger clerk in the Old Mill at the relevant 
time. There were three ledger clerks including him- 
self in the office —one working in connection with 
the New Mill. one in connection with the Old Mill 
and another for both the Mills. After the closure 
of the Old Mill there was work only for one clerk 
in the Ledger Department. One of the clerks had 
retired. As Asit Paul was junior to the other clerk 
in service, he would have been retrenched in normal 
course. But the Company transferred him to the 
New Mill as a measuring clerk without loss of earn- 
ings. The Union's allegation that Shri Paul was 
arbitrarily transferred to an unimportant job is totally 
baseless. In fact, the transfer was to his advantage 
and benefit. Besides, the services of all clerks are 
transferable from one place to another and from the 
Manager’s Office to the Mill and the vice versa. Shri 
Paul was not a trustee of the Provident Fund when 
he was transferred.

DECISION 
Issue No. | 


Admittedly, Shri Asit Ranjan Paul was working 
as a ledger clerk in the office of the Manager of the 
Company. It is undisputed that in all he has put in 
20 years’ service. At present he has-been working 
as the second measuring clerk in the Mill since 1958 
on being transferred from the Manager's Office. His 
case, as deposed by him, is that he is the Vice- 
President of the Bengal Chatkal Mazdoor Union and 
he was agitating for regularising the defects of the 
Provident Fund matters and election of the Provi- 
dent Fund Trustee Board members which was long 
overduc. He also says that subsequently he was 
elected a member of the Provident Fund Trustee 
Board. In the written statement the contention on 
behalf of this clerk is that the Company on the plea 
of an agreement arbitrarilv transferred him with a 
view to creating hindrances to smooth discharge of 
his responsibilities and also that the transfer was 
made to ৪100 which was quite unimportant in com- 
نت‎ with the former job he used to do 1 the 

anager’s Office. It is further in evidence of this 
clerk that in the Mill he has got to work for 48 hours 
a week whereas his duty hours in the office as a 
ledger clerk were 414 hours per week. He says that 
he has been incurring pecuniarv losses and also there 
is difficulty in vetting a proper grade if he remains a 
measuring clerk in the Mill. On the other hand the 
Company's case is that Shri Paul clone with others 
were found to be surplus by reason of the closure of 
the Old Mill of the Company which took 2 most 
sympathetic view in retaining him 11 service and 
making his transfer to the Mill as there was no neces- 
sity of retaining three clerks (including Shri Paul) in 
the Manager’s Office. It is further contended for

Another ground of objection taken by the Com- 
pany is that there was an agreement in view where- 
of the transfer is to be justified. Exhibit A is a 
bipartite ayreement, dated 8th March 1958. It

The contention of Shri Pathak on behalf of the

not bind him at all. It is said that Ext. A is con-

by notices dated 28th December 1957 and 30th

ary 1958, was superseded and four clerks including 
Shri Paul were asked to continue their services in 
the Company from the first day of March 1958. 
Thus, on 8th March 1958, when Ext. A came into 
existence, the notice of 30th January 1958 was also 
superseded. It appears, theretore, that by the notice 
Ext. 4, dated 28th February 1958, the name of Shri 
Paul appearing in the notice of 30th January 1958 
was withdrawn and he was allowed to continue in 
service. It is said for the Company that Ext. 4 did 
not cancel the agreement. But from what I have 
found above, this contention of the Company can- 
not be accepted and it must be held that the agree- 
ment per Ext. A is not binding upon Shri Paul by 
virtue of the notice Ext. 4.

of all descriptions sick leave on half pay up to 15 
days in a year shall be allowed on the basis of 
medical certificate from the Medical Officer of the 
Mill or from a qualified and registered medical prac- 
titioner approved by the Mill authorities. It is said 
by the Company that no such medical certificate as 
contemplated in that award had been filed by any of 
the 12 workers mentioned above. It is also said that 
none of them applied for sick leave before or 
immediately after leave, and that none of these 
rersons has come to depose before this Tribunal. 
For these reasons it is said that the contention of 
the Union must fail and the said workers are not 
entitled to any relief. 


in the relevant paragraph of the Company’s state- 
ment the period of absence of these workers has 
not been denied. It is also not denied that they 
were sick or that they were absent on ground of 
sickness. If the Company's contention be accepted 
at ull, then the period of absence of these workers 
could be considered as unauthorised leave, and in 
that case the Company was expected to issue charge- 
Sheets against them for unauthorised absence. But 
no such step was at all taken by the Management. 
¢ is true no formal application was filed by these 
12 workmen for sick leave. But in the written 
Statement of the Company it has not denied the 
Union's statement that they were examined by the 
Medical Officer of the Mill and were granted leave 
Originally, and subsequently they took “و٣‎ certifi- 
cates” from the attending physicians and submitted 
the same to the Company. In the absence of such 
denial the statement of the Union is to be accepted 
as correct. The Company’s action in refusing wages 
to these workmen for the period of their respective 
illness might be justified if the Company had follow- 
ed the principle of natural justice by issue of 
charge-shects to the workmen and by holding enqui- 
ries. In the absence of such things, therefore, the 
Company's action is considered to be amounting to 
arbitrary one and hence unjustified. Accordingly, 
these workmen are entitled to get their wages for 
the period of their illness at the rate of half basic 
wages and full dearness. The Company shall make 
these payments to them within one month from the 
date of publication of this award in the “Calcutta 
Gazette”. The issue is disposed of accordingly.

in question was filed in connection with Government 
Order, dated 17th December 1957, whereas the work- 
man was dismissed on 156 April 1957, i.e., eight 
months earlier than the date of reference itself. Thus 
there was no dispute pending at all when the dismis- 
sal of the workman took place. On that ground alone 
the application could have been at once rejected as 
being non-maintainable. On _ the contrary, the pro- 
ceedings in connection with that application proceed- 
ed for a pretty long time till 6th December 1958 when 
the Company was ready through its Advocate, but 
the petitioner was absent and took no step. The 
Tribunal then rejected the application for default. 
The question is whether such an order, though pub- 
lished as an award in the “Calcutta Gazette”, would 
be taken as a real award in the true and legal sense 
of the term. 


Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act requires 
that on receipt of a complaint under this section the 
Tribunal shall adjudicate upon the complaint in 
accordance with the provisions of this Act and shall 
submit its award to the appropriate Government. In 
view of thegfacts stated above, it may be said that 
there was no real adjudication upon the complaint of 
the workman concerned. Under rule 2] of the West 
Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules of 1958, if without 
sufficient cause being shown any party to a proceed- 
ing before the Tribunal fails to attend or to be repre- 
sented the Tribunal may proceed as if such a party 
had duly attended or represented. This rule does 


‘ not appear to have been strictly followed in reject- 


ing the complaint for default. In the circumstances, 
آ‎ am unable to consider the order of rejection to be 
an award in its true sense as the dismissal was long 
before the making of the reference itself, in connec- 
tion with which the complaint was made. It may be 
considered that the rejection of the application would 
mean nothing more than non-maintainability of the 
application, as no dispute was pending about the time 
of the workman's dismissal. In this view of the 
matter, therefore, I hold that the present reference is 
quite tenable under law. 


Coming to the question of merit also, J find that 
the contention of the Company cannot stand. The 
alleged occurrence took place on 27th February 1957, 
and the workman was charge-sheeted by the Com- 
pany on 20th March 1957 according to him. The 
Company’s case is that he was charge-sheeted on the 
very date of the occurrence. Whatever that may be, 
the point is whether any proper enquiry was held and 
the principle of natural justice was followed by the 
Company. The Manager says that after the work- 
man’s reply to the charge-sheet he was called to his 
office when he said that as a police case was then 
pending, he would not make any statement and 
refused to give evidence at that enquiry. The 
Manager also says that Shyamnarayan durwan made 
a statement in the verv presence of the workman 
concerned and he took down that statement in 
writing. The workman, Shri Narendra Nath Banerji 
(P.W. 4), denies that the Manager called him to his 
Office and that the durwan made a statement in his 
presence or that the Manager took down that state- 
ment in writing. In Ext. 6, the written statement 
filed by the Company in the case brought by the 
workman under section 33A, it was not specifically

The Company has put in a certified copy of the 
judgment (Ext. B) of the Authority under the Pay-

In view of the above considerations, it appears in 
connection with this issue also that the Company did 
not follow the principle of natural justice in regard 
to these nine masons of the Building Department, so 
that its action in keeping these workers under sus- 
pension for three weeks without issue of timely 
charge-Sheets and without holding any proper enquiry 
is also to be considered unreasonable and unjustified. 
In the result, these workers are also entitled to get 
wages for the period of suspension from 10th Novem- 
ber 1958 to 30th November 1958, and this must be 
paid within one month from the date of publication 
of this award in the “Calcutta Gazette”.

The workman’s Provident Fund book (Ext. 1) 
shows that contribution towards the fund was cut 
from July 1958 to January 1959, and there was no 
such cut for two months following. It is an admitted 
fact that the workman rendered continued service for

have been due to his getting chicken-pox and taking 
leave. But the fact remains that there was conti- 
nuity of his service even in February to April 1959. 
There is, therefore, no good reason for denying him 
the benefit of Provident Fund contribution after 
January 1959. 


The position of this workman is that of a badli 
durwan. According to the definition in the First 
Jute Tribunal Award, a badli is a worker who is 
appointed to the post of a permanent workman or 
probationer who is temporarily absent. The Com- 
pany’s books produced before this Tribunal do not 
Show against whom Sher Bahadur was working as a 
badli worker. It is contended by Shri Pathak on 
behalf of this workman that the position in the cir- 
cumstances is that he is really a permanent work- 
man. It is contended that the Manager refused to 
give him appointment after the expiry of his leave 
inasmuch as he wanted his job to be made perma- 
nent. The question whether this workman is to be 
regarded 01 made a permanent worker is not before 
me in this present reference and, as such, this parti- 
cular guestion is out of the mark 70 remains 
undecided. 


The workman prays for being reinstated with 
other consequential relief on the ground 06 the 
Manager’s arbitrary refusal to allow him to resume 
his duties. It is to be seen whether this prayer is 
to be allowed or not. The Manager stated that Sher 
Bahadur gave up the job and did not turn up after 
the Manager refused to appoint him as an additional 
driver. ] have already seen that the story of Sher 
Bahadur’s coming for the job of a motor driver and 
the refusal of the Manager to appoint him as such 
is not correct, I do not find any sufficient reason as 
to why this man would give up his regular jeb of his 


mentioned that Shri Banerji appeared at the enquiry 
and refused to make a statement. This is admitted 
by the Manager in his cross-cxamination. If any 
enquiry was at all held by the Manager, it must have 
been some days after the occurrence so that the 
statement of the durwan, if at all taken down by the 
Manager in his office during the enquiry, must be 
some time later than the time of the occurrence. But 
the alleged statement of Shyamnarayan (Ext. E) 
reveals a very strange state of things. This statement 
does not bear any signature or thumb-impression of 
the durwan, but bears the date 22nd February 1957 
in the handwriting of the Manager himself, this date 
being the very date of the occurrence. So there can 
be no doubt, if this statement was at all made by 
the durwan, this was on the date of the occurrence, 
and not later. As such it cannot be said to have been 
made during any enquiry. From this fact alone, 1 
can hold confidently that the deposition of the 
Manager as well as the contention of the Company 
is totally unreliable. In the circumstances I cannot 
believe that any enquiry was really held by the 
Manager in regard to the incident in question. No 
paper of procecdings has been filed by the Company 
to show when the alleged enquiry was held, if it was 
held at all. That being so, the principle of natural 
justice was clearly violated and hence the dismissal 
of the workman cannot be justified. Tithe result is 
that the Company shall reinstate this particular 
workman Shri Narendra Nath Banerji to his former 
job with all back wages and continuity of service 
within a month from the date of publication of the 
award in the “Calcutta Gazette”
