سہسیےےےیمییمممم۔م.۔مممتجتےےےے۔۔۔مممےےممسسویت ۔۔ a‏ 


was present on 28th July 1961. So he was aware that 
the date of hearing was 27th October 1961; but he 
did not care to come to the court on that date. On 
that day the case was adjourned to 5th December 
196] for hearing. So, if Shri H. K. Banerjee was not 
aware that the case would be taken up for hearing 
on 5th December 1961, he is to thank himself alone 
on that score. Hence this is no ground for reopen- 
ing of the case. So I rejected that petition and held 
that my order, dated 5th December 1961, would 
Stand. 


The case of the complainant Shri K. N. Ratnam, 
briefly stated, is as follows:— 


He was working under Messrs. Spences Hotel Ltd. 
as a confectioner for about eight years. On 22nd 
March 1961 a charge-sheet was issued to him on the 
ground that he prepared bread and butter pudding 
in a deep bowl and thereby spoiled the food. On 
that very day he gave a reply to the charge-sheet 
explaining the reasons sb he prepared the pudding 
in a deep bowl and why he was not responsible for 
the spoiling of the pudding. In spite of the above 
reply he was suspended on account of the above 
charge. On 8th April 1961 the Managing Director 
of the hotel called him and advised him that he 
should prepare even small quantity of pudding in a 
big flat dish in future. The complainant replied that 
he had no objection to abide by that instruction, 
though the previous instruction was to the contrary. 
Thereafter the complainant was dismissed by a letter, 
dated 3rd May 1961, on account of the above charge. 
No enquiry about the charge-sheet was held. At that 
time a dispute between the Company and its work- 
men was pending before the Second Labour Court. 
The Company contravened section 33 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act by not seeking the approval of 
the Second Labour Court and by not paying him 
salary as mentioned in the proviso to section 33(2)(b). 
So the complainant contends that his dismissal is 
unjustified. 


The Company, on the other hand, in its written 
Statement contends that two enquiries were held 
about the charge-sheet issued to the complainant. On 
those enquiries his guilt of carelessness and ineffici- 
ency in preparing the pudding was proved beyond 
any shadow of doubt. Hence the management decid- 
ed to dismiss him. The management applied to the 
Second Labour Court for approval of its action and 
also gave a cheque, to the complainant for the 
moneys due to him as per the provisions of section 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. So the Company 
contends that the dismissal of the complainant is 
justified. 


Findings 


As stated already, the Company did not adduce 
any evidence in this case. The complainant examined 
himself in support Of his case. He was not cross- 
examined by anybody on behalf of the Company. He 
Says in his evidence that he was given a cheque by 
the managing director of the Company; but he could 
not cash it on account of some objections raised by 
the Bank. He then approached the managing director 
to remove the defects for which the Bank refused to 
honour the cheque; but the managing director did 
nothing of the sort: so the cheque remained un- 
cashed. In the circumstances it cannot be held that 
handing over of the cheque is payment as contem- 
plated in proviso to section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. It is true that the Company applied to 
this Court for approval of its action. But the fact 


THE CALCUTTA: GAZETTE. MARCH 153, 62 805 


that he does not press for any wage on behalf of the 
workman from 12th December 1960 till 18th June 
1961. In a case under section 33A of.the Industrial 
Disputes Act, the Tribunal has to find out, first of 
all, if there was any contravention of the provisions 
of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is 
only if there be any contravention of the said pro- 
vision of law that the Tribunal would enter into the 
merits of the complaint and determine what relief 
the workman is entitled to. The provisions of sec- 
tion 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act at once gives 
a right in favour of the workman to move _ the 
Tribunal and to demand an adjudication as to the 
action taken by the employer as in the case of a 
reference made by the appropriate government under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act provided, of 
course, it is first of all shown that the provisions of 
Section 33 had been contravened. In the- instant 
Case the fact that the workman had resumed his 
duties virtually gives him the psincipal relief which 
he prayed for in this complaint case, no matter 
whether section 33 had been contravened or not. 
It is thus not necessary to determine if the employer 
had taken any action in contravention of section 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. The question 
whether he would get back wages is also solved by 
the admission of the representative of the. workman 
that no claim is made on that account. The parties 
also agreed that there would be no break in service 
of the workman concerned for the period he was 
out of enzagement under the Company, and that his 
continuity of service would be maintained. Naturally 
he would get same wages as he was getting before 
being laid off. Virtually, therefore, on the consent 
of the parties, an award in the above terms is passed. 


K. K. MITRA, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 15tL February 1962.

This is an application under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, filed by Shri Santosh 
Bhowmik, a workman of Messrs. Oriental Rubber 
Works. It is contended by the applicant workman 
that the employer Company in contravention of the 
provisions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, verbally dismissed him from service on 12th 
June 1961. It is alleged that the Company laid off 
a large number of workmen including Santosh 
Bhowmik, with effect from 8th August 1961, and 
after the lay-off was lifted on 12th December 1960, 
he reported to dutv but was refused work. On the 
15th December 1960 he was served with a charge- 
sheet on an allegation of his refusal to work and for 
“conduct subversive of discipline’. The petitioner 
claims that he should be reinstated and paid _ full 
wages from 15th December 1960 till the date of his 
reinstatement as the action of the employer was 
completely unjustified. 


Messrs. Oriental Rubber Works. the cmplover,

lay-off on 12th December 1960 when all the laid-off

refused to do so, and when such state of things was 
continuing, he was duly charge-sheeted on 15th 
December 1960 and was placed on suspension. The 
employer denied the allegations made by the com- 
plainant that he had at any time been dismissed. On 
the contrary, it is alleged that the workman since 
resumed his dutics some time after the withdrawal of 
lay-off of workmen and that there was no violation 
of the provisions of section 33. 


After several adjournments the case came up for 
hearing on 14th February 1962. The case was opened 
at length by Shri Parimal Das, Advocate, represent- 
ing the workman and also by Shri Nalini Mukherjee,

from the pleadings as well as the statements of the 
lawyers that the workman concerned had resumed 
his duties from 19th June 1961. It is 21509 the 
admitted case of both the parties that this workman 
along with others had been laid off with effect from 
8th August 1960 and the lay-off was lifted on 12th 
December 1960. In view of the fact that the work- 
man concerned has already resumed his duties, it is 
conceded by the learned lawyer for the workman,

Audit Branch 


The Audit Branch is vested with the responsili- 
lity of scrutinising the accounts of private licensees 
throughout the Stute and reporting instances ot 
infringement of any of the provisions of the Sixth 
Schedule to the Electricity (Supply) Act. The 
branch is in immediate charge of an Audit Officer. 
The Chairman of the Board has heen appointed 
authority under section 1101) of Indian Electricity 
Act, 1910, to examine these accounts with effect 
from December 1955. 


The Secretariat . 


The Secretariat besides functioning as a receruit- 
ing body serves as a co-ordinating link between thie 
Board and its different departments. 

For consultation in legal matters, the Board hus 
uppointed the Government Solicitor as a retainer.

CHAPTER 1 
OUTLINE OF SCHEMES—PROCRESS MADE 
80 FAR 


An attempt has been made in this Chapter to

(1) The North Calcutta Rural 


Scheme. 

This was the most ambitious of al! schemes 
taken up under the First Five-Year) Plan. The 
scheme was designed to open up a number of 
towns covering about an area of 1,000 square miles 
to the north of Calcutta from Chord Road (a place 
udjacent to Shamnagar Railway Station, which is 
ut a distance of about 22 miles trom Caloutta 
proper) to the use 01 electricity at moderate yates. 
The entire scheme was executed in রী stages. 
The first phase of development which was completed 
in 195] carried electricity up to Krishnayar in the 
north electrifying en-route the towua of Ranaghat, 
Shantipur, Kalua, Birnagar, Habra, Badkulla and 
Walvani township besides giving bulk supply to 
Haringhata Agricultural Farm, Kanchrapara T. B. 
Hospital and the licensees of Krishnagar and 
Nabadwip Electric Supply. 


Electrification 


The power is purchased under this scheme from 
the (Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation’s Power 
House at Mulajore in bulk at 33,000 volts and then 
stepped up to 66,000 volts ut the main receiving 
station 181 Cherd Road, wherefrom this ما‎ 


transmitted to the towns en-route through a 
16.000 volts 11. T. Line. 


Under the second phase, lines were extended 
from Krishnagar to Berhampore and_ thence to 
Jiaganj connecting the towns of Beldanga, Deba- 
gram, Aziingunj, Katwa, Matiari and Dainhat and 
hulk supply given to the licensees of Berhampore 
Klectric Supply. The connection to Kalna, Katwa 
and Agimgunj has been given by means of sub- 
marine cables, Completed in 1954 at a total cost 
of Rs. LOO dakhs, the seheme covers 14 towns, 170 
miles of H. T. Imes, 8 sub-stations and 6 bulk 
consumers, The earning from this scheme in 
1955-46 amounted to Rs. 8.39 lakhs on the basis of 
North Caleutta grid tariff rate.

F. Jaldhaka and Balasun Hydro Projects 


The important and = ambitious electrification 
achemes of North Bengal areas are the two hydro- 
electric projects, viz., Jaldhaka Hydro-Electric 
Scheme and Balasun Hydro-Electric Scheme. The 
salient features of the two schemes are given below 
separately :— 


(a) Jaldhaka Hydro-Elcctric Scheme 


This scheme envisages harnessing the water of 
the Jaldhaka river near its point of entry at Bindu- 
khola near the boundary of Bhutan. From this 
point, water will be conveyed by an open flume to 
a forebay noar Paren and thereafter by individual 
penstocks to each of the two units of 12 mw 
generator to be housed in a power house near 
Jhalung. By the end of 1960-61, Jaldhaka will 
develop firm generating capacity of 12 mw (during 
dry season for about four months) and 24 mw 
during the period of monaoon lasting for eight 
months in the year, and thereby will be in a 
position to cater to the load demanda of the tea 
gardens of North Bengal. 


be made available to the existing townships near 
the Dam and also to industrial consumers in the 
area nearabout, which will in course of time 
develop into centres of industrial activities, as also 
to the adjoining coalfields. Requirement of power 
for town electrificution was estimated to be about 
2,000 kw and that for pump irrigation, the umount 
was almost the same. Two 2,800 H.P./2,000 kw 
turbo-generating sets were planned for installation 
at the power station at Massenjore. To meet the 
growing demand of power of the different towns 
in the project area and also to have a stand-hy 
source of power in times of exceptional drought, 
provisions were made to import power from the 
Damodar Valley Corporation via their Pandaveswar 
sub-station. Kstimated to cost Rs. 63 lakhs, the 
scheme was divided into two phases. The first 
Phase comprises the erection of 41 miles of double- 
circuit transmission line from Pandaveswar to 
Massenjore via I)ubrajpur and Suri, 34 miles of 
transmission line from Suri to Bolpur via Ahmed- 
pur and Sainthia with the provision of future 
extension up to Nalhati in the north and Guskara 
in the south, 10 miles of transmission line from 
Suri to Mohummnadbazar, generating station at 
Massenjore, retail distribution in the towns of 
Dubra)jpur and Sainthia and bulk supply to the town 
of Dumka in Bihar. The second phase is mainly 
concerned with the extension of lines to the towns 
of Guskara, Mollarpur, Rampurhat and Nalhati ind 
to different irrigation pumping areas. The entire 
project is expected to be completed by the end of 
the current financial year. The cost of the hydro- 
electric portion of the scheme amounts, as already 
stated, to Rs. 68 lakhs and the equipment and 
machineries for this project are being received from 
Canada as gifts under the Colombo Plan.

CHAPTER IV 


THE BOARD'S FINANCE, ACCOUNTS AND

1. General principles for Board’s Finance 


Prior to the formation of the Board, the State 
Government used to provide in the State Budget 
under appropriate budget heads, amounts required 
for Capital expenditure as well aa Revenue expendi- 
ture (including depreciation and interest charges) 
for execution of the electrical schemes duly sanc- 
tioned und for maintenance of those schemes com- 
pleted and put into operation respectively. The 
Revenue Receipts derived from the operative 
schemes in turn were fully credited to the consoli- 
dated fund of the State Government under proper 
head of account opened for the purpose in the State 
Wadget. The net profit or loss arising from the 
working resulta of the operative schemes was also 
shared or horne by the Government. 


With the formation of the Board with effect from 
lst May 1955, a separate fund was crented in the 
Reserve Bank of India, Calcutta, known as ‘State 
Electricity Fund’ under Government order 
No. 2740/TB—57/55, dated 30th April 1955, and 
operated by the persons authorised in the 8ء‎ 
Government order. Subsequently, the fund has 
heen declared as “Local Fund’? under Government 
order No. 9986/TB—57/45, dated 21st December 
195. Tor execution of the schemes (Capital 
expenditure) and maintenance of schemes put into 
operation (Revenue expenditure) no fund

CHAPTER V 
Commercial Activities 


The commercial activities of the Board consist 
in carrying out load survey throughout the State 
with a view to working out the economics of each 
new connection or extension, formulation of tariff 
for different =o purposes and collection 78176 
maintenance of statistics relating to electric supply 
industry. 


Tariff Policy of the Board 


A great variety of retail tariffs was in existence 
at the Vesting day. The following tariffs were 
also framed by the Bourd in addition to the elready 
existing ones :— 


(a) Howrah-Amta and Singoor aren. 
(b) Durgapur-Sonamukhi area. 

(c) Burdwan-Mogra area. 

(0) Small Diesel Schemes. 


The Bourd also framed grid tariff for bulk 
supply to the licensees of Bankura and Vishnupur. 


The absorption of many individual 0110 self- 
contained undertakings, e.g., Burdwan, ‘Tamluk, 
Suri, Santiniketan, عات‎ inevitably brought into 
the fore anomalies of charges inherited from the 
former undertakings. Such anomalies and 
inequalities called for an early treatment on the 
ground of equity alone. 


Section 49 of the Electricity (Supply) Act 
provides that the prices to be charged by the Board 
shall be in দর with tariffs as may be fixed 
by the Board from time to time. The primary 
question for decision by the Board was whether 
there should in fact be one tariff or different tariffs 
for different areas of supply. 


The Board has been purchasing energy in bulk 
from different supply rindartal ities or retail 
distribution in the Board’s area of supply which 
ore not contiguous. As such, the pooling cf the 
cost of purchase of energy and transmission "۳۲ 
the ne areas of supply was not considered 
advisable. Pending further examination of tariffs 
in general, the Board decided to retain os an 
interim measure the same tariff for bulk supplies 
as was in vogue before the vesting date. At the 
same time, as a step towards the cheapening of 
supplies in mainly rural areas, the Board in 
approprite cases has reduced the flat rate charges 
which were in excess of 6 annas per unit. 
Realising that detailed cost analysis would not be 
practicable until the organisation has x«dvanced 
further, the reduction of certain high flat retes 
was the first step to the removal of anomaloua 
variations in actual changes from area to 8۰ 


To suit seasonal consumers to that they may not 
be penalised during adverse period of low energy 
consumption, provision for levy of mitlimum

ہا‎ harmonise as much as possible its commercial

Mayurakshi Hydro-Electric Scheme 


All the construction work envisaged under the 
scheme and devolving on the Board for execution 
was carried through in course of the year under 
review at a total cost of Rs. 63 lakhs. The Hydro- 
Electric Station which has an installed capacity 
of 4000 kw. was switched on by Sir D. N. Mitra, 
the Chairman of the Board, on 16th December 19546, 
in presence of a large and distinguished gathering 
where the High Commissioner for Canada in [ndin 
was represented through his First Secretary 
Mr. Hampson. 


The commissioning of the Hydel Power Station 
ul Muasenjore has opened up the towns of Surt, 


Mohammad Bazar, Mollarpur, Rampurhat, Nal- 
hati, Sainthia, Ahmedtpur, Bolepur, Gushara, 


Dubrajpur, Pandaveswar and the adjoining coal- 
field arenas in the State of West Bengal and the 
town of Dumka in the State of Bihar to the use 
of electricity at a cheaper cost. 


The construction phase over, the question of fix- 
ing responsibility for operation and maintenance 
of the stations came to the fore. It was held that 
us the Power Station is situated at Massenjore 
which is outside the territory of West Bengal, the 
Board could not have any jurisdiction over the 
maintenance of the station in terms of the provi- 
sions of section 18 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 
1948. This view was also upheld hy the Legal 
Remembrancer to the Government of West Bengal 
and accordingly the State Government in the Irri- 
gation and Waterways Department brought out an 
order transferring the management and mainten- 
ance of the Massenjore Hydel Power Station and 
13 miles of Transmission System from Maasenjore 
16 Bihar-West Bengal border to the charge of the 
Chief Electrical Engineer and Electrical Adviser 
to the Government of West Bengal with the Irri- 
gation and Waterways Department of the State 
(tovernment retaining all financial and Executive 
control of the station. 


Ever since the station went into operation, the 
Board has been purchasing power from the Irri- 
gation and Waterways Department of the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal from its Massenjore Tlydel 
Station at 33 kv. in the capacity of a bulk con- 
sumer and then selling this power to its consumers 
in the towns referred to in this report through a 
number of 33/11 kv. and 11/.4 kv. sub-stations— 
the major ones being situated at Suri, 
Pandayeswar and Sainthia,

CHAPTER ITl 


THE BOARD'S FINANCE, ACCOUNTS AND 
AUDIT 


1. General principles for Board’s finance 


Since the formation of the Board with ۷ء‎ 
from lst May 1955 the Board did not take any 
loan from the State Government for meeting its 
operating, maintenance and management expenses 
except a loan of Rs. 10.89 Jakhs drawn during 
1955-56 for meeting its revenue expenses. The 
entire amount was, however, refunded during the 
same year. The revenue earnings of the Board are 
now sufficient to cover the gross expenses including 
the depreciation charges. The Board takes loan 
from the State Government only for capital outlay 
in connection with the execution of the schemes 
under Second Five-Year Plan and the norma! 
extetisions of the existing schemes of capital 
nature. The normal extensions are financed hy 
State Revenue proper.

from the grid or transmission system neces- 
sitates supply in the areas by disel genere- 
tion which incidentally raises the unit cost 
of production over the grid rate. The chronic 
slump in the rural sector has combined with 
higher cost of unit production to complicate the 
situation to the point of intriguing even the most 
ingenious business talent to carry through a com- 
prehensive scheme of rural electrification consistent 
with the objective of safeguarding business 
interest. 


Committed however to a policy of rationalising 
the distribution and transmission of electricity in 
the countryside by progressively bringing ever- 
increasing number of کا‎ under electrification, 
the Board cannot afford to let its decision be 
influenced by considerations of earning alone in 
drawing up schemes of rural electrification. Once 
the insularity of the villages is broken by the 
initial thrust given through supply of power other 
forces will be set in motion and under the gather- 
ing momentum gained from the original impact, 
channels will open up of themselves for increased 
development activities in other directions. 


The Electricity Board is cut out to play this 
vital role in initiating the process of secondary 
developments in the rural sector by offering the 
potential ipower thrust to the withering fabric of 
the rural economy. 


Such a benign role can hardly be possible for a 
business concern to assume of its own volition and 
should as such be left to be filled up by an orga- 
nisation ready to finance the scheme even at the 
cost of initial financial loss. And this is exactly 
what the Board proposes to do. It intends to 
carry through its programme of electrification in 
the years to come by subsidizing supply to rural 
areas out of surplus from its earning schemes. 


The magnitude of the programme justifying, the 
Board may have to have recourse to subvention 
from the Government to supplement the surplus 
resources available under its earning schemes. 


Load Survey 


A judicious selection of places based on survey 
report may as well keep the amount of subsidy 
well within the limit of surplus from its earning 
schemes without inflating the financial burden of 
the Board which may not otherwise be avoided. 
|| is precisely here that the importance of the 
01٦ and technique of survey would manifest 
ا تسگا‎ 


The planning of survey pattern and of methuda 
10 be employed is in no way less important than 
the survey operation itself. Before deploying the 
survey teams in the hugs areas lying mapped out 
before it, the Board has to take the initial decision 
on the technique of team deployment in the areas 
based on considerations of their administrative 
importance. According to the grading of adminis- 
trative importance, the areas with police-stations 
come next to the district and subdivisional towns. 


6. Gepreciation Reserve 


Depreciation Reserve Fund is created on Sinking 
Fund method at 4 per cent. compound interest. As 
the amount is not invested outside the Board’s 
Fund the interest is credited to the fund by the 
Board and the Depreciation Reserve Fund remains 
merged in the State Electricity Fund. The 
amount accumulated in the a aera Reserve 


Fund up to 9181 March 1957 is Rs. 8.13 lakhs. 
7. Accounts and Audit 


The audit of the Board’s accounts for the year 
1955-56 has been entrusted by the State Govern- 
ment to Messrs. G. Basu & Co. in accordance with 
the provision of section 69(2) of the Electricity 
(Supply) Act, 1948. But the above section of the 
said Act has been recently amended providing for 
the audit of the Board’s accounts by the 
Comptroiler and Auditor-General of India or by 
such other person as may be authorised by him. 
The audit of the accounts of the Board for the 
year under report has not been taken up by the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India or by his 
authorised person as per provision of section 69(2) 
of the Electricity (Supply) Amendment Act, 1956, 
although negotiations were giong ov between the 
Board and the Accountant-General, West Bengal, 
during the year in this respect. 


CHAPTER IV 
COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES 


Commercial activities comprise continuous load 
survey operations, formulation of tariff and out- 
lining the policy behind tariff formulation, 
examination of all cases for permission to supply 
power under section 27 of the Indian Electricity 
Act, 1910, initiating proceedings for revocation of 
licence, assessment of valuation in respect of 
acquired undertakings, drafting of all Commercial 
agreements for supply of power and disposal of 
cases involving application of the provisions of the 
Indian Electricity Act, Electricity (Supply) Act 
and the rules framed thereunder. 


We shall give in this Chapter an account of the 
comparatively important of these activities 101 some 
detail. 


The Paradox of Rural Electrification 


By 1955-56 all the district towns and most of 
the subdivisional towns were electrified in addi- 
tion to a number of important towns and villages. 
The remaining subdivisional towns were also pro- 
grammed for electrification during the vear under 
review. With all the district and  subdivisional 
towns ulready electrified or under process of electri- 
fication, the Board enters from now on ٥ menac- 
ingly wide and unchartered field comprising of no 
less than 42,000 villages scattered throughout the 
length and breadth of the State to direct its survey 
operations for chalking out its future programme 
of rural electrification for the years that lie abead. 
The use of electricity is as much the function as it 
is the cause of economic prosperity. The paradox 
of rural electrification lies precisely in this situa- 
tion. The remoteness of the rural hamlets

plun.

for the territories annexed to the State following

1956, were based on data collected by intensive

» Tariff 


Since tuking over of Burdwan, Suri and Santi- 
niketan Undertakings from private licensees 
further reduction of rates was under consideration 
although some reduction of rates was effected 
immediately after taking over. In the year under 
review a considerable reduction of rate has been 
effected at Burdwan, in conformity with the 
standard rates for Burdwan-Mogra Grid. On being 
connected to the Mayurakshi Grid, consumers of 
Suri, Saniniketan, Nalhati, etc., were offered 
North Calcutta Grid rate which was much less 
than the prevailing rate. In the year under con- 
sideration two more private undertakings, e.g., 
Sodepur and Jhargram were taken over by the 
Board. Sodepur is contiguous to Barrackpore and 
hence our Barrackpore rate which is the lowest rate 
has been applied in the case of Sodepur. Power is 
generated at Jhargram by diesel-electric genera- 
tion and as such our standard diesel-rate has been 
offered. In both the above cases consumers were 
relieved of the burden to a considerable extent. 
In November 1956, the district of Purulia was 
transferred to West Bengal and all the existing 
undertakings of the Bihar Government came under 
the control of the Board. The prevailing rates 
were superseded and our standard rate for 
Burdwan-Mogra Grd was enforced. Among the 
amendment of the standard rate the cases of 
industrial rates of Burdwan-Mogra and Durgapur- 
Sonamukhi Grids may be mentioned. Some con- 
sumers having an installed capacity of above 
15 H.P. are now gradually taking supply in some 
small undertakings where power is generated by 
diesel electric generation. Hence the limit of the 
rate has been extended from 15 H.P. to 50 kW. 
A special tariff has been introduced for bulk con- 
sumers whose maximum demand is above 60 kW, 
und the consumption of energy for lights and fans, 
etc., exceeds 10) per cant. of the total monthly 
consumption, Last but not the least in importance 
8 the concessional rate for small-scale and cottage 
industries. This concession is only applicable to 
those who have an installed capacity up to 10 H.P. 
and consume energy for the above purposes. 
Consumers under this category are relieved of the 
burden to a very great extent by the introduction 
of this new ۰

the Engineers of fhe Board acted with remarkable

industrial possibilities of the areas. 


By January 1957, the departmental officers of 
the Board collected all relevant data after inten- 
sive survey and prepared a comprehensive scheme 
for extension of the supply system in the district 
of Purulia entailing an estimated capital expendi- 
ture of Rs. 41.5 lakhs for the whole of the merged 
areas. 


Prior to merger, bulk power was purchased by 
Bihar Electricity Department at 11 kv from 
D.V.C.’s Digwadih sub-station. Pending finalisa- 
tion of an agreement for purchase of bulk power 
from D.V.C. at Purulia by the Board for which 
negotiations were started during the year, the 
Board continued to purchase power in bulk at 
11 kV from the Bihar Electricity Department from 
the Digwadih-Anara line. This Digwadib-Anara 
transmission line which is insulated for 33 kV, but 
sia کر‎ at present to 11 kV is the mainstay of 
supply in the Purulia district. The line is 19 miles 
long of which 13.3 miles have come to the share 
of West Bengal within the transferred areas. 
The total value of the transferred assets is approx!- 
mately Rs. 11.5 lakhs. In the context of the load 
potential and the extent of transmission system 
required to serve the area with a well connected 
system of net work, the inadequacy of the existing 
Digwadih-Anara line was self-evident. Dua 
ownership of the existing line by the State Gov- 
ernments of Bibar and West Bengal also pointed 
to the necessity of going in for independent source 
of -supply. To overcome this difficulty in the 
management problem and to serve the area’s grow- 
ing load demand, a scheme was prepared providing 
for three way ramification of a separate and 
independent 33 kV transmission line from Purulia 
to Jhalda, Purulia to Balarampur and finally from 
Purulia to Manbazar. Advantage may then he 
taken of these 33 kV lines to supply power 6০ 
Jhalda, Tulin, Joypur, Balarampur, Hura, Bara- 
bhum, Puncha and Manbazar.

Shri ٥. K. Sen, I.A. & A.S., a retired officer 
of the Government of India in the Ministry of 
Finance, was appointed Administrator to the 
Board and he took over charge of his office with 
effect from 6th January 1958. 


Shri T. 8. Mukherjee continued to be the 
Secretary of the Board. 


Dr. M. Datta, the Senior Superintending 
Eugineer of the Board, was elected President of 
the [ngineering and Metallurgy Section of the 
Indian Science Congress Association for 1958-09. 


The Board renewed its membership of the 
Central Board of Irrigation and Power and th- 
Indian Standards Institution under section 24 1ہ‎ 
the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. 


As mentioned in the previous reports, the Legal 
Adviser to the 70910 is the Solicitor to the 
Government of West Bengal, who was appointed 
on a retainer during the year under review. 


The foundation of the Central Testing 
Laboratory of the Board was 1910 by its Chairman 
on 18th June 1957, the construction of the building 
was completed in February 1958 and_ the 
Luboratory commenced functioning from 10th 


March 1958. 


Recruitment and Promotion 


As in the previous years, the recruitment and 
promotion policy of the Board has been to fill up 
higher posts as far as possible by promotion from 
the existing personnel, outside recruitment being 
resorted to only when suitable and qualified 
persons are not available amongst the existing 
hands. In the lower technical posts, recruitment 
is made, as far as practicable, from the 881 
employed on daily wage basis on work-charged 
establishment in connection with construction 
work with a view to progressively absorb those 
staff in the regular cudre. This ensures continued 
utilisation of the useful experience gained by the 
employees through their previous work on Board’s 


grid. 
Selections for filling up the various posts 
under the Board are entrusted to the two 


Committees as follows :— 
Selection Committee I (for filling up Class ا‎ and

Accounts and Audit 


The audit of the Board's account for 1953-56 has 
not yet been completed by Messrs. G. Busu & Co., 
to whom the audit has been entrusted by the State 
Government under section 69(2) of the Electricity’ 
(Supply) Act, 1948. The section has been 
amended to provide for the audit of the Board’s 
account being done by the Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India or by his authorised person with 
effect from dist December 1957, i.e., from the date 
of the publication of the amendment. But it 
would be difficult to prepare two separate accounts 
for a financial year and to get these audited by two 
different audit agencies. So the Accountant- 
General, West Bengal, has agreed to audit the 
entire period of 1956-57 as there is no legal bar to 
the uudit of the entire period of 1956-57 being 
undertaken by him. 


The Accountant-General, West Bengal, has 
taken up the transaction audit of Board’s account 
for 1956-57. 116 is also carrying out the audit of 
arrear accounts of the pre-Board peniod. 


Decentralisation of Board’s account 


Under the present system of working of the 
Board all payments are made centrally trom the 
Head Office and the accounting of receipts and 
expenditure is also made centrally. The Divisional 
سح‎ have been vested with very little finan- 
clal powers nor have they been made drawing and 
disbursing officers in respect of the expenditure 
relating to their respective divisions. 


This system results in delay in making pty ments 
and also makes correct budgeting and control of 
expenditure difficult. Further more with the rapid 
expansion of the activities of the Bourd, the cen- 
tralised svstem has been proving .o he unwork 
able. The Board has টব نا‎ introduce the 
system of accounts on the model of the (dovern- 
ment P.W.]). system. Necessury steps ure alreaty 
being taken to introduce the P,W.T). accounting 
system with effect from Ist April 1959 and 
Divisional Accountants for the purpose are heing 
provided by the Accountaut-General, Went Bengal, 


During the year the Bourd decided 10081 
under the powers vonferred by rule 50 of the West 
Bengal State Electricity Board Rules, 1935, the 
surplus funds of the Bourd may be invested in 
Government of India Treasury bills.

Tariff 


With the introduction of the decimal currency 
system since Ist April 1957, all the standard and | 
special rates and charges of the Board for supply 
of power were converted into decimal currency. 


During the year under review there had been 
only a few cases of rate amendments. The main 
reason for the amendments was the maintenance of 
uniformity in tariff in difficult zones. 
In this connection it may he mention- 
ed that there are at present only five 
types of rates—(l1) Rates which are  appli- 
cable to the consumers of North and South Calcutta 
Grid, (2) rates applicable in the whole of West 
Zone (other than South Calcutta Grid), (3) special 
rates applicable to Cooch Behar, Kurseong, Sili- 
guri, Barrackpore and Sodepur, (4) special indi- 
vidual rate toa few bulk consumers and (5) 
standard rates for isolated diesel supply under- 
takings. However, during the period under review 
the following amendments of rates, were made. 
For the sake of uniformity the standard tariff of 
the West Zone (Burdwan-Mogra Grid rate) was 
extended to Mayurakshi area where the North 
Calcutta Grid rate was applicable up to 30th June 
1957. On introducing the standard tariff of the 
West Zone in the said area consumers have been 
relieved to a very great extent. Again, the old 
standard rate for collieries which was applicable to 
Pandaveswer area was reduced and the standard 
tariff of West Zone was introduced in this area 
also. Some minor amendments in the rate strue- 
ture were made in the case of rate H of the 
standard tariffs of the Board. In addition to this, 
the rate of Power Factor surcharge was amended 


in the case of thos id hich 1

No, 1F.—1st February 1962.—In exercise of the power conferred by sub- 
seciion (3) of section 20۸ of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act IV 
of 1866), and in supersession of all previous regulations on the subject, 
if, 7. Mukharji, Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, hereby frame the follow- 
ing regulations, with the approval of the State Government :— 


THE CALCUTTA SPECIAL POLICE OFFICERS RECULATIONS 
CHAPTER | 


Organisation 
Short title 


1. These regulations may be called the Calcutta Special Police Officers 
Regulations, 1962. 


Defiritions 


2. In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) “‘the Act’? means the Calcutta Police Act, 1866; 


(b) “authorised Deputy Commissioner’? means a Deputy Commissioner 
of Police for the town of Calcutta, who may be authorised by the 
Commissioner of Police, Caleutta, under the proviso to sub 
section (2) of section 20A of the Act to exercise the power of 
appointment of a specia] police officer of any class or rank; 


(c) ‘the Commissioner’? means the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta: 


(1) 50186101661) means the force of Special Police Officers for the towa 
of Calcutta: 


(e) “Special Police Officer’’ means a Special Police Officer reterred to 
in section 201 of the Act; 


(f) ‘‘town of Caleutta’’ shall include all places within the local limits 
of the jurisdiction of the High Court at Caleutta. 


Name and character of the force 


3. (1) The force of Special Police Officers for the town of Calcutta shall 
he 0 purely voluntary force raised as an auxilary wing of the regular police 
force under the Commissioner, and shall be known as the Calcutta Special 
1১116 Officers Force. 

(2) A Special Police Officer shall not be entitled to receive any salary

functions or for journeys undertaken in connection with such duties, parade 
or functions,

CHAPTER II 


Recruitment, Appointment and Promotion 
Eligibility 


12. (1) In order to be eligible for appointment as a Special Police 
Otticer, a person shall— 


(i) be a citizen of India; 


(11) ordinarily reside or carry on business, trade or profession in the 
tuwn of Calcutta or the suburbs of the town of Calcutta as defined 


by notification under section | of the Calcutta Suburban Police 
Act, 1866; 


(ili) be between twenty-five and fifty years of age; 


(iv) not belong to any political party or froup or take any active part 
in politics; 


(৮) have a fair knowledge of English, Bengali and Hindi languages; 


(vi) be physically fit, willing and able to attend parades, rallies, route 
marches and the duties which may be allotted to him; 


(vii) be willing and 1১16 to render voluntary and non-remunernative 
service to the Government ; 


(viii) be in a position to purchase at his own cost his uniform, equipment 
and badges; 


(ix) not have been convicted of any offence by any court of law; 


(x) not be an officer of any regular or auxiliary, military unit or 
essential service, or hold any honorary rank therein; 


(xi) be a person fit to hold a position of responsibility, 


Relaxation on sufficient grounds 


(2) Any of the conditions mentioned in sub-reguintion (1) may be 
relaxed by the appointing authorny if im his opinion there are sufticient 
grounds for making such relaxation. 


Form and procedure of application for appointment 


13. Applications for appointment as a Special Police Officer shall be 
made in the form in Appendix 1. Such form may be obtained from the 
headquarters of the force at Lalbagar or from the offives of the Group 
Commanders of the force. The application form duly filled in by the 
applicant shall be sent to the Commandant of the force at Lalbazar. After 
proper enquiry, the Commandant shall forward the application with his 
recommendations to the Commissioner. On receipt of the application form 
together with the recommendations as aforesaid, and after making any 
further enquiry, if thought necessary, the Commissioner may direct the 
cundidate to appear for an interview before a sclection board,

CHAPTER 8 1 
Duties, liabilities and obligations 
Calling Out in aid of the Police 


23. It shall be the duty of every officer of the force to assist the reguiur 
police whenever called out by the competent authority to do so in discharge 
of legal duties by the Police. 


Social welfare work 


24. It shall be the duty of the Sperial Police Officers to assist the 
Government in undertaking social welfare work in their own localities and 
to undertake such work, if possible, of thei own accord. 


Assistance to Vigilance Parties 


25. It shall be the duty of the Special Police Officers to assist in the 
formation of local Vigilance Parties. 


Assistance to the Police in night rounds and collection of intelligence about 
bad characters 


26. It shall be the duty of the Special Police Officers to assist. the 
regular Police in night rounds, to collect intormation and intelligence about 
bad characters in their own localities and pass it on to the Police through 
the proper channel. 


Assistance to the Police whenever required on the spot 


27. It shall be the duty of every Special Police Otteer to go to the 
assistance of a Police Officer when called upon to do so on the spot. 


Hours of duty 


28. Ordinarily, the hours of duty of such officers, except in cases of 
emergencies and except under unavoidable circumstauces, shall be settled 
after consulting the convenience of such officers. 


CHAPTER IV 
Jurisdiction 
Jurisdiction and organisational set-up Croups 


29. (1) The jurisdiction of the force and organisation of the Special 
Police Officers for the town of Caleutta shall extend to the town of Calcutta. 
This organisation shall be divided into four Groups, namely, North Group, 
Central Group, South Group and = eadquarters (iroup. The area and 
jurisdiction of the first three Groups will correspond to the area and jurise 
diction of the local police division within the town ot Calcutta. The Tlead- 
کت‎ Group will have jurisdiction over the whole of the town of 
valeutta, 


Sub-Croups 


(2) Each of the Groups except the Headquarters Group shall be sub- 
divided into two Sub-Groups. The area and jurisdiction of each Sub- 
Group will correspond to the area and jurisdiction of the loca) Assistant 
Commissioner of Police within the town of Calcutta. 


Sections 


(3) Bach Sub-Group shall be subdivided into as many Sections as there 
are police-stations in its area and jurisdiction. The area and jurisdiction 
of each Section will correspond to the area and jurisdiction of the local 
police station within the town of Calcutta. 


Blocks 


(4) Mach Section shall be split up tuto Blocks according tp necessity. 
The area and jurisdiction of cach Block will correspond to the area and 
jurisdiction of the corresponding beat of the Jocal police station. 


Headquarters Croup 


(4) For smooth and efficient administration, management and control, 
the Headquarters Group may be divided into such Sub-Groups, Sections or 
Blocks, as the Commissioner may, from time to time, determine.

CHAPTER V 
Training 


Course of Departmental training 


30. After enrolment, every Special Police Officer shall undergo a 
prescribed course of departmental training which shall be arranged by the 
Commissioner or the authorised Deputy Commissioner. 


Drill and lecture 


This course shall consist of drill and lecture classes and the Special 
Police Officers shull be encouraged through such a course to learn such 
subject or matter as is, in the opinion of the Commussioner, necessary tor 
enabling them to discharge their duties as officers of such a 10108, 


Musketry 


Such a course shall also include a course of musketry formulated by the 
Commissioner. Subsequent to this course, the Commissioner may also 
indicate a period during which the officers of the force may be called upon 
to receive practical training in their work. The course of the practical 
training also shall be decided by the Covinissioner. 


CHAPTER VI 
Leave and Transfer 


Casual leave and long leave 


31. (1) A member of the force can be given either casual leave or long 
leave. Casual leave may amount to 18 days only in a year. Long leave 
may be given for an indefinite period not exceeding one continuous year. 
lf a member remains on leave tor more than one continuous year, his 
membership of the force shall automatically be terminated. 


Grounds for leave 


(2) Casual leave may be granted for private or urgent reasons. The 
cause for long leave may be equally varied, and it shall be in the discretion 
of the authority granting leave to consider whether any particular ground 
constitutes a sufficient ground for long leave or not. Medical yrounds will 
naturally be one of them, as well as absence from Calcutta on business. 


Authority competent to grant casual leave 
(3) The following officers are empowered to grant casual leave: 
Group Commander—To all ranks below him. 
Commandant—To Deputy Commandant and Group Commanders. 


Commissioner of Police—To the Commandant. 


Account of Casual leave to be maintained by C.8.P.0. 


(4) Whenever casual leave is given to any particular officer, the fact 
shall be intimated by the Officer granting leave to the office of the Special 
Police Officers Force. The said office shall keep an account of casual leave 
of each individual officer. 


Authority to grant long leave. Leave account to be maintained 


)5( Tiong leave may be granted by Group Commanders to officers up to 
the rank of Deputy Section Leader. Long lenve to an officer of the rank 
of Section Leader and ahove may be granted only by the Commandant. 
The Deputy Commandant shall have equal powers as the Commandant in 
this respect. The Commissioner may grant long leave to the Commandant 
The fact of such long leave being given shall be intimated to the office of 
the Special Police Officers Force which shall keep an account of such long 
leave of ewch imdividual officer.

CHAPTER VIII 
Discipline and Punishments 
Breaches of discipline 
$4. It shall be a breach of discipline for any member of the forre— 
(i) to violate any provisions of the Act or of any rules, regulations, 
or orders made thereunder; 
(ii) to abuse hia official position; 
(iii) to indulge in party politics; 
(iv) to interview any person connected with the Press or to supply any 


information to any such person, without orders from his imme- 
dinte superior officer ; 


(v) 10 interview an officer superior in rank to bis immediate superior

rapacity by any competent authority; 

(vii) to do anything or to avoid doing anything which is likely to 
bring the foree into disrepute; 
(viii) to wear his uniform in an locorrect manner.

Punishment 


30. (1) A Special Police Officer who has committed a breach of discip- 
line shall be liable to punishment. 


(2) A punishment may be either major or minor. 


(1) A major punishment may be as follows: 
(3) Dismissal from the foree; or 
(11) Dischatye from the force; or 


(iui) Black Mark, 


(4) .A minor punishment may be as follows: 
(1) Warning; or 
(11) Reprobation; or 


(211) Censure. 


Procedure in awarding punishment 


36. (৫) A minor punishment shall not be awarded except after giving 
the officer concerned an opportunity of beimg heard, either orally or in 
writing. 


(2) A major punishment shall not be awarded except after proceedings 
have been drawn up against the officer concerned. Subject to these recula- 
tions, such proceedings shall be drawn up and disposed of as _ nearly as 
possible in the same manner as proceedings against member of the regular 
police foree, but no mere technical defect or error, not affecting the merits 
of the case, shall vitiate such proceedings. 


Person entitled to order and conduct proceedings 


37. (1) The Commissioner may order and conduct proceedings against 
Special Police Officers of all ranks. 


(2) Subject to the control of the Commissioner, the authorised Deputy 
Commissioner may order proceedings against any Spevial Police Officer 
in respect of whom he is the appointing authority and may conduct such 
proceedings himself or through such Police Officer or Special Police Officer 
as he may nominate. 


Persons empowered to award punishment 


38. Any Special Police Officer may be awarded any minor punishment 
by any officer superior to him in rank. But no major punishment shall be 
awarded to any Special Police Officer except by the authority appointing 
him or any higher authority. 


Appeal 


39. (1) An appeal shall lie from any order awarding a major punish- 
ment,— 


(i) to the State Government, if the order is passed by the Commis- 
sioner ; 


(ii) to the Commissioner if the order 18 passed by the authorised 
Deputy Commissioner. 


(2) An order passed on appeal shall be final and conclusive. 


Power of cancellation of appointment under section 20A(5) not affected or 
prejudiced 


4). Nothing in this Chapter shall in any way affect or prejudice the 
power of cane 5 of any appointment of a Special Police Officer, con- 
ferred by sub-section (5) of section 20A of the Act.

No. 2F.—Ist February 1962.—In exercise of the power conferred by 
sub-section (3) of section 14A of the Calcutta Suburban Police Act, 1866, 
(Bengal Act II of 1866), and in supersession of the previous regulations on 
the subject, I, U. Mukharji, Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, hereby 
frame the following regulations, with the approval of the State 
Government: 


THE CALCUTTA SUBURBAN SPECIAL POLICE OFFICERS 
RECULATIONS, 1962 


Short title 


1. These regulations may be called the Calcutta Suburban Special 
Police Officers Regulations 1962. 


Definitions 


2. In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires,— 
6 


(u) ‘‘the 40৮77 means the Calcutta Suburban Police Act, 1866. 


(b) ‘‘authorised Deputy Commissioner’? means 2. Deputy Commissioner 
of Police for the town of Calcutta who may be authorised by the 
Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, under the proviso to sub- 
section (2) of section 14A of the Act to exercise the power of 
appointment of a Special Police Officer of any class or Rank; 


(c) ‘‘the Commissioner’? means the Commissioner of Police. Calcutta; 


(0) ‘‘the force’? means the force of Special Police Officers for the 
suburbs of the town of Calcutta; 


(e) “Special Police Officer’? means a Special Police Officer referred to in 
section 14A of the Act; 


(£) ‘‘the suburba’’ means the suburbs of the town of Calcutta as defined 
in the notification under section 1 of the Calcutta Suburban Police 


Act, 1866. 


Name and character of the foroe 


3. (1) The force of Special Police Officers for the suburbs shall be a 
purely voluntary force raised as an auxiliary wing of the regular police 
force under the Commissionr, and shall be known as the Calcutta Suburban 
Special Police Officers Force. 


(2) A Special Police Officer shall not be entitled to receive any salary or 
allowance or uny payment whatsoever, either in cash or in kind, for perform- 
ing his official or departmental duties or for attending at parades or functions 
or for journeys undertaken in connection with such duties, parades or 
functions. 


Jurischction and organisational set-up Croups 


4. (1) The jurisdiction of the force and organisation of the Special 
Police Officers for the suburbs shall extend to the suburbs. The organisation 
shall be divided into four Groups,. namely, North Group, Cenfral Group, 
South Group, and Headquarters Group. The aren and jurisdiction of the first 
three Groups will correspond to the area and jurisdiction of the local police 
division within the suburbs. The Headquarters Group will have jurisdiction 
all over the suburbs.

Sub-Croups 


(2) Hach of the Groups except the [eadquarters Group shall be subdivided 
utto two Sub-(lroups. The area and jurisdiction of each Sub-Group will 
correspond to the raea and jurisdiction of the local Assistant Commissioner 
of Police within the suburbs. 


Sectione 


(3) Each Sub-Group shall be sub-divided into as many Sections as there 
are police-stations in its area and jurisdiction. The area and jurisdiction of 
each Section will না to the area and jurisdiction of the local police 
station within the suburbs. 


Blocks 


(4) Each Section shall be split up into Blocks according to necessity. 
The area and jurisdiction of each Block will correspond to thé area and juris- 
diction of the corresponding beat of the local police-station. 


Headquarters Croup 


(5) For smooth and efficient administration, management and control, 
the Headquarters Group may be divided 10৮০ such Sub-Groups, Sections or 
Blocks as the Commissioner may, from time to time, determine.

Exceptions

“Calcutta Special Police Officers Force’’ shall be read. 


(ii) Applications for appointment referred to in regulation 13 of the

(iv) In sub-regulation (1) of regulation 4, sub-regulation (4) of ae

Special Police Officers’’ shall be read.

of the Act’’ respectively, shal] be read.

No. 1440/10A-1/58.—15th February 1962.—The 
Governor is pleased to make the following amend- 
ments to the Building Rules for Kalyani, published 
under the Development Department notification No. 
4875 /KPA-81/52, dated 3rd October 1953, at pages 
3708 to 3733 of Part I of the “Calcutta Gazette”, 
dated the 19th November 1953, as subsequently 
amended, namely:— 


Amendments 
In the said rules— 


after rule 135 insert 
namely:— 


the following rules, 


CHAPTER VIII 
Rules for Industrial Plots in Block ‘D’, Kalyani 


136. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary 
contained in the foregoing rules the following rules 
shall apply to buildings or workshops to ৮০০৩ con- 
structed on declared industrial plots at Kalyani. 


137. No residential quarters shall be allowed to 
be erected within the essential staff জা except 
for the purposes of the essential staff. Such essen- 
tial staff shall be defined by the Kalyani Authority. 


138. The minimum plinth height of non-residen- 
tial building in this area shall be 1 foot except in cases 
in which it may be otherwise specifically sanctioned. 


139. The buildings, workshops, etc., may cover 
threc-fourth of the area of the plot area leaving one- 
fourth area as open space including a minimum of 
6 ft. wide side space on two sides and open space of 
at least 10 ft. at the back and 10 ft. on the front. 


140. In case of corner pee 10 ft. front space 
shall be obligatory on both the road fronts and the 
side space shall be 6 ft. 


141. Every building proposed to be constructed 
within the premises, shall be in conformity with the 
provisions of West Bengal Factories Rules, 1958, as 
amended from time to time. 


142. All latrines, urinals, bathing places, etc., shall 
be connected with the public sewer. Plans for all 
such latrines and urinals shall be approved by the 
Chief Engineer, Public Health Engineering. 


143. The trade-effluents if required by the autho- 
rity, shall be treated prior to its discharge into the 
public sewer by adopting any of the methods or com- 
bination of methods, such as sedimentation, screen- 
ing, coagulation, chemical precipitation, activated 
Sludge process, bio-fithation method followed by 
chlorination, superchlorination or any other chemi- 
cal treatment as may be demanded by the authority. 


144.—The surface-water shall be discharged in the 
nearest road side drain. 


145. Nobody shall be allowed to tap underground 
resources without permission from the Authority. 


By order of the Governor, 
H. BANERJEE,

Subject: Realisation of dues of Rehabilitation 
Finance Administration, New Delhi, together 
with interest from their borrowers as arrears of 
land revenue. : 


No. TM/TF.IV/RFA/827.—2nd March 1962.— 
The Rehabilitation Finance Administration, New 
Delhi, having been merged with the Miunistry of 
Finance, it has been decided in supersession of this 
Office notification Nos. TM/TF/356, dated 4th April 
1952, and TM/TF/372, dated llth June 1952, that 
the dues of the Rehabilitation Finance Administration, 
New Delhi, should henceforth be remitted by the 
District Collectors direct to that office by means of 
Bank Drafts. The District Officers in West Bengal 
are, therefore, requested to ensure that the dues of 
the said Administration, realised in their districts 
during a month are remitted by Bank Draft to the 
“Government of India, Ministry of Finance (D.E.A.), 
Rehabilitation Finance Administration, Church Road, 
New Delhi”, by the 5th of the following month duly 
supported by schedules containing full particulars in 
the enclosed form. Any particulars regarding the 
name of the borrowers or the loan Account Numbers 
subsequently required by the Government of India, 
Rehabilitation Finance Administration, for proper 
adjustment of the amounts against the accounts of 
io respective loanees should be promptly supplied to 
them.

Subject: Draft corrections to the Central Govern- 
ments’ Compilation of Treasury Rules, Vol. I 
[First Edition, Fifth Reprint]. 


No. TM/23-3/61-62/825.—23rd February 1962.— 
All Treasury Officers and Sub-Treasury Officers in 
West Bengal, all Heads of offices of the Central 
Government under the audit control of this office 
and the Manager, Reserve Bank of India, Calcutta. 
may please note the following further corrections 
made to the Central Treasury Rules, Vol. 1 


Page 126 
No. 337 


Substitute the following for rule 430 


Rule 430: “All bills, cheques and other docu- 
ments passed by Treasury Officers and Offices of 
Accountants-General for payment at the Bank, as 
well as Interest Payment Orders, etc., being non- 
negotiable instruments, warrant special precaution on 
the part of the Bank in the matter of identification 
of the payee. All such claims have normally to be 
presented by the payee personally, but where pay- 
ment is desired to be made to an endorsee (other 
than a banker) or a messenger, the provisions otf 
rule 30302) or 437, as the case mav be, should he 
strictly followed by the Drawing Officer. The Bank 
will not, however, disburse payments of such claims 
unless the Bank is satisfied about the identity of the 
person receiving payment as attested by the Drawing 
Officer in accordance with rule 303(2) or 437, as the 
case may be. The Bank shall also verify before 
making the payment that the signature of the 
Drawing Officer attesting the payees’ signature tallies 
ns that on the bill as passed by the Treasurv 

cer.” 


Page 54 
No. 338. 


Substitute the following for rule 180(1) 


Rule 18008): “When a bill is presented by a 
person who is not the Drawing Officer himself or his 
duly authorised Agent (banker), he shall be required 
to produce a letter, in Form TR72, authorising him 
to receive payment. The signature of the messenger 
or his thumb impression, if illiterate, shall be taken 
on the as a proof that the messenger actually 
received the money on behalf of the Drawing Officer,”

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 
ORDERS 


AWARD 


Thereafter the workmen represented by the 
Associated Pigments Workers’ Union filed the 
written statement on 19th July 1961 signed and 
verified by one Shri Ram Babu Saha described as 
the President of the aforesaid Union. 


The employers, i.e., Messrs. Associated Pigments 
Ltd. (No. 2) then filed the written statement on 
28th December 1961 duly signed and verified by 
Shri J. P. Narain described as the Factory Manager 
of the Industry. 


The Company authorised their Labour Adviser, 
Shri J. R. Jain, to represent them in the proceed- 
ings before the Tribunal. 


After several adjournments the dispute was fixcd 
for positive hearing on 20th February 1962. In the 
meantime on 8th February 1962 a petition was filed 
by the Company stating therein that a tripartite 
settlement through the intervention of the Concilia- 
tion Officer had been arrived at between the parties 
on 12th January 1962. The Company along with 
the petition filed a copy of the memorandum of 
settlement which had been arrived at between the 
parties. It appears from the memorandum of 
settlement that it was duly signed for the work- 
men by Shri. Ram Babu Saha, President of the 
Union, Md. Hadish, Secretary of the Union and Tej 
Pratap Singh, workman, and on behalf of the 
employers it was signed by Shri J. P. Narain, Factory 
Manager and Shri J. R. Jain, Labour Adviser. It is 
clearly stated in paragraph 5 of the memorandum 
of settlement that the workmen entering into the 
Settlement are not interested in pursuing the case 
before the Tribunal. It is also to be noted that in 
spite of the fact that the memorandum of settle- 
ment was filed on 8th February 1962, none on behalf 
of the workmen came forward to challenge the 
memorandum of settlement or, otherwise, to pro- 
ceed with the case. Apparently, the memorandum 
of settlement is signed by the proper repre- 
sentatives of the parties. Therefore, the posi- 
tion is that in accordance with the settlement made 
between the parties, the workmen represented by 
the Union as mentioned in the order of reference 
are not willing to pursue the dispute and wish that 
the proceedings might be dropped and that a “no 
dispute” award might be passed. I accordingly pass 
a “no dispute” award. 


K. K. MITRA, 
Judge, 
Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 22nd February 1962.

of their misdeeds. Thus, in short, the case of the 
Company is that these four workers were never 
dismissed or discharged as alleged, but they were 
simply absenting themselves from work and thus 
abandoned the employment. 


Other facts will appear from the body of the 
award that follows: 


Decisions 


Before considering the issue on merit, I must 
consider the preliminary objection raised on behalf 
of the Company in respect of the maintainability 
of the reference itself. ا1‎ is urged that the present 
dispute is an individual dispute and not = an 
industrial dispute, and so this Tribunal has no 
jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the matter in issue. It 
is contended that the Union which has taken up the 
cause of the workman has got no representative 
character to raise the dispute. The workmen 
concerned are being represented by Calcutta Leather 
Workers’ Union, and this Union is undoubtedly not 
a Union confined to the employees of this particular 
concern or this particular employer. The present 
workers concerned are no doubt employees of the 
leather section or leather unit of the present 
employer, and the Union in question is an omnibus 
Union for the leather workers of the Calcutta region. 
The evidence is that workers of about 135 such 
Companies are members of this Union. An 
upplication (vide Ext. A) purported to have been 
signed by certain employees of Shri M. A. Sultan 
has been filed before me and the contention of the 
Company is that most of the employees of the 
Company are not members of the said Union, and 
thus the cause of these four workmen was 0٥۶ 
taken up or supported by the workers of the 
concern. Four witnesses have been examined before 
me on behalf of the Company, and only one of them 
SayS something in this connection, and he is 

-P.W. 1, Shri Gani. He says that he is not a 
member of the said Union. He 81509 adds in his 
examination-in-chief that Ram Nagina, Sukdeo, 
Hariram and Jhari Ram also are not members of 
that Union. The application (Ext. A) is purported 
to have been signed by about twenty persons. But 
in his cross-examination, Shri Gani says that he 
never saw the Membership Register of the Union 
and that he thinks (thus simply surmises) that the 
said four persons are not members of the Union. 
Thus 1 have reasons to believe that the witness Gani 
has no personal knowledge or competence to say 
that the said four persons are not really members 
of the Union. None of those four persons have 
been examined before me. Shri Gani was one of the 
three coolies employed by Shri Sultan at the relevant

The only issue referred.to this Tribunal for

AWARD 


Briefly stated, the case of the workmen in their 
written statement is this: Messrs. M. A. Sultan & 
Co. 18 a proprictory concern—the proprietor being 
Shri M. A. Sultan. Shri Sultan carries on manu- 
facture of leather goods under the name and style 
of Messrs. M. A. Sultan & Co. Lately the proprietor 
changed the signboard of the firm and named it as 
Messrs. S. Mahmood & Co. and this change in the 
name of the firm has been with an ulterior motive. 
Nevertheless, Shri Sultan continues to ০৪ the 
proprietor thereof. The present four workmen were 
dismissed previously also by the present employer 
and an industrial dispute was raised 11) that 
connection. The local First Labour Court was, 
however, pleased to direct reinstatement of all of 
them. The Management was also directed to pay 
the said workmen their entire back wages for the 
period of their forced unemployment. But despite 
the award of the First Labour Court, the employer 
failed to reinstate the workmen concerned or pay 
their back wages in terms of the award. So, these 
workmen had to move the Labour Directorate, and 
on the intervention of the Conciliation Officer only 
they were reinstated on 15th November 1958. The 
workmen had to take steps for realisation of their 
dues also in terms of the award. On Ist January 
1959 these workers as usual went to the factory to 
join their work, but the Management did not allow 
them to enter into the workshop. The Manage- 
ment further told the workers that they had heen 
dismissed from service. No charge-sheet was issued 
against these workers nor was any enquiry held 
against them. آ٥‎ reason even’ was assigned for 
their dismissal and, hence the present dispute. 


The Company, on the other hand, inter alia, 
alleges in its written statement that the present 
Union has got no representative character to raise 
the present dispute and thus the dispute is not an 
industrial onc. As to merits of the case, the 
Company’s case is that the present workers after 
their reinstatement in terms of the previous award 
intentionally set fire to certain properties of the 
Company on 30th December 1958 and _ caused 


damage to the extent of Rs. 500. The Company 
lodged an information with the Police in this 
connection and subsequently filed a_ regular 


complaint before the Criminal Court. On the final 
date of hearing, however, the Management failed to 
appear in person before the Criminal Court and did 
not proceed with the case. It is alleged that the 
Company has been paying back wages to the workers 
in terms of the previous award in monthly instalment 
of Rs. 80 and denositing the same with the Provincial 
State Bank of India. It is further added that the 
workers in question did not turn up to join their 
duties after the said fire on 30th December 1958, 
and presumably they were afraid of the consequences

order of reference, as it stands, prima facie shows 
that the Government is satisfied that there has been 
dismissal actually, and I am required to see if the 
dismissal is at all justified. The case of the work- 
men alsq is that they have been arbitrarily dismissed 
or discharged verbally by the proprietor without any 
charge-sheet or انس‎ and for no fault or offence 
of theirs. The employer, on the other hand, 
contends that the workmen concerned were never 
dismissed or discharged as alleged. It is added that 
after an incident of outbreak of fire in the factory 
premises on 30th December 1958 the workers failed 
to report themselves for duty, kept themselves 
absent from duty without Icave or permission and 
without showing any cause whatsoever, and thus 
forfeited their licn on the employment. It is not 
in dispute that these four workmen were permanent 
employees of this concern. It is nobody's cage that 
any charge-sheet was issued against these persons on 
or after 30th December 1958 in respect of any 
offence or that they were dismissed or discharged 
after any departmental enquiry. It is also not in 
dispute that they worked for this employer at least 
till 30th December 1958, and that they did not work 
or were not allowed to work from Ist January 
1959. The question is whether the employer really 
discharged or dismissed them and thus refused to 
employ them after 315 December 1958 or whether 
the workmen voluntarily absented themselves for 
any reason from 30th December 1958. All the four 
workers have identical and common case on the 
point. They allege that they had worked as usual 
till 315 December 1958, but they were refused 
employment from Ist January 1959 by the employer 
for extraneous reasons only. The Company alleges 
that the workmen concerned after their reinstate- 
ment in accordance with ‘a previous award 
intentionally set fire to certain properties (some 
leather goods) of the Company on 30th December 
1958 with an evil motive and thus caused damage to 
the extent of Rs. 500 and thereafter they started 
absenting themselves from duty without any notice 
to the employer. 


Thus while the workers allege that the Manage- 
ment purposely refused employment to them, the 
Management alleges that the workers intentionally 
withdrew themselves from work and absented them- 
Selves after setting fire to some leather goods. It 
may be mentioned here that the Management filed 
a criminal case also against these four workmen 
under section 427, I.P.C., but this case was not 
proceeded with, and the accused were all discharged 
under section 259, Cr.P.C. No  charge-sheet was 
issued. by the Management against them and they 
were not found guilty by any domestic tribunal also 
The criminal case, it appears, was filed long after 
the alleged occurrence. The Union 170 alreadv 
moved the Labour Commissioner in the matter on 
Ist January 1959, If the workers themselves decided 
to abandon the work voluntarily as alleged by the 
Management, they surely would not have gone so 
rromptly to the Union and complained to the 
Labour Department without waiting for the reaction 
of the Management in respect of the incident of fire. 
Whatever be the incident on 30th December 1958, 
the Union was approached within a day or two and 
by Ist January 1959 the Union had already taken 
up the cause and wrote to the Laboug Commissioner. 
Thus this conduct of the workmen definitely 
militates against the probability of the Company's 
story of voluntary rclinquishment of job by the 


the leather factory. It is also clear accordingly that 
some of the signatories thereof were not the 
employees of Shri Sultan at the relevant time. On 
the other hand, a register has been produced by the 
Union to show that nine workers of this leather 
factory (including the workmen concerned) were 
members of the said Union. None of these nine 
employces has been examined by the Company to 
say that he was not a member of the Union. The 
name of Ram Nagina appears in the said petition, 
but it is not proved properly if all or any one of 
the persons named therein actually signed the same. 
Shri Gani'’s evidence is vague and not sufficient to 
prove this aspect of the matter or the genuineness 
of the signatures and thumb impressions thereof. 
The Seeretary of the Union swears that Shri Nagina 
is still a member of the Union. So, I cannot attach 
much importance to this petition (vide Ext. A). The 
General Secretary of the Union swears that at least 
Seven workers of the leather factory in question 
were members of the Union at the relevant time. 
The number of workers in’ the factory evidently 
fluctuated at different times, and accordingly the 
number of Union members also may have fluctuated 
at different points of time. But this much is clear 
that most of the workers of the leather factory 
were members of the Union at the relevant time. 
It is also clear that most of the workers of this 
leather factory were Hindus at the relevant time. 
So, there is no substance in the contention that the 
Union which has espoused the cause of these four 
aggrieved workers is or was not sufficiently 
representative. According to Shri Parash Ram and 
Shri Ekadashi Ram, three of the workers of this 
leather factory (besides the aggrieved workers) were 
also consulted in the matter of this dispute and they 
also supported the cause and went with the workmen 
concerned to the Union office to report about the 
dismissal in question. So, there is not the least 
doubt that the majority of the workers of this 
particular leather factory supported the cause and 
moved the Union to take up the case with the 
authorities. In short, I find that at the relevant 
time there were 7/8 workers including the workmen 
concerned in the leather factory in question, and at 
least seven of these workers made a common cause 
and moved the Union actively. So, a very large 
section of the employees of this particular industry 
having Supported the cause, the particular dispute of 
the four aggrieved workers has actually been 
transformed into an industrial dispute. Even if I 
assume that Shri Nagina, who is still an employee 
of this very Compary, no longer supports the case 
of the workmen conccrned for some reason, yet the 
dispute cannot be any longer held to be an individual 
dispute, because he had lent such support when the 
dispute was initiated. If some supporting workmen 
subsequently resile from their previous stand and 
withdraw their support during the pendency of the 
proceedings, the jurisdiction of the Tribunal is not 
legally affected thereby. However, I think, the 
majority of the workmen of the relevant time really 
supported the dispute irrespective of the question 
whether Nagina also supported the same or not. 
So, the reference is valid and this Tribunal has 
every jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the matter in 
dispute.

Tribunal for adjudication. The point for adjudica- 
tion is whether there was any _ justification for 
dismissal of the four workmen concerned. The

question of the justifiability of the dismissal of an 
individual workman, namely, Shri Upendra Nath 
Haldar, is an individual dispute. Section 2(k) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act which defines an industrial 
dispute is in these terms—* ‘industrial dispute’ 
means any dispute or difference between employers 
and employers or between employers and workmen, 
or between workmen and workmen, which 05 con- 
nected with the employment or non-employment or 
the terms of employment or with the conditigns of 
labour of any particular person.” The use of the 
olural number in the word “workmen” does not of 
৩0:5৩ necessarily mean that 01) industrial dispute 
must always be between one employer and a number 
ot workmen. The use of the plural may be accounted 
101 in either of two ways. It may be that the plural 
number had to be used in the word “workmen” 
because of the use of the plural number in the word 
“employers”. It may also be that the plural number 
was used because the plural includes the singular 
also according to the rule of construction laid down 
in section 13(2) of the General Clauses Act which 
provides that in all Central Acts and Regulations 
unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or 
context, words in the singular shall include the plural 
und vice versa. If, therefore, the question is looked 
at purely as a matter of the language, as used in this 
definition, “industrial dispute” would not necessarily 
exclude an individual dispute from its ambit. But 
there is the whole scheme of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. and the background in which this Act had to be 
enacted. In the light of that background and_ ۶ 
whole scheme اہ‎ the Act it has been held in a 
number of cases that an individual dispute is exclud- 
ed from the definition of “industrial dispute,” 
although even an individual dispute can ০০ trans- 
formed into an industrial dispute if a majority of 
the workmen of the particular employer or a consi- 
derable section of these employees takes up _ the 
cause of the individual employee primarily concern- 
ed in the dispute and makes the dispute their own. 
The earliest Supreme Court decision on this point is 
the case of D. N. Banerjee versus P. R. Mukherjee 
1952, VI, F.J.R. 443 and the latest case on the point

Hindu, Bombay and another. That was a 85 in

workman. At the relevant time the Management of

was a member. The Union had other journalists 
working in different establishments as its members. 
The validity of the reference was successfully chal- 
lenged by the Management of The Hindu before the 
Industrial Tribunal on the ground that there was 
121 an individual dispute which was not supported 
by an appreciable number of the emplovees of The 
Hindu, Bombay. Their Lordships of the Supreme

Mangement except where there are compelling cir- 
cumstances to justify such a step, namely, when 
there is want of good faith, when there is victimisa- 
tion or unfair labour practice or when the Manage- 
ment is guilty of a basic error of violation of principle 
of natural justice, as 1910 down by the Supreme Court 
in Indian Iron & Steel Co, Ltd. versus their workmen 
(1958-II L.L.J. 260) and reiterated in 1৬101617260 & 
Co. Ltd. versus its workmen (1959-II, L.L.J. 285). It 
must accordingly be found that the order of dismis- 
Sa! is justified and the employee is entitled to no 
relief. 


But as I have already found, the reference in itself 
is invalid. It has thus to be rejected on that ground 
and there cannot be any award on the point referred 
to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Lictated and corrected by me. 


5. N. GUHA ROY, Judge. 


S. N. GUHA ROY,

24th May 1960 onwards there is little excuse. On 
top of that, there is the fact that Shri Upendra Nath 
Haldar appears to have been a_ habitual absentee. 
shri Nani Gopal Dutta prepared Ext. 6, the state- 
ment of his absences during the years 1958-59 and 
1959-60. In 1958-59 he appears to have been absent 
altogether for 71 days and during the year 1959-60 
he appears to have been absent altogether for 58 
days. According to the evidence of Shri Nani Gopal 
Dutta, for a part of these absences he was on leave. 
Under section 12 of the Bengal Shops and Establish- 
ments Act, a person employed in an establishment 
for public entertainment or amusement is entitled 
for every 12 months’ continuous employment to 
privilege leave on full pay for 14 days, to sick leave 
on half pay for 14 days and to casual leave on full 
pay for 10 days and privilege leave can be accumu- 
lated up to a maximum of not more than 28 days 
and sick leave can be accumulated up to a maximum 
of not more than 56 days and casual leave cannot be 
accumulated at all. It appears that Shri Upendra 
Nath Haldar was absent in 1958-59 and 1959-60 for 
71 and 58 days respectively. Although a part of 
these absences was accounted for by the leave that 
was sanctioned to him the whole of it was not. It 
was open to the Management to take those facts 
into consideration in awarding the punishment for 
the atfence which he committed by absenting him- 
Self without leave from the 24th May 1960 onwards. 
Although therefore the Tribunal if it was left to 
take its own view might not have awarded this 
punishment for his absence from the 24th May 1960 
onwards, coupled with the fact that he had absented
