The Government of West Bengal by its Labour 
Department, order No. 1123-1.R./IR/10L-57/61, 
dated 10th March 1961, referred to this Tribunal an 
industrial dispute between Messrs. B. D. Engineering 
Works, 2/12 Ultadanga Main Road, Calcutta-4 
(hereafter referred to as the Company), and their 
workmen represented by Peco Engineering Mazdur 
Union, 1 Gauritbari Lane, Calcutta-4 (hereafter 
referred to as the Union), for adjudication under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


The only issue referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication in this case runs as follows: 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Manya Kumar 
Mondal and Shri Mantu Ranjen Das 15 
justified? To what relief, if any, are they 
entitled? 


AWARD 


Briefly stated, the case of the workmen concerned 
in their written statement is this. The employees of 
the opposite party Company were very much ill-paid, 


| PART I 


case, and on the last date of hearing the workmen 
in the absence of any Union official engaged a 
lawyer at the last moment to conduct the case. 
Thus it is more than clear that the Union concerned 
was never a Union of the employees of the present 
employer, and that the Union is really a Union of 
the employees, of another particular employer. No 
worker of the present Company ever became member 
of this Union so long he had retained relationship 
with the present employer. So, the support, if any, 
of the Peco Engineering Mazdur Union is not 
sufficient to transform the individual dispute of these 
two workmen into an industrial dispute. There is 
no evidence or legal presumption in favour of these 
two workers to show that the dispute of these two 
workers was ever supported by any section of the 
workers of this particular industry or the employees 
of this particular employer. It is also not in evidence 


that any section of the 010 91010105985 of this 
employer ever supported the cause of these two 
workmen. Thus in any view of the case, the 


present dispute is not an industrial dispute, simply 
because a Union purports to represent the employees 
concerned, the dispute does not cease to be an 
individual dispute. The Union concerned is not 
connected with the cmployer, and there cannot be 
any presumption that the employees of this particular 
industry do support the dispute. If the Union 
would have been a Union of this particular industry 
alone, there might have been a presumption—though 
rebuttable. In the case of Express Newspapers (P.) 
Ltd. (A.ILR. 1959 Cal. 265) his lordship has held that 
a Union unconnected with the employer, the employ- 
ment or the particular industry concerned cannot 
transform an industrial dispute into an industrial 
dispute. In the case of Dimakuchi Tea Estate vs. 
Their workmen (1958 I L.L.J. 500 S.C.) their lord- 
ships of the Supreme Court also have held that the 
person regarding whom the dispute is raised must be 
one in whose employment, non-employment, terms 
of employment or conditions of labour, the parties 
to the dispute have a direct or substantial interest. 
In the present case, the Peco Engineering Mazdur 
Union have no direct or substantial interest in the 
employment or non-employment of the workmen 
concerned, because the members of the Union are 
unconnected with this particular industry or the 
particular employer. So, I finally hold that this 
dispute is not an industrial dispute and consequently 
the reference itself is invalid, and this Tribunal has 
no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the dispute. So. 
I intend to express no final opinion on the merit of 
the issue. | 


However, ا‎ may incidentally mention that iboth 
the parties have adduced evidence before me on the 
merit of the issue also. It is the case of the Manage- 
ment that these two workmen voluntarily abandoned 
their employment and no opportunity was given to 
the Management to dismiss them. The evidence 15 
that Shri Mandal committed or attempted to commit 
a theft ٠ respect of three pieces of brass rods and 
kept the same concealed under his machine. The

Mandal’s fellow workers intervened in the matter 
and requested the Management not 00 start a 
prosecution but allow him to vacate the job. Shri 
Mondal left the job voluntarily and did not report 
for further duties. As to Shri Das, he was only an 
apprentice worker for about four months. After the 
above incident of Shri Mondal, Shri Das once abused

employer concerned, the prima facie individual 
dispute cannot be transformed into an_ industrial 
dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. It has been held in numerous cases by 
Superior Courts that a dispute between an individual 
employee and his employer cannot be an industrial 
dispute unless the cause has been espoused by the 
other workmen of the cstablishment or at least by 
a substantial or appreciable section thereof and it 
becomes a collective dispute. So, according to the 
accepted view of law on the point, the dispute of 
these two particular employees with their employer 
cannot be an industrial dispute unless a substantial 
section of the employees of the same employer 
espouse their cause. There are at present 5/6 
employees only under the employer concerned, and 
it is the positive evidence of the Company that none 
of the present employees actually support the cause 
of these two workmen. This evidence not only 
goes unchallenged, but the workmen concerned also 
admit before me in their deposition that no other 
workmen of B. D. Engineering Works are members 
of the Union which took up their cause before the

From the deposition of Shri Mantu§ Ranjan Das

in the matter. Shri Das does not say that he at all

even according to the workers concerned, the Union 
represents Shri Mandal alone, and not both the 
aggrieved workers. The Company challenges the 
allegation that either of these two workers ever 
became a member of the said Union. Shri Mondal 
concedes in his cross-examination that he has

a Union of the workers of that particular industry

AWARD 


This is an application under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act by Shri Sewji Singh, a work- 
man of Messrs. Hindusthan Gas Company Ltd. The 
allegation in the application is that the Company 
dismissed him from service on the pretext of 
accepting his resignation and this fact was intimated 
to him by the Company. The Company in its written 
Statement pleaded that the application was not 
maintainable because the Company’s action in 
accepting the workman’s resignation would not bring 
the facts within the purview of section 33A and 
secondly that there was actually a resignation by the 
workman and when the workman denied this, the 
Signature to the letter of resignation was examined 
by a handwriting expert Shri P. K. Bakshi at the 
instance of the Company and it was found by him 
to be the signature of the same person as the writer 
of the admitted signatures also placed before him 
for examination. On the 2nd of February 1962 the 
date of hearing was fixed for 16th February 1962 and 
Shri Sewji Singh in token of his having seen the 
order signed against the order in the order-sheet. 
Even then on !6th February 1962, there was no 
appearance for him and Shri P. Dasgupta who was 
to have appeared for him told me that he was not 
able to contact his client. It also transpired on that 
day that Shri P. Dasgupta had not filed any letter 
of authority. The case was then fixed for the 2150 
of February 1962 for hearing so as to give the work- 
man a chance of appearing and prosecuting his 
application. Even then, the workman did not turn 
up on the date of hearing. Shri P. Das Gupta came 
along on the 215 and told me that he had failed to 
contact him. The matter had therefose to be heard 
ex-parte. Two witnesses were examined for the 
Company. The first is Shri Tarit Kumar Bakshi, 
the handwriting expert, who examined the signature 
purporting to be that of Shri Sewji Singh to the 
letter of resignation, Ext. 1. along with a number of 
signatures of Shri Sewji Singh before his alleged 
resignation. The expert's opinion is that these were 
all written by the same man, and he has also said 
this in his evidence. The other witness examined 
for the Company, is Shri P. I Tain. the Production 
Engineer, who merely proves the signatures of the 
Manager to certain relevant gocuments including 
Exts. 3 and 4. By Ext. 3, dated the 10th July 196], 
Shri Singh was told that his letter of resignation, 
dated the 8th of Julv 1961, had been accepted with 
effect from the 11٤١ of July 1961. Exhibit 4 is 
another letter, dated the 20th of Tuly 1961, by which 
the Factory Manager asked Shri Sewji Singh to 
deposit his attendance-card and other relevant 
documents confirming and establishing his identity 
as a workman of the establishment. The first was 


Shri Dhirendra Nath Chatterjee, one of the partners 
of the concern, and failed to report for work there- 
after. Of course, no charge-sheet was issued against 
either of them and no enquiry also was held. But 
as the evidence stands, prima facie, there were 
definite charges against these two men and they had 
left the job, it is alleged, before any charge-sheet 
could be issued. However, as ] have no jurisdiction 
to adjudicate on the matter in issue or interfere 
with the Management decision in this case, ] come 
to no definite finding on the point. 


In view of my above decision, I may at once find 
that the workmen concerned are not entitled to any 
relief in the present case before this Tribunal.

F Tribunal 


An industrial dispute between Messrs. Bengal 
Rolling Mills, Sodepore, 24-Parganas, and their work- 
men represented by the Bengal Rolling Mill Workers’ 
Union. 292/7 Upper Chitpore Road, Calcutta-5, over 
the following issue, has been referred to this Tribu- 
nal for adjudication, by the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, Order No. 2931-LR./IR/ 
LOL-109/61, dated the 5th June 1961. 


Issue 


1. Whether the discharge of Shri Prabhu Singh is 
justified? To what relief, if any, is he entitled? 


acknowledged by Ext. 3(2), dated the 12th of July 
1961, and the second was acknowledged by 
Ext. 4(2), dated the 22nd of July 1961. The Sewii 
Singh appears to have written the letter, dated the 
31st of July 1961 (Ext. 5) to the Company saying 
that he had not actually resigned from his service 
as falsely and maliciously alleged. It is strange that 
although Shri Sewji Singh received the notice of the 
acceptance of his letter of resignation by the 
Company on the 12th of July 1961, he did not write 
to the Company till the 3150 of July 1961 alleging 
that he had not actually resigned. This, together 
with the fact that Shri Sewji Singh does not now 
turn up to prosecute his application seems to me 10 
prove conclusively that Shri Sewji Singh did in fact 
submit his letter of resignation (Ext. 1) and that 
the handwriting expert is right in his opinion that 
Ext. 1(1) is the signature of Shri Sewji Singh who 
had also signed the other documents produced before 
him for examination. In the circumstances, on the 
merits it must be found that Shri Sewji Singh had. 
actually resigned and what the Company accepted 
was in fact Shri Sewji Singha’s resignation. - 


The next question is whether this application is 
maintainable. Section 33A presupposes the contra- 
vention of the provisions of section 33 which again 
prohibits the alteration of the conditions of service 
of a workman during the pendency of a reference 
under section 10. Such an alteration of the 
conditions of service must mean an alteration by 
the Company’s action independent of any action on 
the part of the workman concerned. If the Company 
accepts the resignation of an employee what the 
Company does is really to give effect to something 
which is done by the employee himself, and it 
cannot be said to be the Company’s independent 
action. There are two steps into termination of a 
workman’s service by the employer’s acceptance of 
his resignation. The first of these two steps is the 
voluntary resignation by the workman and the 
employer's acceptance of this resignation constitutes 
only the second and final step with which his employ- 
ment terminates. Obviously, the second and final 
step would be impossible without the first. Hence, 
such termination of a workman's service is really 
caused by the workman’s voluntary act of resignation, 
the employer playing merely a secondary role in the 
matter when he accepts the workman's resignation. 
The position, however, may well be different when 
the 11 Sosa does not submit any resignation 
but the Employer received a letter of resignation 
purporting to bear the workman's signature and 
believing it to be his genuine signature, the 
employer accepts the resignation. The whole thing 
in such a case is due to a mistake and what the 
effect of that mistake on the ultimate termination 
of the workman’s employment would be, need not 
be considered here, because on the facts found this 
question does not arise. 


The termination of the service of the workman in 
this case, is, as already found, the result not of the 
independent action of the Company but the result 
primarily of the action of the workman himself and 
what the Company did was merely to accept what 
the workman had done. This view is supported by 
the view of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta, 
in the case between Messrs. Macfarlane & Company 
Ltd. and Shri Sudhir Kumar Dhar and Ors., 1953 
L.A.C. 695. On the preliminary point, therefore, it 
must be found that the application of Shri Sewji 
Singh under section 33A is not maintainable at all.

and their workmen to the First Industrial Tribunal

pute Shri Bibhuti Singh Roy, a workman of the 
above Company, filed a complaint under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act before that Tribunal 
on 14th November 1957. That Tribunal, as authori- 
sed by the Government of West Bengal nctification 
No. 1916-I.R./IR/3A-1/58, dated 13th May 1958, 
transferred the above complaint to this Court on 9th 
June 1959 for disposal. 


Upon receipt of the order of reference on 12th 
June 1961, notices were issued upon the parties for 
appearance and for filing written statements. 


After service of notices the workmen represented 
bv the Bengal Rolling Mill Workers’ Union filed the 
written statement on 100) July 1961 duly signed and 
verified by Shri Nepal Roy, described as President of 
the aforesaid Union. The case as made out by the 
Union in the written statement is to the effect that 
Shri Prabhu Singh who was working as durwan in 
the said Company had been wrongfully dismissed on 
the 16th February 1961], after he had put in eleven 
months continuous service with a spotless service 
record. The Union along with the written statement 
filed a copy of the order of dismissal given to the 
workman by the employer. 


Messrs. Bengal Rolling Mills Ltd., thereafter, filed 
the written statement on 14th August 1961 duly 
signed and verified by one Shri M. M. Singh described 
as Works Manager of the concern. It is contended 
by the Company that Shri Prabhu Singh was appoint- 
ed as durwan on 12th September 1960 on probation 
for a period of six months and in course of his pro- 
bationary period the employer received adverse 
report regarding the work of the durwan from the 
immediate superior officer. It is further alleged that 
the durwan Prabhu Singh flouted the orders of the 
Head Jamadar on many dates as_ specified in the 
written statement. Consequently when it was found 
that Shri پت‎ did not improve his conduct in spite 
of the verbal warnings given to him, the Company 
had no other alternative but to discharge him from 
service as he was found unsuitable for the job. It is 
thus contended that the employer took the action 
against Shri Singh acting bona fide and the workman 
concerned was still in his probationary period when 
the discharge took place. 


After completion of preliminary stages the case 
was fixed for hearing on 29th November 1961. On 
that date none appeared on behalf of the Union. On 
29th December 1961 Shri M. M. Singh representing 
the employer filed an application for time on _ the 
ground that a talk of settlement was going on and 
the said prayer was allowed ex-parte. Next the case 
was adjourned to 27th January 1962 and on_ that 
date an application was filed by Shri Ashu Mukherjee, 
the Vice-President of the Union, praying an adjourn- 
ment to 28th February 1962. The prayer was allow- 
ed. The case was fixed for hearing on 28th February 
1962. On that date none appeared for the workman. 
The employer was present before the Tribunal. In 
the circumstances I find that the Union is not 
earnest to proceed with the dispute. Prima facie it 
appears that the employer’s action is justified inas- 
much as the said workman had been discharged 
during the period of probation on the ground that 
his service during the period of probation was found 
to be unsatisfactory. Be that as it is, when the 
Union does not proceed with the case, the dispute 
ends in a “no dispute” award. 


K. K. MITRA, 


Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 


The 12th March 1962.

No. 964-I.R./IR /11L-276/59.—19th March 1962... 
Whereas under the Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, order No. 4177-LR./IR/llle 
276/59, dated the 27th August 1959, the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Spences Hotel ا٤.‎ 
4 Wellesley Place, Calcutta, and their workmen 
represented by Spences Hotel Employecs’ Union, 


{Part | 


i উন পি লি ++‏ ا 


which the Company has informed the complainant 
that it was not possible for the Company to extend 
leave up to 4th March 1961. In that letter the 
Company also informed the complainant that it had 
been necessary for the Company to employ another 
durwan. The Company contends that the service 
of the complainant was terminated according to rule 
9d) of the Standing Orders of the Company. 
Rule 9(d) reads as follows: 


“If any workman remains absent beyond the 
period for which leave has been originally granted 
or subsequently extended, he shall lose his lien 
on his appointment. The Managing Director 
may, however, condone at 1115 discretion such 
absence if (1) the workman concerned returns 
within eight days of the expiry of leave and gives 
an explanation to his satisfaction of the inability 
to return before the expiry of the leave.” 


That rule clearly says that if a workman remains 
absent beyond the period of sanctioned leave, he 
will lose his lien on his appointment. Loss of lien 
is not the same thing as termination of service. Loss 
of lien by a workman only justifies an employer to 
take action for the dismissal of a workman. It is 
on evidence that the complainant was in the enjoy- 
ment of a sanctioned leave up to 4th February 1961. 
The only question is about his absence after that 
date. In Ext. Al4 the Company has refused to 
extend the leave prayed for by the complainant; but 
the Company has not informed him that unless he 
joined by a certain date, his service would be 
terminated. It is true that when an _ employer 
terminates the service of an employee in accordance 
with the provisions of the Standing Orders which 
may be termed as conditions of service, it is not 
necessary to issue a charge-sheet, unless the 
termination of service is on account of a misconduct. 
I agree that the Company in the present case could 
terminate the service of the complainant in 
accordance with the rule 9(d) of the Standing Orders 
but the Company must satisfy me that it applied 
the above rule of the Standing Orders properly. 
The Company has produced copies of the corres- 
pondence that passed between it and the complainant. 
In some of the letters the Company has informed 
the complainant that another durwan was appointed 
in his place. But this was not sufficient. In my 
opinion the Company ought to have warned the 
complainant of its intention to dismiss 01 
complainant unless he turned up by a certain date. 
If the Company had given such a warning, it was 
quite likely that the complainant would have tried 
to join his duty by that date in spite of his illness 
or he might have made a representation which the 
Company could think reasonable. So in this case 
the complainant has been kept in the dark as to the 
threatened dismissal, and when he turned up to 
resume his duty, he was told that his service had 
been terminated. It is true that the Director of the 
Company offered him an employment in a sister 
concern. Whatever may be the reason or motive 
behind this offer, this offer cannot justify the 
previous dismissal. 


In view of the above considerations, I hold that 
the dismissal of the complainant Shri Asaibar Singh 
is unjustified. Hence I order that he should be 
reinstated as a durwan of the Spences Hotel Ltd. 
As the Company had allowed him leave for a very 
long period, I do not allow him any compensation 
for his forced idleness. 


992 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, MARCH 29, 1962 


sent two petitions on 7th March 1961 and 17th 
March 1961 requesting the Company to allow him 
to join his work. The Company wrote him a letter, 
dated 17th March 1961, to the cffect that he would 
have to convince the Director of the Company that 
he would do his duty faithfully and loyally. He 
replied on 18th March 1961 to the effect that he 
had done his duty faithfully and would continue to 
do so. Thereafter the Company remained silent and 
did not allow him to resume his duty. So the 
complainant has been virtually dismissed from 
service. An industrial dispute between the Company 
and its workmen was pending before this Court, 
viz., Second Labour Court. The Company did not 
apply to this Court for approval of its action nor 
did it pay one month’s wages to the complainant. 
Hence the complainant contends that the Company 
has contravened the provisions of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act and that its action in 
dismissing him is unjustified. 

The Company admits that the complainant was 
allowed leave from 2nd November 1960 and that the 
leave was later extended. But the Company denies 
that he was allowed leave up to 3rd March ۰

application inasmuch as there has been no contra-

The Company has also denied the other allegations 
of the workmen. 


Generally two issues require decision in a 
complaint under section 33A of the Act. They are: 


(1) the fact of contravention, and 
(2) the merits of the order of the employer. 


Decision

Disputes Act. There is no mention of any pending 
proceeding before this Tnbunal in the workman's 
application itself filed under section 33A. Thereupon 
the Company seriously questioned the maintainability 
of the present application in its written statement. 
In the evidence of the concerned workman also 
there 15 nothing to show that any proceeding was 
pending before this Tribunal at a time when there 
has been the alleged contravention of the provisions 
of section 33. The alleged contravention if there be 
any must take place during the pendency of a 
proceeding before this Tribunal. In the present 
case there is nothing to show that the alleged 
contravention took place during the pendency of a 
proceeding before this Tribunal. Thercfore, the 
present application is not maintainable.

(2) the person regarding whom the

From the above decision, it will be clear that an 
individual dispute will be transformed into an 
industrial dispute if the members of the Union 
concerned have a community of interest with the 
workman concerned or if they are vitally interested 
in the employment, non-employment, terms of 
employment or conditions of labour of the workman 
concerned. This matter was considered by his lord- 
ship of the Calcutta High Court in a case between 
Express Newspapers (P.) Ltd. vs. First Labour Court, 
West Bengal and Others (vide A.I.R. 1959 Cal., 265). 
His lordship observed in this connection as follows: 


“It is now finally settled that an individual 
dispute between an employer and one of his 
workmen is by itself not an industrial dispute 
which can be referred under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, but such an individual 
dispute might be transformed into an industrial 
dispute, provided that the cause of the particulars 
workman concerned is taken up by a majority 
of the workmen concerned in the particular 
industrial establishment or by a Union of sueh 
workmen. The Industrial Disputes Act is a 
legislation to ensure industrial harmony and 
when an individual case is taken up by a class of 
workmen then it becomes an industrial struggle 
and loses its limited scope. But a workman's 
case cannot be taken up by a Union unconnected 
with the employer or the industry concerned. 
The employer is not concerned with the work- 
men who are not in his employ. He _ cannot 
possibly have an industrial dispute or any dispute 
with such persons. The real test appears to be 
that as to whether the majority or a large portion 
of the workmen employed in the particular 
industry are concerned in the dispute or not. 
Where the Union is of the workmen employed 
in that particular industry, it may be presumed 
that when the union takes up the cause of an 
individual -workman it signifies a concerted 
action on the part of the workmen who are 
members of that Union. But it is not possible 
for a Union of workmen unconnected with the 
particular industry concerned to take up such a 
cause and transform it into an industrial dispute 
between a particular employer and his workmen. 
In an industrial dispute, it is not always for the 


employer to prove the facts relating to the 
representation by the Union of the workman 
concerned in the dispute. In 5001) cases, the 


ordinary rule of throwing the burden or onus 
should be followed, mainly as to who should fail 
if no evidence is given. When a workman is 
represented by a Union of the workmen of the 
employer or a large portion thereof, and the 
employer alleges that the Union does not 
represent the views of the majority of the work- 
men or a large portion thereof, then in the first 
instance it would be for him to prove the same. 
But if it is admitted or not disputed that the 
Union is not a Union of the workmen of the 
particular employer or industry and if there is

Decisions 
From what I have mentioned above, it will be 
clear that the Management raised a_ preliminary

reference itself. The learned lawyer fomthe Manage- 
ment urges before this Tribunal that the present 
dispute is only an individual dispute, and that it 
has not been transformed into an industrial dispute, 
even though the Hosiery Working Men’s Union is 
purported to have espaused the cause of the 
aggrieved workman. So, before J consider the issue 
on merit, I must consider this preliminary objection 
and see if the reference is at all valid. From the 
issue framed, it will be clear that the subject 
matter of the present dispute is the dismissal of Shri 
Biswanath Das. Thus the dispute is apparently 
between the individual worker and the employer. 
So, this individual dispute cannot be transformed 
into an industrial dispute, unless the cause of Shri 
Das is actually espoused by other workmen of the 
concern. Shri Das’s cause has been taken up and 
represented before this Tribunal by the Hosiery 
Working Men’s Union. As the very name of the 
Union suggests, it is an omnibus Union and not a 
Union of the workmen of this particular unit of 
industry. Further it is the definite case of the 
Management that the workmen of the present 
hosiery factory are not members of the said Union. 
It is contended that this Union does not represent 
a single workman of this factory. If this contention 
of the Management be correct, there is no escape 
from the conclusion that the Union has no locus 
Standi to espouse the cause of the workmen 
concerned and that it cannot raise any industrial 
dispute before this Tribunal. The expression 
“industrial dispute” has been defined in section 2(k) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. This definition, was 
considered by their lordships of the Supreme Court 
in a case between the ‘Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea 
Estate (Assam Cha Karmachari Sangha) and Dima- 
kucha Tea Estate’ reported in 1958 I L.L.J. page 500. 
There was considerable uncertainty regarding the 
meaning of the words “any person” used in the 
definition. Their lordships observed in this con- 
nection as quoted below: 


“the expression ‘any person’ in section 2(k) 
means a person in whose employment or non- 
employment or terms of employment or 
conditions of labour, the workmen as a class have 
a direct or substantial interest— with whom they 
have under the scheme of the Act a community 
of interest. Having regard to the scheme and 
objects of the Act and its other provisions, the 
expression ‘any person’ in section 2(k) of the Act 
must be read subject to such limitations and 
qualifications as arise from the context; the two 
crucial limitations are— 


(1) the dispute must be a real dispute 
between the parties to the dispute as intended 
in the first two parts of the definition clause, 
50 as to be capable of settlement on adjudication 
by one party to the dispute giving necessary 
relief to the other; and

evidence on record, whether adduced by the

Similar view has been expressed in a case between 
Mahaboob Shahi Kulbarga Mills Ltd. vs. K. Bittal 
Kamath and another (vide 1959 IT L.L.J. 196). In 
deciding this case, their lordships have observed as 
follows: 


“The crucial test to determine whether an 
individual dispute has been transformed into an 
industrial dispute as defined in the Act is to see 
whether the workmen who espouse the cause of 
the individual have any direct or substantial 
interest in the employment, non-employment or 
conditions of employment of that person. The 
mere fact that a trade union espouses the cause 
of the person will not furnish necessary nexus 
between the dispute of the parties to the dispute 
to convert his dispute into an industrial dispute 
as to give jurisdiction to an Industrial Tribunal 
to adjudicate upon the same.” 


These principles have been approved and confirmed 
by Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Bombay 
Union of working Journalists and _ others vs. 
“Hindoo” Bombay and another (21 F.J.R. 207).

in one voice that Shri Das used to work so badly 
that they came across with maximum number of 
defects in the hosiery products dealt with by him. 
These are questions of facts and I should not 
express any final opinion on the point in view of 
the decision already made. This much I can point 
out that Shri Das was warned in writing once on Ist 
June 1956 and again on 13th April 1957, and there 
is no other written warning after 1957 and before 
1960. It is alleged on behalf of the Management 
that in between 1957 and 1960 also several verbal 
warnings were given to Shri Das, but without any 
tangible effect on him. It is conceded by the 
Management and its witnesses also that defects are 
at times noticed in the work of other workmen as 
well, but it is alleged, Shri Das used to top the list 
of bad workers, and so the Management was 
compelled to take action against him. The Manage- 
ment contends that in spite of this, it was prepared 
to treat him sympathetically and give him three 
months’ time to improve his work. But he proved 
adamant in his attitude and refused to comply with 
the Company’s direction or improve his work. It is 
not unlikely that greater number of defects were 
noticed in his work, and this might have indirectly 
told upon the good name of the Company itself. 
But it is to be considered whether in the present 
case there should have been a discharge or 
termination of service pure and simple or outright 
dismissal without any formal enquiry. Shri Das 
served the Company for about eight years and all 
along he used to work as a Chainman. If he was 
tolerated for cight years 1 do not know why all on 
a sudden he was found so _ inefficient as to be 
discharged summarily without any enquiry and 
without any compensation. Be that as it may, as 
the dispute between the parties is not an industrial 
dispute, 1] have no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon 
the casc on merit. In any case, the workman 
concerned is not entitled to any relicf before this 
Tribunal. 


This is my award.

The Company raised a preliminary objection at 
the time of hearing that the reference was originally 
made to the First Labour Court and a further refer- 
ence to this Tribunal is illegal and not maintainable. 


Decision 


] first take up the preliminary objection raised by 
the Company. The Government first made a refer- 
ence under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act to the First Labour Court by Order No. 6630- 
I.R./IR/9L-6:'58, dated Ist December 1959. The 
First Labour Court was replaced by the Sixth Indus- 
trial Tribunal constituted under Notification No. 
3115-I.R./IR/3A-6/59, dated 215 June 1960, and 
was in consequence abolished by Notification No. 
3508-1.R. 'IR/3A-9/59, dated 11) July 1960.  Para- 
graph 4 of the present reference runs as follows: 
‘Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
by section 10(1)(d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased to refer 
to the said Sixth Industrial Tribunal the proceedings 
of the industrial disputes between the said Company 
and their workmen, relating to the matter specified in 
the Schedule below, for adjudication in supersession 
of the orders contained in Order No. 6630-1 / 
9L-6/58, dated Ist December 1959, referring the said 
dispute to the First Labour Court.” Now the ques- 
tion is whether the present reference to the newly 
constituted Tribunal is in respect of the proceedings 
of the First Labour Court or it is in respect of the 
dispute itself which was subsisting and surviving the 
abolition of the First Labour Court. In my opinion, 
the obvious answer to the question is that the present 
reference is in respect of the dispute which was 
subsisting and surviving the abolition of the First 
Labour Court. The abolition of the First Labour 
Court did not certainly extinguish the industrial dis- 
pute though the adjudication proceedings relating to 
that dispute before the First Labour Court were 
wiped off. The dispute having survived the abolition 
of the First Labour Court the Government was, in 
mv opinion, competent to make a fresh reference of 
that dispute to this Tribunal under section 10(1)(d) 
of the Act. I, therefore, hold that the reference is 
legal and maintainable. 


I now take up the matter in dispute. 


There was admittedly a demonstration by Sreeman 
Bhujel and some other persons and shouting of 
slogans. There was a demand for supply of firewood. 
The Manager says that firewood was being supplied 
to the workers and there could be no agitation in 
respect of supply of firewood. [ do not see any- 
thing to disbelieve the Manager on this point. There 
is no Satisfactory evidence on the side of the Union 
that the Company did not supply firewood to the 
workers in the garden. P.W. 1 Shri Nani Bhatta- 
Charjee, the President of the Union, said: “The 


This reference is in respect of termination of em- 
ployment of Srceman Bhujel, a workman in the Tea 
Garden of the Dalmore Tea Estate, Jalpaiguri (here- 
inafter called the Company). 


The admitted facts are as follows: 


Sreeman Bhujel was a workman in the garden of 
the Company for a number of years. The Manager 
of the garden warned him on two  occasions—on 
11٠٦5 February 1955 and Ist June 1956—on allega-

there was a demonstration by a number of Com-

shouted slogans demanding bonus for the year 1955 
and supply of firewood. The Manager Md. Tod, 
who was proceeding towards his bungalow from the

officer, who happened to be there cleared the way 
for him to proceed, the Manager drove to 1115 
bungalow. Next day, charge-sheets were given to 
Sreeman Bhujel and four other employees and all the 
five employees replied to the charge-sheets on 9th 
July 1955. Enquiries were held and the Manage- 
ment having found Sreeman Bhujel guilty of gross 
misconduct removed him from service. 


The Union alleges that Sreeman Bhujel was the 
the Assistant Secretary of the Garden Committee of 
the Union and the Company victimised him for his 
Union activities. It is the case of the Union that 
the two warnings to Sreeman Bhujel in 1955 and 
1956 were given to him without giving him any 
opportunity of defending himself. Regarding the 
incident on the 2nd July 1957, the Union’s case 15 
that there was a simple demonstration of the work-

supply of firewood, that the demonstrators assem- 
bled outside the office premises on the P.W.D. Road 
and they never obstructed the Manager from proceed: 
ing to his bungalow, that when the Manager stopped 
his car Sreeman Bhujel and some other employees 
went towards him and the Manager suddenly start-

had to be removed from the spot, first to the hospi-

against him contained false allegations, that there 
was no proper enquiry held and Sreeman Bhujel was 
not given permission to be represented by Shri 
Besterwitch, the Union Sccretary, that the finding is 
perverse and the order of dismissal unjust and 
improper. ‘ 


The Company’s case is that Sreeman Bhujel was 
all along an ordinary garden labourer and his past 
record of Service was unsatisfactory and he _ had 
been twice charge-sheeted and warned for insubordi- 
nation. The Company denies that Sreeman Bhujel 
was ever victimised for Union activities. It is alleged 
that at about 5-30 p.m. on the 2nd July 1957 a

thereby disturbing the work in the office. When the

the Manager’s jeep and obstructed him from going 
to his bungalow and they demanded that the 
Manager must pass orders for payment of bonus for 
1955. <A police officer who happened to be at that

It is therefore the admitted case of the parties that

Now regarding payment of bonus for 1955, the 
Manager Mr. Tod (O.P.W. 1) says that he had 
received a letter sometime in June 1957 from the 
Head Office regarding the profit position of the 
Company and two days after receipt of the letter he 
personally informed Sreeman Bhujel and others that 
no bonus for 1955 could be paid to the workers as 
the Company had sustained loss for that year. The 
Manager also says that a notice to that effect was 
hung up in the notice board in the garden. The

1957. So it is clear that although the Manager had

for the reason that the workers could not suitably 
explain the details to him. The demonstration was, 
therefore, made at the instance of the President of 
the Union and not exactly at the instance of workers 
themselves who had already been told about the loss 
suffered by the Company in 1955 and about non- 
availability of bonus for that year. P.W. 1, the 
President of the Union, further admits in his cross- 
examination: “there was an agreement that in case 
of loss of the Company, no bonus was to be paid for 
that year.” If that was so, then it is not understood 
why an agitation was started demanding bonus for 
the year 1955. The Union President’s only grievance 
is that the Profit and Loss Account of the Company 
was not given to the Union. From the evidence dis- 
cussed above, it is clearly proved that the Company 
having suffered loss in 1955 the Head Office informed

The main demand of the demonstrators was for

Regarding the charge under section 13(c)(18), it is 
admitted by the Union that the workers were hold- 
ing a demonstration which, according to them, was a 
peaceful one. O.P.W. 2 Shri Roy Chowdhury says 
that he heard shouting of slogans by the demonstra- 
tors from the office where he had been sent by the 
Manager to close the office. The obstruction to the 
freedom of movement of the Manager, I have found, 
was inside the Tea Estate, i.e., within the office com- 
pound. The workers were therefore holding a demon- 
tration there at that time even if they had _ first 
assembled on the P.W.D. Road. P.W. 3 Ramlal 
Sharma said that they had assembled on the P.W.D. 
Road and then started their march. Sreeman Bhujel 
was the Assistant Secretary of the garden unit of the 
Union and as such was the chief of the demonstra- 
tors holding the demonstration within the office com- 
pound and near the office when the officers were 
working there. This being the case, Sreeman Bhujel 
is also guilty of misconduct under section 13(c)(18) 
of the certified Standing Order. 


The Union then alleges that there was no proper 
enquiry in respect of the charge levelled against 
Sreeman Bhujel. The charge-sheet (Ext. 5) was given 
to the workman under reference on 3rd July 1957 
and the workman admitted in his reply (Ext. A), 
dated 9th July 1957, that he had been given the 
charge-sheet. That an enquiry was held was admit- 
ted by Sreeman Bhuyjel in his letter to the Manager, 
dated 9th July 1957 (Ext. D2). He stated in this 
letter: “After the enquiry of today which was held 
by your good self you asked me if I wanted anyone 
to represent my case to you.....” No allegation 
was made by the workman under reference in this 
letter that the enquiry had not been properly held or 
that he had not been given opportunities to defend 
himself. On the contrary, he thanked the Manager 
for having given him opportunity to have his case 
represented by Shri Ramlal Sharma, the garden 
Secretary of the Union. So the allegation of the 
Union that the Company proceeded with the enquiry 
in a perfunctory manner is not true. It is then argued 
that the Manager was the prosecutor and the judge 
and the enquiry and the findings were therefore 
vitiated as offending against the principles of natural 
justice. Such an objection was not taken at the 
initial stage although the workmen concerned in this 
reference had all sorts of help and advice from the 
Union. A preliminary objection like this must be 
taken at the initial stage and as the workmen did not 
raise such objection when the enquiry was started it 
must be held that there was a waiver. In this 
garden, the Manager. is the Chief Administrative 
Officer and the second officer was the Engineer 
Assistant. Both of them were witnesses to the occur- 
rence. There was no third officer who could have 
held the domestic enquiry. This being the case, the 
Manager was the only person in authority who could 
have held the enquiry. Besides, the entire dispute 


the Manager about the profit position of the Com- 
pany for that year and the Manager in his turn 
explained the position to the workers and informed 
them that no bonus for the year 1955 could be paid 
to them. The workers must have understood what 
the Manager had told them about the non-payment 
of bonus for the year 1955. If the President of the 
Union had any grievance he should have taken up 
the matter with the Head Office through proper 
channel but instead he thought it fit to advise the 
workers to start an agitation for bonus for 1955 and 
thus invite trouble for all concerned. That is exactly 
what had happened. In holding demonstration some 
of the workers surpassed limits and came under the 
mischief of the Standing Orders. There is no clear 
proof that the demonstrators numbering about 200/ 
250 had been holding demonstration all along on the 
P.W.D. Road, opposite the office premises. P.W. 1

The Manager then turned the face of the car 
towards his bungalow and we came and stopped in

office compound and the demonstrators having come

that the demonstrators entered the office compound 
and stopped in front of the Manager’s car and there 
was therefore an obstacle for the Manager to proceed. 
It appeared to both P.W. 2 Sreeman Bhujel and

called them but O.P.W. 1 Mr. Tod, the Manager, 
denies this. P.W. 1 Sreeman Bhujel says that when

he had to be removed. P.W. 3 Shri Ramlal Sharma 
Says that Sreeman Bhujel had to be removed to the 
hospital and then to his residence. I believe Mr. Tod 
that he never called the demonstrators to talk to 
them again regarding the bonus demand as it is the 
admitted case of the parties that the Manager had 
already told them about the non-availability of bonus 
for 1955. When the Manager did not call the demon- 
strators who might have assembled on the P.W.D. 
Road, it is admitted that a number of demonstrators 
came inside the office premises on seeing the 
Manager and stopped in front of his car and if Sree- 
man Bhujel was said to have been knocked down, it 
must be said that he was one of the persons, if not 
the only person, who must have tried to prevent the

ted fact that*at that moment a police officer happened 
to be present in the Manager’s office in connection

that time. O.P.W. Shri Roy Chowdhury who was an

his provident fund rules in accordance with the 


provisions contained in paragraph 61 of the 
Employees’ Provident Funds Scheme, 1952. 
12. The amount of contributions shall 0৩ 


calculated to the nearest quarter of a rupee; that is 
12.5 naye paise or more shall be counted as the 
next higher quarter of a rupee and fractions of a 
rupee less than 12.5 nave paise shall be ignored. 
The amounts of inspection charges and damages 
shall be calculated to the nearest 5 naye paise that 
is, 2.5 naye paise or more shall be counted as 5 naye 
paise and any amount less than 2.5 naye paise shall 
be ignored. 


13. On all repayable loans granted by factories 
interest shall be charged at the rate of 44 per cent. 
or | per cent. above the rate allowed on the balance 
to the credit of the members whichever is higher. 


14. The employer shall pay to the Regional Con- 
missioner inspection charges payable, failing which 
damages shall be paid at a rate fixed by the Central 
Government from time to time. 


15. (a) Wherever there is an agreement between 
the employers and the employees in any manner, it 
should be left undisturbed, and the election 
procedure would apply only to future cases. The 
Boards of Trustees in existence need not be 
disturbed during their current terms of tenure. 


(b) Subject to what has been stated above, where- 
ever there is a registered union, such unions may 
nominate workers’ representatives. ] there is a 
single registered union recognised statutorily or by 
a bipartite agreement, such a union shall nominate 


notification, amend the constitution of the Provident 
Fund maintained in respect of the factory in regard 
to the following matters, namely:— 


(a) the provident fund shall vest in a Board of 
Trustees and there shall be a valid instru- 
ment in writing, which adequately safe- 
guards the interests of the employees and 
such instrument. shall be duly registered 
under section 5 of the Indian Trusts Act, 
1882; 

(b) the Board of Trustees shall consist of an 
equal number of representatives of the 
employees and the employer and _ all 
questions before the Board shall be decided 
by a majority of votes; 

(c) the employer shall nominate one of 1:15 
representatives on the Board as the Chair- 
man who may exercise a casting vote if so 
rovided under the rules of the factory. 

here a casting vote is exercised or where 
no casting vote is exercised but the opinion 
of the representatives is equally divided, 
the matter shall be referred to the Regional 
Provident Fund Commissioner appointed 
under the said Scheme (hereinafter referred 
to as the Regional Commissioner) within 
whose jurisdiction the factory to which the 
matter relates is situated and whose 
decision in the matter shall be final. 


3. The provident fund rules of any factory shall 
not be amended except with the previous approval 
of the Regional Commissioner. Where any amend- 
ment affects the interests of the employees, before 
giving his approval. the Regional Commissioner shall 
give a reasonable opportunity to the employees to 
explain their point of view. 


4. (a) The employer shall maintain accounts of 
the provident fund in such manner and submit such 
returns to the Regional Commissioner as the Central 
Provident Fund Commissioner may, from time to 
time, direct. 

(b) The employer shall furnish to the Regional 
Commissioner such accounts relating to the provident 
fund of the factory as the Central Provident Fund 
Commissioner may prescribe from time to time. 
He shall also furnish an annual statement of 
account or a pass book, in such form as may be 
approved, to each subscriber who, but for the 
exemption, would have been a member of the Fund 
established under the Employees’ Provident Funds 
Scheme, 1952. 


(c) The employer shall make all investment of 
accumulations accruing after the date of exemption 
in securities of the Central Government. The 
reinvestment or conversion of securities on maturity 
shall also be in the securities of the Central Govern- 
ment. The employer shall formulate a procedure for 
prompt investment of provident fund moneys 2110 
shall get it approved from the Regional Commissioner. 


5. The employer shall afford such facilities for 
inspection of the accounts of the provident fund 
as the Central Provident Fund Commissioner may 
from time to time specify. 


6. All expenses involved in the administration of 
the Provident Fund Scheme including the 
maintenance of accounts, submission of accounts 
and returns, transfer of accumulations and payment 
of inspection charges shall be borne by the employer.

“Calcutta Gazette” of the 20th of October 1955, at 
pages 4263-4267, vide the Government notification 
No. 2215-SD, dated the 7th October 1959, as sub- 
sequently amended up to date, delegated to me by 
the Director of Consumer Goods, West Bengal, by his 
order No. XVII(82)55/3294(FU), dated the 6th July 
1956, I, the District Magistrate of Nadia, do hereby 
fix in partial modification of this office order No. 
4664JG, dated the 22nd July 1961, the maximum retail 
selling price of soft coke indented by dealers of the 
Ranaghat Subdivision of this district by road only 
at Rs. 2.40 per maund (exclusive of sales tax). 


This enhanced rate of maximum retail selling price 
of soft coke shall apply onlv in respect of stock 
brought into Ranaghat subdivision of this district 
within 90 days from the date of this order. 


A. K. DATTA,

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 
ORDERS 


Issue 


1. Whether the closure of the factory is real and 
bona fide and whether in the present circumstances 
it is justified? To what relief, if any, 215 the 
following workmen entitled? 


(i) Shrimati Gita Ghose. 

(ii) Shrimati Santi Ghose. 

(iii) Shrimati Kamala Das. 

(iv) Shri Panchu Dhali. 

(v) Shri Sukumar Das. 

(vi) Shri Radha Gobinda Saha. 
(vii) Shri Ram Narayan Basak. 
(viii) Shri Ranga Ram Ghose. 
(ix) Shri Haru Goswami. 

(x) Shri Ashananda Saha. 


This reference came from the Government in 
respect of an industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Anjana Scientific Glass Apparatus of 30 Raja Naba 
Kishan Street (hereinafter be referred to as the 
Company) and their workmen represented by Glass 
Blowing Mazdoor Union (hereinafter be referred to 
as the Union). 


This reference was received here on 23rd 
December 1960. As usual, immediately thereafter, 
notices were issued for service upon both the parties, 
who entered appearance and filed their respective 
statements. They did not put in any 
documents even though called for. On the Union's 
prayer the case was adjourned to 16th February 
1962 for preliminary hearing in view of certain 
Statements appearing in the written statements 
regarding complete closure of the business after 
Satisfaction of the dues of most of the work- 
men. On the date fixed the ex-proprietor of the 
Company appeared before the Tribunal, but the 
Union did not in spite of fresh notice served upon 
the Union by registered post with acknowledgment 
due on 5th February 1962. However, the Union, 
was given a last chance and the case was adjourned 
to 2nd March 1962 for hearing and disposal. On 
the date fixed again the Union has failed to turn up 
or to take any step. The ex-proprietor of the 
Company (since defunct) has attended with docu- 
ments. I have perused the documents and also the 
petition which he has just filed and prima facie I 
am satisfied about the bona fide closure of the 
Company after some payment of the dues of the 
workmen. 

The Union has not placed any material on the 
record and has not cared to proceed with the case 
in spite of service of fresh notice lastly on 5th 
February ۰ 


Therefore, in the circumstances, it is presumed 
that the dispute under reference 15 no longer in 
existence and as such a “no dispute” award is given. 

This is my ۹۰ 

Dictated and corrected by me. 

J. N. MANDAL, 
Judge. 
JITENDRA NATH MANDAL, 
Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal. 
The 3rd March 1962.

Company paid the workmen as well as the members 
of the staff bonus at the rate of one month’s basic 
wages and also of dearness allowance. 


At the hearing there was no appearance for the 
Union, although I waited up to 11-20 am. _ before 
taking up the case. Even during the hearing, there 
was no appearance for the Union. The case had 
been fixed for hearing on 5th February 1962 but at 
the instance of Shri D. L. Sen Gupta, Advocate, who 
appeared for the Union on that date, it was adjourned 
to the 5th March 1962. But as the 5th March was 
later declared to be a holiday, the date was shifted 
to the 6th March 1962 on the 13th February 1962 and 
notices were issued accordingly to the parties. It 
appears from the acknowledgment that the notice 
ان‎ accepted by someone for the Secretary of the 

nion. 


On behalf of the Company its balance-sheet for the 
year 1959-60 has been proved. The profit and loss 
account shows a loss of Rs. 11,606.34 nP. To this 
loss have to be added back the bonus paid in the 
eye year and the depreciation shown, The 

onus paid for the previous year to the workmen and 
the members of the staff appears from Ext. 3 series to 
be Rs. 6,115.31 nP. and the depreciation of machinery 
and furniture and buildings as it appears from the 
balance-shect is Rs. 14,512.30 nP. There is thus a 
gross profit of Rs. 9,021.27 nP. From this the normal 
depreciation has to be deducted. In the absence of 
any evidence to the contrary this normal deprecia- 
tion may be taken to be the same as that shown in 
the balance-shcet, namely, Rs. 14,512.14 nP. showing 
thereby a loss of Rs. 5,490.87 nP. If return on invested 
capital is taken to be 6 per cent. the loss will increase 
by Rs. 8,880, 1.9, the total loss will now be 
Rs. 14,370.87 nP. The cost of rehabilitation charges 
has been estimated by the Company in Ext. 4 at 
Rs. 10,142. What the Company appears to have done 
in arriving at this figure is to take the book value of 
the machinery and furniture as shown in the balance- 
sheet to the nearest rupee, to divide it by 5 and then 
multiply it by 2.7 and then divide by 15 so that 
the total figure on this head comes to Rs. 3,053.00. 
In the same way it takes the book value of buildings 
at Rs. 79,042, divide it by 5 and multiply it by 2.5 
and then divide it by 30. In this way the figure arrived 
at is Rs. 1,317.00. The total under the two heads 
comes to Rs. 4,370.00. This figure is deducted from 
the total depreciation of Rs. 14,512.00 as shown in 
the last page of the balance-sheet and the “esiduc 
represents according to the Company the rehabilita- 
tion charges for the year. Evidently, in this calcula- 
tion the life of machinery and furniture has been 
taken to be 15 years and the life of buildings such as 
the Company possesses namely tin sheds with pucca 
walls and plinth has been taken to be 30 years. Mr. 
Das Gupta relied for this calculation on the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal’s decision in Trichinopalli Mills 
Ltd. and National Cotton Mill Workers’ Union 
1953 II-L.L.J 361. I find, however, that in this case 
5 per cent. of the original value of machinery, fur- 
niture and buildings was taken to be the breakdown 
value. Even if this decision is taken to he correct 
the calculation in Ext. 4 is wrong because the hook 
value has to be divided not by 5 but bv 20 and 19011 
multiplied by 2.7 in one case and by 2.5 in the other. 
These figures may have been appropriate for the nur- 
nose of the case which the Learned Appellate 
Tribunal decided. But to my mind to apnlv them in 
all cases in general would he arbitrary and it is really

AWARD 


This is an application under section 33A, Ivdus- 
trial Disputes Act, by Shri Rabindra Nath Misra 
against Shri Ashutosh Kundu, the opposite party. 


The complaint made in the application is sub- 
stantially that the applicant was a permanent 
employee in a public bus bearing No. W.B.U. 73 
owned, and operated by the opposite party on a 
certain route in Howrah, but the applicant was 
illegally dismissed from service by the oppostte 
party in the circumstances alleged in the applica- 
tion without complying with the provisions of sec- 
tion 33, Industrial Disputes Act, during the pendency 
of the adjudication proceedings of another dispute 
between the opposite party and his workmen, which 
was referred for adjudication to this Tribunal by 
the Government of West Bengal. Labour Depart- 
ment, order No. 4083-I.R./IR /4L-34/59, dated the 
2nd August 1960. The applicant claims reinstate- 
ment to his service under the opposite party witn 
continuity of service and all back wages. 


After service of notice of the present application 
upon the opposite narty he entered appearance 
through a representative, but no written statemert 
was finally filed on his behalf though several 
adjournments were taken for the purpose. The 
applicant too defaulted in annearance on several 
dates up to 15th Januarv 1962 On 15th Januarv 
1962 the Tribunal suo moto adjourned the case to 
30th Tanuarv 1962, directing that the case would 
be disposed of according to law if no written‘ 
statement was filed within 12 am. on that = date. 
On 30th Tanuary 1962 Shri M. Saha, Advocate, 
anncared for the applicant. hut on an application for 
adjournment made on behalf of the annosite nartv, 
the case was adjourned to 16th Fehruarv 196? with 
the same directions as on 15th Januarv 1962. There 
was no annearance for the onposite partv on 16th 
February 1962, but an applicant for adjournment was 


impossible to calculate the ‘cost of rehabilitation in 
any particular year without appropriate data being 
placed before the Tribunal. I am not, therefore, dis- 
posed to accept the calculation of the rehabilitation 
charges in Ext. 4 as correct. But whatever the 
correct figures of rehabilitation charges for the ycar 
might be, there will be a little addition to the losses 
already amounting to Rs. 14,370.87 nP. without such 
charges being included. In any case, therefore, there 
was no available surplus for distribution to the work- 
men for the year in question and there was therefore 
no question of paying any bonus to the workmen 
for that year. But as I have already said the Com- 
pany has already paid to the workmen as well as the 
members of the staff bonus at the rate of one month's 
wages, inclusive not merely of basic wages but also 
of dearness allowance. The workmen therefore are 
not entitled to any further bonus for the vear. 


The issue is whether for the year 1959 the workmen 
are entitled to any additional bonus. The Company's 
first objection is that its year is not the English 
Calendar ٣٥٢٢ but was from 17th April 1959 to 4th 
April 1960. The issue, therefore, must be taken to 
mean the Company's accounting year which in that 
particular year corresponded to the period between 
17th April 1959 and 4th April 1960, both days 
inclusive. 


My award accordingly is that for the Company's 
accounting year 1959, from 17th April 1959 to 1 
April 1960, the workmen are not entitled to any 
extra bonus.

Decision 


Admittedly the Company is a private proprietory 
conetern. It is also admitted that it has got two 
factorics, one at 117 Raja Dinendra Strect, Calcutta, 
and the other at Dum Dum under the ownership of 
Sm. Manada Sundari Saha. D.W. 1 Shri Dinesh 
Chandra Saha is her husband. It is very clear from 
his evidence that he is the de facto Malik of the 
concern and at the same time receives a monthly 
salafy for his services. He says that he serves the 
Company but having no designation just as he claims 
to be possessed of general qualifications but with- 
out any educational qualification. Be that as it may, 
he is the man who ts overall in charge of concern 
Standing in the same of his wife. He takes the final 
decision in all matters of the Company. 


Admittedly, the concerned five workmen (1) Pran 
Krishna, (2) Dwijendralal, (3) Ram Prosad, (4) 
Sreenath and (5) Radhakanta were laid off after 
notice with effect from 9th November 1959. [Vide 
Exts. 1 to 1(d).] But four of them were paid lay 
off compensation for 45 days only even though they 
were laid off continuously for a longer period up 
to April 1961. They were not retrenched after a 
period of 45 days, for which they were paid 


[Part I 


already found from the Company's letters issued to 
the workmen that the Company’ could not assign 
any reason for withholding lay-off compensation to 
one of the workmen Radha Kanta Poddar and also 
could not offer any explanation for non-compliance 
with the provisions of section 25C(2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act in respect of the other four workmen. 
The Company could have retrenched them in 
accordance with the provisions of section 25F at any 
time after the expiry of the first 45 days of the lay- 
off. But the Company arbitrarily stopped payment 
of lay-off compensation after the first 45 days and 
the workmen were kept in suspense for more than 
one year. Some of them were taken back in May. 
1961 but that was done probably with some motive 
because they were again charge-sheeted within a 
couple of months of their joining and they have 
been kept in suspense indefinitely although it is said 
that there has been a domestic enquiry made by the 
Company’s Secretary Shri C. R. Chakravarti, but 
the result of the enquiry still remains unknown to 
the workmen. 


It is in the evidence of almost all the P.Ws., who 
were employees of the Company and one of them 
P.W. 2 Shri Jitendra Nath Bag who is still in the 
employ of the Company, that immediately after the 
lay-off of these five workmen in November 1959, 
the Company recruited new hands. P.Ws. have 
specified the names of newly recruited workmen. 
The Company’s solitary witness D.W. 1 Shri D. C. 
Saha could not altogether deny this fact. Therefore, 
the Company’s mala fide motive is not very far to 
seek. The Company, as it appears, in a very high- 
handed manner laid off these five workmen without 
any justification. The Company, as I have found, 
could not deny that these five workmen were 
prominent workers of the trade union. In the matter 
of payment of lay-off compensation the Company 
also showed some _ discrimination without any 
justification, and could not offer any satisfactory 
explanation for non-compliance with the provisions 
of section 25C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act and 
altogether denying any lay-off compensation to the 
workman Radha Kanta Poddar. D.W. 1 Shri D. C. 
Saha has attempted in his evidence to describe these 
workmen as purely temporary hands having served 
as helpers. But he had to admit the incorrectness 
of his own statement. One of them 91001798107 
Majumdar was a Drill-man as admitted by him who 
has been in service from the very start of the factory 
at Dum Dum in the year 1957. He says that 
Radha Kanta Poddar was in service for a month 
only before he was laid off. This statement of the 
de facto malik of the Company is found to be 
absolutely false. He was laid off with effect from 
9th November 1959 but the attendance register 
(Ext. D/1) which he produced before the tribunal 
shows that he was in service at Icast from July 1959. 
The evidence of P.W. 3 Radha Kanta Poddar is that 
he joined service in January 1959. This evidence of 
him was not challenged in his  cross-examination. 
Therefore, hardly any reliance can be placed on the 
evidence of Shri D. C. Saha the only witness of the 
Company. His own evidmence is being contradicted 
by the documents he has produced before the 
tribunal. According to him Ram _ Prosad_ and 
Dwijendralal were employed in 1958. It is in 
evidence of P.W. 2 Shri Jitendra Nath Bag who is 
still in service of the Company as a marking mistry, 
that there was plenty of work in the factory at the 
time these workmen were laid off by the Company.

Therefore, 1 am unable to be convinced about the 
alleged scarcity of work pleaded by the Company in 
order to justify the lay-off of these five workmen 
who were active members of the Union which fact 
remains unchallenged. 


The Company has, at the time of hearing, taken 
another plea to justify its non-payment of 
compensation to the workmen. The Company's 
contention is that the factory at Dum Dum having 
employed less than 50 workmen, the Company is 
under no obligation to pay any lay-off compensation 
as provided in section 25C of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. No doubt there is such a provision in section 
25A of the Industrial Disputes Act, but the Company 
has only to satisfy that there are less than 50 work- 
men employed by the concern. I have alread 
concluded from the evidence of D.W. 1 Shri D. C. 
Saha that the Company is a single unit having its 
different varieties of works done and completed at 
two different places but for all practical purposes 
under the same management and administrative set 
up and ownership. The Company has placed before 
this tribunal the attendance registers (Exts. D, 
D/1) in respect of workmen working in Factory 
No. II at Dum Dum. No doubt these two registers 
will show that there are workmen numbering less 
than 50 working in the factory at Dum Dum. The 
Company has not produced the register in respect of 
workers designated as learners. D.W. 1 Shri Saha 
admits employment of such workers in that factory. 
Then again the Company has not produced another 
সি in respect of workmen employed in the 
other factory attached to the Head Office at 117 Raja 
Dinendra Street. The Company did not take this 
plea in the written statement, but it was pleaded 
only at the time of hearing. The plea was not taken 
earlier in the lay-off notices or in the written state- 
ment, presumably because it was well aware of the 
truc position and as such the Company paid lay-off 
compensation under section 25C to the four work- 
men for the first 45 days only. To support. this 
belated plea the Company has placed some 
documents like Ext. E (order register) before this 
tribunal but I have already recorded the reasons for 
rejection of these documents. Hardly any reliance 
can be placed on this document in order to praye 
Scarcity of work or its financial stringency as pleaded 
by D.W. 1 Shri D. C. Saha at the time of hearing, 
the Company could have placed hefore the tribunal 
its books of account and balance-sheets and income- 
tax returns but these documents have been withheld 
eh the Company and I believe, it was purposely 
one. 


Therefore, I have no hesitation to come to the 
conclusion that there was no justification for the 
Company's action to lay-off these five workmen and 
to withhold payment of lay-off compensation to 
which they were entitled to. The action taken 
against the workmen was mala fide and with a 
motive of victimisation and unfafr labour practice.

Thereafter the workmen represented by the Otis 
Elevator Employees’ Union (hereinafter referred to as 
the Union) filed the written statement on 7th April 
1961. The case as made out by the Union is that this 
Company having its Head Office at Bombay and 
branches at Calcutta and New Delhi carries on the 
business in installation, adjustment and testing of 
Escalators and is associated with Messrs. Waygood 
Otis Ltd., London, a very renowned 384 well- 
established concern of United Kingdom. Since 1954 
the Company started functioning its own business 
independently and before that such business was 


[Part I 


: teh -. 


Besides, the agreement, Ext. 3, clearly indicates that 
this Company assumed liability for social benefit for 
the employees of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. from 
the time the workmen took their engagement under 
this Company with the consent of Messrs. Balmer 
Lawrie & Co. It is contended by the Company that 
whatever might be the state of things regarding pay- 
ment of bonus prevailing under Messrs. Balmer 
Lawrie & Co. this Company was not bound by that 
when it started functioning as a new Company. The 
auestion as to if there was complete termination of 
Service of the employees by Messrs. Balmer Lawrie 
& Co. and whether the employees were appointed as 
new recruitment by this Company had _ been 
considered by me in the previous adjudication case, 
between the same puartics, the award of which was 
published in the “Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary”, 
dated the 4th November 1961. After consideration 
of all the facts and circumstances in the light of the 
evidence therein adduced, I came to the conclusion 
that there was complete termination of employment 
of the workmen by Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. 
and that the engagement of the workmen by this 
Company was, in fact, new appointment as direct 
recruitment. The question, therefore, becomes 
Immaterial for the purpose of this case to find out 
what bonus the then workmen had been paid when 
they were the employees of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie 
& Co. For the purpose of creation of relationship 
as master and servant, I take it that such connection 
between the employer and the employees _ started 
from September 1954 and the liability as to fulfil- 
ment of the benefit available to the workmen as 
social benefits cannot be traced back to a period 
prior to that time. 


It is also significant to note that the question 
whether the workmen at the Calcutta Office were 
entitled to get additional bonus for the years 1955 
and 1956 came up for decision in a_ previous 
reference case, the award of which was given b 
Shri P. K. Sarkar, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal, 
<s published in the “Calcutta Gazette, Extra- 
ordinary”, dated the 26th September 1959, at page 
2049, From that award it appears that the learned 
Tribunal found the available surplus at a sum of 
Rs. 32,052 for the year 1955, and the sum paid as 
bonus in that year at Rs. 3,718 making Rs. 35,770 
and thus held that the workkmen were entitled to 
get additional bonus for one month's basic pay 
which was found to be Rs. 14,234 taking into account 
cll the employees of the Company including high 
salaried staff in Bombay and Calcutta when the 
Company oa paid one month’s pay as bonus. 
The learned Tribunal found that the workers were 
not entitled to get any additional bonus for the year 
1956 when the available surplus was found to be 
Rs. 30,333 and the workers were paid as bonus 
Rs, 30,19,211 and one month’s basic wage for the 
entire staff of the three branches—Bombay, Calcutta 
and New Delhi—amounted to Rs. 22,470. 


So, for the purpose of determining the claim of the 
workers employed in Calcutta for additional bonus 
for each of the years 1955 and 1956, the Tribunal on 
the basis of the trading result of the Company 
applied the Full Bench Formula to find out the 
available surplus for each of the years 1955 and 1956 
Separately and after taking into account the pay- 
ment already made by the Company towards bonus 
came to the concluston that additional one month's 
basic pay as bonus should be paid to the workmen 
for the year 1955 could be sustained. The learned

agreement and the business was taken over directly 
by Messrs. Otis Elevator Co. (India) Ltd. An agree- 
ment was made as between Messrs. Otis Elevator 
Co. (India) Ltd. and Messts. Balmer Lawrie & Co. 
on the 18th August 1954 (vide Ext. 3). In terms of 
that agreement Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. made 
over to this present Company all its existing service 
contract as agent of Messrs. Waygood Otis Ltd., 
London, and this Company as such assumed complete 
responsibility for their fulfilment. One of the terms 
in the said agreement was to the effect that Messrs. 
Balmer Lawrie & Co. will transfer or make available 
to this Company those of its employees that are 
engaged in the lift business and as are desired by 
Otis (India) Ltd. and that Messrs. Otis (India) Ltd. 
will assume all liability for social benefits for such 
employees of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. from and 
after the time their services are terminated and that 
Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. will assume all such 
liabilities for the period prior to their transfer to 
Messrs. Otis (India) Ltd. The question of fixation 
of grades and scales of pay of the clerical and sub- 
ordinate staff of this Company was decided by the 
Tribunal in a recent award published 11 the 
“Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary”, dated the 4th 
November 1961, at page 2880C. According to the 
version of the Company they are paying bonus to 
the workmen at the Calcutta Office since 1955. In 
the notice declaring bonus, issued on 28th September 
1955, it was categorically stated by the Company 
that the Puja bonus equivalent to one month’s basic 
pay would be paid to every permanent workman 
provided that the workman had been present on 
duty not less than 226 days within the period of last 
12 months ending on the 3lst July 1955 (vide Ext. 1). 
It was also mentioned in the aforesaid notice that 
a portion of this bonus covering the months of 
August and September would be paid by Messrs. 
Balmer Lawrie & Co. and the rest by this 
Company. There is no evidence to show’ what 
bonus the workmen were getting at the time when 
Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. happened to be the 
Agent of Messrs. Waygood Otis Ltd., London.

lawyer appearing for the Company urged that the 
said Tribunal in giving the award considered the 
payment of one month's basic wage towards bonus 
in the years 1955 and 1956 as nothing but profit 
bonus and, therefore, it is too late in the day for the 
Union to urge a case that the workmen had already 
acquired a right to get one month’s basic pay as 
bonus either as a condition of service or as a Puja 
bonus. 

The Supreme Court in the case of Messrs. Graham 
Trading Co. and their workmen, reported in 1959, 
Il, L.L.J. p. 93, had formulated the several tests 
which are to be satisfied for the purpose of 
determining whether a right in favour of the work- 
men had accrued in the matter of claiming bonus 
either as a condition of service or as customary one. 
There is, of course, some differences in the terms 
and factors to be considered as to when a claim of 
bonus can be sustained as a condition of service and 
that based on a customary right. But in either case 
it has got to be shown that such payment had been 
made by the Company for an unbroken series of 
years for a systematically long period and that the 
payment had been made irrespective of the question 
of profit and loss. As already found by me the 
workmen under this Company entered into their 
engagement in relationship as master 101 servant 
under this Company since September 1954. The 
workers got bonus in Calcutta on the eve of Durga 
Pujas in 1955, 1956, 1957 and 1958 at the rate of 
one month’s basic pay. The employees at Bombay 
and Delhi got the same rate of bonus on the eve 
of the Dewali and Christmas. At the same time the 
bonus as was paid in 1955 though amounting to one 
month’s basic pay was shared by Messrs. Balmer 
Lawrie & Co. in view of the fact that Messrs. Balmer 
Lawrie & Co. happened to be the employer for the 
months of August and September and that the work- 
men came under the employment of this Company 
from October 1954. Even ignoring the fact that the 
payment of bonus in 1955 had been shared between 
the two Companies, it can at best be said in favour 
of the workmen that they got bonus at the rate of 
one month’s basic wages in 1955 and in 1956. Such 
payment of bonus for two years is not a sufficiently 
long peried in order to ripen into a custom to 
create any right in favour of the workmen to justify 
a claim for such bonus in the following years. Nor 
can it be said that a implied condition of service 
for a bonus had developed in their favour. I, there- 
fore, hold that in deciding the claim of additional 
bonus for the years 1957 and 1958, I shall have to 
take into account the amount already received by 
the workmen in the shape of bonus at the rate of 
one month’s basic wages for each of the years 
treating the same as profit bonus in order to 
determine if the claim for additional sum can be 
sustained, on the basis of the profits earned in those 
years. 

There is no controversy on the point that all the 
workmen including the গন staff engaged in 
Calcutta, Bombay and New Delhi had been paid one 
month’s basic pay as bonus in 1957 and also in 1958. 
Exhibit A is the notice, dated the 30th September

bonus to be made on the 3rd October 1958 for the 
year 1958. It is admitted by both the parties that 
similar notice had been issued by the Company in 
1957. Admittedly the trading years of the Company, 
both in 1957 and 1958, were from the Ist of 
January to the 3lst of December of — those years.

There is no doubt that when the accounts of the

the Company’s officers prepared the balance-sheet 
and Profit and Loss Account, and that the labour

Sufficient opportunities must be given to the Union

sheet and profit and loss accounts. 


But before the accounts can be thrown off, it is 
necessary to remember the principle stated by the 
Supreme Court in the case of Associated Cement Co. 
as reported in 1959, I, L.LJ. p. 644. The 
observations run as follows: 


“As a general rule, the amount of 51955 
profits thus ascertained is accepted without sub- 
mitting the statement of the profit and 1955 
account to a close scrutiny. If, however, it 
appears that entries have been made on debit 
side deliberately and mala fide to reduce the 
amount of gross profits, it would be open to the 
Tribunal to examine the question and if it is 
satisfied that the impugned entries have been 
made mala fide it may disallow them.” 


“It would likewise be open to the parties to 
claim the exclusion of items either on the credit 
or on the debit side on the ground that the 
impugned items are wholly extraneous and entirely 
unrelated to the trading profits of the year. In 
considering such a plea the Tribunal must resist 
the temptation of dissecting the balance-sheet 
too minutely or of attempting to reconstruct it 
in any manner. It is only in glaring cases where 
the impugned item may be patently and obviously 
extraneous that a plea for its exclusion should be 
entertained.” 


Besides showing that the Company had followed 
the mode of accounting in the preparation of Profit 
and Loss Account somewhat different from what is 
done by other Companies, I do not find any reason 
to hold that the Profit and Loss Account do not 
show the correct state of things and that any items 
of income and expenditure which are extraneous 
trading result of the Company had been incorporated 
therein to make a show of lesser profit than what
