Engineers and Chemico Industrial Plants, the second 
and third concerns being described as associated 
concerns of Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel 
Co., and their workmen represented by Wolver- 
hampton Iron & Steel and Associated Concerns 
Workers’ Union. The relevant case of the Union 
under the issue referred for decision in so far as it 
relates to the said three concerns may be briefly 
Summarised as follows. Messrs. Wolverhampton 
Iron & Steel Co., hereinafter referred to as the 
Company, was established in or about the year 1939. 
In 1958 and 1959 respectively, the said Company 
purported to put up two other concerns under the 
names Modern Engineers and Chemico Industrial 
Plants, within the factory premises of the said 
Company by putting up two signboards bearing 
those names. The said two concerns were not real 
industrial concerns independent of and separate from 
the Company. They existed only in name. The 
work of the said Company was really done in th 
particular premises where these signboards were pu 
up. These fictitious concerns had no_ separate 
establishment, plant or machinery at all. Their work- 
men were appointed by the Management of the said 
Company and these workmen were paid their wages 
from the pay office of the Company. The Company 
resorted to this subterfuge of creating fictitious 
concerns with the mala fide intention of evading 
taxes and cheating the workers in various ways. 
Ten of the workmen, excluding workmen Nos. 8 and 
9 named in the issue, were appointed in the two 
fictitious concerns on the dates and years given in 
the list made Annexure A to the written statement 
of the Union. But on 3rd November 1959, the 
Company put the names of these workmen in the 
attendance register of the Company indicating 
thereby that they were appointed as from that date. 
Thus, their past service with the Company was 
arbitrarily wiped out and they were treated as new 
recruits of the Company from 3rd November 1959 
and their service periods were counted from that 
date. Their service periods under the Company 
should really be counted from the dates of their 
appointments under the two fictitious concerns 
according to the list made Annexure A to the written 
Statement and they should be deemed to be regular 
employees of the Company from the said dates. 
The Union prays for this relief in regard to the 
10 workers excluding workers Nos. 8 and 9, whose 
case is not pressed on the ground that they have 
left the service of the Company since the reference.

the Companies by Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & 
Steel Co. It is first submitted in the written state- 
ment that the issue as referred is vague and nb 
relief can be claimed on such issue. Then it is 
submitted that workers Nos. 8 and 9, 686 
Sarma and Dukhiram Sarma were never in the 
Company’s employment at any time and so, there 
can no industrial dispute regarding them. It is 
further submitted that worker No. 12 Sudhir Mondal 
was formerly an employee under the Company, but 
his services were terminated in March 1956 and he 
was employed anew under the Company on 31 
November 1959. It is admitted that the other 
workers named in the isSue are in the employ of 
the Company since 3rd November 1959 and it is 
contended that they first became the employees of 
the Company on and from that date. It is 
categorically denied that the two other concerns,

dated the 5th January 1961, the industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co. 
and Associated Concern (Modern Engineers & 
Chemico Industrial Plant), 3/1 Kashinath Dutta 
Road, Calcutta, and their workmen represented by 
Wolverhampton Iron & Steel and Associated Concern 
Workers’ Union, 90 Gopal Lal Tagore Road, 
Calcutta-36, regarding the issue mentioned in the 
said order being a matter specified in the second 
schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV 
of 1947), was referred for adjudication to the Seventh 
Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Seventh Industrial Tribunal 
has submitted to the State Government its award on 
the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of

the said award as shown in the annexure hereto.

AWARD 


The above dispute over the issue given in the 
order of reference and reproduced below was referred 
for adjudication to this Tribunal by the Government 
of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 31. 
I.R./IR/1OL-77/59, dated the 5th January ۰ 


The Issue referred for decision is as follows:— 


Issue 


Service period of the following workmen— 
Sarbashree (1) Subal Basak, (2) Krishna Guin, 
(3) Manoranjan Acharjee, (4) Mrityunjoy 
Bijali, (5) Hematfulla Mondal, (6) Jitendra 
Nath Das, (7) Khudiram Mondal, (8) 
Ramanand Sharma, (9) Dhukhiram Sarma, 
(10) Amarendra Nath Roy, (11) Bhadreswar 
Ghosh, and (12) Sudhir Mondal. 


It will appear clearly from the order of reference 
that the dispute under reference covers only the 
three concerns named in the order of reference, viz., 
Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Stcel Co., Modern 


[PART I 


admissions of both parties, appointed under Messrs. 
Wolverhampton Iron & Stcel Co., is based upon the 
lea that Modern Engineers and Chemico Industrial 
lants had 170 separate existence 1ء0۲‎ 
and functionally from Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron 
& Steel Co. and they were really component parts 
of the said Company and the said Company used to 
have its own work done through the said two 
concerns which were shown to be nominally separate 
from the Company for some ulterior purposes. As 
indicated above, this plea has been denicd by the 
Company in the written statement and it has been 
contended ir effect that all these three industrial 
concerns were and are Separate and independent 
units, both organisationally and functionally and 
there was or is no functional integrality between 
them. The crucial point for decision would be which 
of the aforesaid cases of the contending parties is 
to be accepted upon the evidence produced in the 
case. If the Union’s case is accepted, their claim 
must succeed, but if it is rejected and the Company’s 
case is accepted, their claim must fail. 


The physical existence of the three industrial 
concerns named in the order of reference, Messrs. 
Wolverhampton Jron & Steel Co., Modern Engineers 
and Chemico Industrial Plants, cannot be disputed 
and this fact is borne out by the order of reference 
itself and also by the admitted agrecment, Ext. B, 
between the said concerns and_ their employees 
through their Union. This fact is also proved by 
Exts. ہنا‎ D(1), E and F, which considered together, 
clearly point to the position that each of these 
concerns has a factory covered by a separate licence. 
P.W. ۱ Shri Subal Chandra Basak, a member of the 
Union Executive Committee, has practically admitted 
the physical existence of the three concerns by 
saying “I say that these are all the same Company 
because their works are carried on within the same 
compound.” P.W. 2 Shri Nirmal Kanti Ghosh, the 
Secretary of the Union, has also admitted that the 
concerned workers served in Modern Engineers and 
Chemico Industrial Plants before 3rd November 
1959. They could not certainly serve in these 
cortcerns unless they physically existed. It is further 
proved by Exts. G, ৫1 and 0302), the three wages 
registers of the three industrial concerns, that wages 
of the employees of each concern were paid 
separately and accounted for separately. This fact 
clearly indicates that the finances of these three 
concerns were kept separate and there was no 
unitariness in respect of the financial transactions of 
the three concerns. It is proved by the evidence of 
O.P.W. I Shri Hari Narayan Chatterjee, the General 
Manager of Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel 
Co., that Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co. 
and Chemico Industrial Plants are partnership 
concerns and Modern Engineers is a proprietory 
concern owned by Shri R. N. Chatterjee, a son of 
Shri P. N. Chatterjee, a partner of Messrs. Wolver- 
hampton Iron & Steel Co. It is also proved by him 
that the factory of Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & 
Steel Co. is situated at 3/1 Kashi Nath Dutta Road 
and the factories of Modern Engineers and Chemico 
Industrial Plants are situated at 65 Nainam Musal- 
manpara Lane, but both the premises are covered by 
the same municipal holding. The evidence of this 
witness in regard to these facts has not been 
seriously challenged in  cross-examination and J 
accept this evidence as correct. He has _ further 
produced and proved two separate balance-sheets of, 


1062 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 5, 1962 


Modern Engineers and Chemical Industrial Plants, 
were false and fictitious concerns set up by the 
Company for some ulterior purposes and they used 
to do the work of this Company and it is asserted 
that this Company had or has no_ functional 
integrality with those concerns and those concerns 
are two independent concerns and they are not 
associated concerns of this Company. These two 
concerns are run with their own capitals and they 
employ thier own workmen and pay their wages 
from: their own funds. It is further submitted that 
the employees of these concerns had and have no 
connection whatsoever with the employees of the 
Company. On the above allegations, it is finally 
contended that the service periods of the concerned 
workmen covered by the dispute under this 
Company is to count from 3rd November 1959, the 
date of their first appointment under this Company 
and their service periods cannot be extended back 
to cover their alleged periods of service under the 
two other concerns. 


Findings 


The issue as framed and referred for decision is 
no doubt somewhat vague and indefinite in that it 
does not clearly specify exactly in what manner and 
with reference to which industrial concern or 
concerns named in the reference the service periods 
of the concerned workmen are to be determined. 
It only refers generally to the service periods of the 
workmen. The proper question under the issue 
should have been as follows:— 


“Whether the service periods of the concerned 
workmen under Modern’ Engineers and 
Chemico Industrial Plants should be counted 
towards their service periods under Messrs. 
Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co.” 


This 1s practically the basic question at issue between 
the parties according to the written statements filed 
by them. The vagueness and indefiniteness of the 
issue, however, cannot affect the reference itself and 
prevent this Tribunal from adjudicating the dispute 
réferred to it because the precise point at issue 
between the parties clearly appears from the written 
stat-ments filed by them before this Tribunal. The 
reference is thus not incapable of adjudication for 
the defect in the issue indicated above. This 
disposes of the preliminary objection raised on behalf 
of the Company on the plea that the issue is vague 
and indefinite and no relief can be claimed on such 
issue. 


As already indicated above, the Union does not 
press the cases of workmen Nos. 8 and 9, Ramanad 
Sarma and Dukhiram Sarma. The position comes to 
this that the dispute in regard to these two workers 
is given up by the Union and in this way the 
dispute in regard to them ceases 100 exist. 
Accordingly, there is to be a “no dispute” award in 
respect of these two workres and I at once award 
accordingly in their cases. 


I now take up the merits of the case for decision 
in regard to the other 10 workmen named in the 
issue, Nos. 1 to 7, 10 to 12 


The Union's claim for counting the service periods 
of these workmen under Modern Engineers and 
Chemico Industrial Plants prior to 3rd November 
1959, or which date they were, according to the 


Part I] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 5, 1962 1063 
47185 
the/two partnership concerns, Messrs. Wolver- holding. The only conclusion that can legally 


follow from the aforesaid factual position is that the 
10166 industrial concerns covered by the dispute were 
ind are actually separate and independent units and 
not component parts of the same unit. There is 
absolutely no substance in the Union's case that 
Modern Engineers and Chemico Industrial Plants 
existed only in name and were absolutely fictitious 
concerns. Necessarily, it must be held that the 
employees of each of theSe concerns were and are 
completely separate and persons who were formerly 
employed under Modern’ Engineers and Chemico 
Industrial Plants but who were subsequently 
employed under Messrs. Wolverhampton 1790 & 
Steel Co. from 3rd November 1959, cannot claim 
continuity of service as between the periods during 
which they served under Modern’ Engineers and 
Chemico Industrial Plants and the periods during 
which they are now Serving under Messrs. Wolver- 
hampton Iron & Steel Co. In other words, they must 
be considered to be new entrants into the service 
of Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co.- from 
3rd November 1959 and their service periods under 
this Company must be counted from that date and 
these cannot be extended back to cover the periods 
of their service under Modern Engineers and 
Chemico Industrial Plants. This decision covers the 
cases of all the remaining 10 workers named in the 
issue including worker No. 12 Sudhir Mondal 
irrespective of the Company’s case in respect of him 
that he was previously in the employ of Messrs. 
Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co. but was discharged 
and then was taken as a new employee on and from 
3rd November 1959. The Union's case in the written 
statement is that all the workers named in the issue 
were entered in the register of attendance of Messrs. 
Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co. on 3rd November 
1959 on the basis that they were appointed from 
that date. There is no evidence to prove that 
Sudhir Mondal had continuity of service under this 
Company before 3rd November 1959. 


On the above decisions and for the reasons given’ 
above, I award in respect of workmen Nos. ] to 7 
and 10 to 12 that their service periods under 
Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co. will be 
counted from 3rd November 1959, on which date 
they became the employees of this Company and 
these periods shall not extend back to cover their 
periods of service under the other two concerns, 
me Modern Engineers and Chemico Industrial 

ants.

hdmpton Iron & Steel Co. and Chemico Industrial 
Plants. From the facts proved by this witness, it can 
be safely held that the three industrial concerns, 
Messrs. Wolverhampton Iron & Steel Co., Modern 
Engineers and Chemico Industrial Plants were and 
are really three separate industrial units 
organisationally, functionally and financially. It does 
not matter that these concerns are situated within 
the same municipal holding. No doubt according to 
the evidence, one of the partners of Messrs. 
Wglverhampton Iron & Steel Co. is the father of 
the owner of Modern Engineers. This fact cannot 
necessarily prove that the said two concerns are 
really one and the same concern organiSationally and 
functionally. On the contrary, it has been proved 
that these concerns have separate licences and have 
separate wages registers showing that their financial 
administrations are quite separate and independent. 
Even assuming that they are associated concerns in 
the sense of being controlled by persons who are 
near relatives or even members of the same family, 
it cannot necessarily be said that they have no 
separate and independent existence apart from each 
other. The most important test in such a case 
would be whether there is functional integrality 
among the industrial concerns so as to make all the 
concerns component parts of a single unit. There 
is absolutely no satisfactory evidence to prove that 
any functional integrality existed or exists between 
the three industrial concerns covered by the present 
dispute in the sense that they are functionally inter- 
dependent on and supplementary to each other. The 
test of functional integrality as between different 
industrial concerns has been held to be the crucial 
and supreme test in order to determine whether 
they form a single industrial unit or not even in 
cases where the concerns are owned and controlled 
by a single owner [vide 1960(I) L.L.J., page 497 ৩.০]. 
In this Supreme Court 0956 another test has also 
been mentioned and it is the test of integration or 
distinctness of finance and employment. I have 
already indicated above that there is ample evidence 
on the record to prove that finances of the three 
concerns were kept separate and wages of the 
employees of-each concern were paid and accounted 
for separately. The same _ test of functional 
integrality and integrality of employment and 
expenditure in respect of several concerns controlled 
by the same Managing Agent was also laid down 
in the case of Bangur Brothers versus Government 
of West Bengal. [1961(IT) L.LJ., page 351}. The 
resultant position in the present case, therefore, 
comes to this. Separate existence of the three 
industrial concerns organisationally and functionally 
and also financially has been proved and no functional 
integrality as between them has been proved, though 
there may he grounds for believing that these are 
associated concerns owned and controlled by some 
persons who are related to each other and the 
factories are situated within the same _ municipal

No. 372Ex.—24th March 1962.—In exercise of the 
power conferred by section 86 of the Bengal Excise 
Act, 1909 (Bengal Act V of 1909), the Governor 1s 
pleased’ to make the following amendments in the 
rules published with notification No. 601S.R., dated 
the 30th March 1915, as subsequently amended, 
namely ; — 

Amendments 

In the said rules— 


(1) for rule 237, substitute the following rule, 
namely,— 

“237. Confiscated country spirit shall be sold 
by auction subject to a reserved price which 
shall be equal to the amount of duty leviabie 
on the article in the place in which the sale 
takes place. If such price is not obtained, the 
article shall be destroyed.”; and 


(2) after rule 237A, insert the following rule, 
namcly,— 


“2378. Confiscated ganja and bhang shall be 
either destroyed or sold at such price as may be 
fixed by the Excise Commissioner with the 
approval of the State Government to a person 
Or persons holding licence under this Act for 
the sale of such article, subject to realisation 
of duty leviable under chapter V of the Act on 
the article in the place in which the sale takes 
place.”. 

By order of the Governor, 


A. M. KUSHARI, Jt. Secy.

No. 6-I. — 16th February “1962, — Whereas by 
notification No. 18-I, dated the 3rd November 1961, 
under sub-section (1) of section 4 of the West Bengal 
Irrigation (Imposition of Water Rate for Damodar 
Valley Corporation Water) Act, 1958 (West Bengal 
Act XXVI of 1958), published at pages 4080-4085 of 
Part I of the “Calcutta Gazette” of the 7th Decem- 
ber 1961, the Governor declared her intention to 
impose a water rate for the kharif season of the 
year commencing from July 1961 at the rate of ten 
rupees per acre in the area included within the 
boundaries specified in the schedule below: 


And whereas the period for prefering objections 
referred to in sub-section (2) of the said section has 
expired and no objection has been received within 
such period; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power ,conferred 
by clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 
West Bengal Irrigation (Imposition of Water Rate 
for Damodar Valley Corporation Water) Act, 1958 
(West Bengal Act VI of 1958), the Governor is 
pleased hereby to impose a water rate for the kharif 
season of the year commencing from July 1961 in the 
area included within the boundaries specified in the 
schedule below at the rate of ten rupees per acre.

This is application under section 33۸ of the 
Industrial Disputes Act by Gokkarn, ticket No. 381 
to 384, of Messrs. Kesoram Cotton Mills Ltd. in 
respect of an order dismissing him from the service 
سا‎ Company with effect from the 22nd July 
1960. 


The facts as far as they are admitted or beyond 
dispute are briefly that Gowkarn was served with a 
Charge-sheet. Exhibit E, dated the 12th July 1960, 
in which it is stated that it was reported by his 
Officer-in-charge that on 12th July 1960 two of his 
four looms were stopped during his duty hours and 
that when Shri Chari, Officer-in-charge, approached 
him during his rounds and asked for an explanation 
for the stoppage, the workman concerned shouted 
at him asking him to leave the place, abused him 
and refused to state to him the reasons for the 
stoppage. There was an enquiry into the charge- 
sheet by Shri R. K. Goel, Labour Officer of the mills. 
During the enquiry Shri Chari and Hiralal who was 
in charge of the Weaving Department “A” shift and 
three workmen, namely, Ramprabesh Singh, Abdul 
Sukkur and Rafiulla were examined. Gowkarn cross- 
examined some of them and declined (0 cross- 
examine the rest. On a _ consideration of the 
materials and evidence before him the Enquiring

The next question is whether the order of 
dismissal is justified. Gowkarn was accused in the 
charge-sheet of having refused to give an explanation 
for the stoppage of two looms asked for by Shri Chari 
and also to have abused him in filthy language. 
Gowkarn’s explanation is Ext. F which is in Hindi 
and there is a translation of this explanation signed 
on behalf of both the parties. In this explanation 
it is stated by Gowkarn that the charge-sheet was 
entirely false and it was Shri Chari Saheb who had 
abused him. In his evidence before the Tribunal 
Gowkarn says in his examination-in-chief that it is 
not a fact that he abused and insulted Shri Chari 
as alleged in the charge-sheet or that he kept the 
looms stopped and he stated the same thing during 
the enquiry. In his cross-cxamination here, how- 
ever, he says that when he inspected the materials 
of his looms he noticed that the pin which fixed the 
bobbin in the shuttle was slightly loose. Then after 
Starting the four looms he went to the carpenters 
for fixing up the loose pin of the shuttle and he was 
delayed there and he found that his looms had 
stopped as a result of the yarn of the bobbin having 
been exhausted and all the four looms had stopped 
and he went running to the looms. At the same 
time Sriman Chari Saheb also reached his looms 
during his rounds and Shri Chari told him he was 
a foolish operator, loitering here and there leaving 
his looms unattended and he also called him an 
“idiot” and an “ass” when Gowkarn told him “Sir, 
you are drunk and you better leave the place.” 


On behalf of the Company four witnesses were 
examined before me, namely, Shri R. K. Goel, the 
Enquiring Officer, M. V. Chari, the Weaving 
Assistant in-charge in Weaving Shed No. 1 “A” 
shift in July 1960. Hiralal, the Weaving Master in 
“A” shift in July 1960 and Rafiulla, Assistant Head 
Jobber in “A” shift shed No. 1. The first of these 
witnesses merely held the enquiry and knows nothing 
of the incident. Hiralal and Rafiulla also did not 
speak of the incident. Shri Chari alone speaks of 
the incident. His evidence is that he found looms 
Nos. 381 and 382 were idle and when he asked 
Gowkarn why the two looms were stopped he could 
not give any proper reason and when _ he again 
insisted on knowing the reasons Gowkarn got wild 
and started abusing him in very filthy language. 
The language used was “you get out of my place and 
go and do your duty” and said in Hindi “laorase 
chalaega” and “get out of this room and I will do 
my duty”. It is further his evidence that after 
saying this Gowkarn stopped the other two looms 
383 and 384 also. Then he went and reported the 
matter to Hiralal and thereafter he submitted a 
written report which is Ext. D. What Hiralal and 
Rafiulla testified to was subsequent to the incident, 
out of which the charge arose. But what they said, 
if believed, would lend support to the allegation of 
Shri Chari. There is no reason at all why Hiralal 
should fabricate an incident as against Gowkarn. 
There is equally no reason why Rafiulla, an Assistant 
Head Jobber, would tell lies against him. The 
attitude of Gowkarn as disclosed in the evidence of 
Hiralal and Rafiulla indirectly confirms the story of 
Shri Chari that he used abusive language to Shri 
Chari and that he had first stopped looms Nos. 381 
and 382 and that after the incident he stopped the 
other two looms also. It is hardly likely that 


hereby dismissed from the service of the Company 
with effect from 22nd July 1960 and he is also told 
here to collect his dues including his month's wages 
in terms of section 33(2)(b) from the Time-Keeping 
office. The application under section 33(2)(b) was 
actually filed on 26th July 1960, although it bears 
the date 22nd July 1960. On the 16th March 1960 
an order was made by me striking off this case on 
the ground that the award in the proceedings arising 
out of the order of reference was published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary”, dated 26th 
January 1961, and the Tribunal had no longer 
jurisdiction to deal with this application, vide order 
of the Tribunal in case No. 1190 of 1991. The view 
ا‎ took in that case and a series of other cases like 
that pending shortly after | joined this Tribunal 


struck me later as entirely wrong in law and 1 have ° 


since followed the rule that an application under 
Section 33(2)(b) validly entertained by the Tribunal 
must be disposed of by it according to law and the 
striking off such an application would not be lawful 
disposal of the matter. On 12th March 1962 when 
this application of Gowkarn under section 33A came 
to be heard this matter was again brought to my 
notice and when | explained to the parties my present 
view in the matter, both the parties agreed that the 
corresponding application under section 33(2)(b) 
should be restored to file. It was accordingly 
restored. But then on 14th March 1962 an 
application was filed on behalf of the Company 
withdrawing the application, 1 have made no orders 
on that application yet. 


There was undoubtedly four days’ delay between 
the order of dismissal and the application and in the 
notice Ext. H itself the workman was told to collect 
his dues although he does not appear to have 
collected his dues. The question, therefore, 15 
whether on these facts it can be held that there has 
been a contravention of the provisions of section 
33(2)(b) by the Company. On behalf of the Company 
reliance has been placed on two decisions of the 
Calcutta High Court, in the case between Metal 
Press Workers Ltd. and Deb H. R. and others 1962 
f—I, LL.J. 75 and in the case between Titaghar 
Paper Mills Company Ltd. and State of West Bengal 
1962—I, L.L.J. 192. Both these cases follow well- 
known Supreme Court decisions. In the case of the 
Metal Press Works Ltd. Sinha J held that the 
application must he made quickly and without a 
time-lag. In the case of Titaghur Paper Mills Co. 
I.td., Banerjee J held that where the employer 
tendered one month’s wages to the concerned work- 
man as required by the proviso to section 33(2)(b) 
of the Act at the time of communicating the order 
of dismissal itself but the workman did not accept 
the same, the fact that the said amount was 
remitted to the concerned workman by money order 
after the filing of the application for approval could 
not be relied upon to refuse the approval. In this 
case also the money was tendered with the natice 
Ext. H, i.c., one day prior to the actual dismissal 
which took effect from 22nd July 1960. The 
application was also filed four days later. Four days 
cannot be said to be unreasonably long, in view of 
the fact that before an application is actually filed, 
it has to pass through several hands. It must 
accordingly be held that there was a substantial 
compliance with the requirements of section 33(2)(b) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act by the Company in 
this particular case, and there has been no contra- 
vention of any of its provisions. The application

My award accordingly is that the Company was 
justified on the facts in dismissing Gowkarn for 
misconduct on the basis of the finding arrived at by 
the Enquiring Officer and that the application of 
Gowkarn under section 33A is not maintainable on 
the ground that there has been no contravention of 
the provisions of section 33 by the Company in 
dismissing Gowkarn.

Gowkarn would have spoken of Chari in the presence 
of Hiralal and others in the language that Hiralal 
and Rafiulla attributed to him if the earlier incident 
as reported by Chari had not taken place. That 
there was an incident between Gowkarn and Chari 
is also admitted by Gowkarn but his case is that it 
was Chari who abused him. The charge-sheet, 
Ext. E, clearly mentions that two out of the four 
looms had been stopped by the workman. In his 
explanation the workman does not 58 that four 
looms had stopped or that even two looms stopped 
as a result of the yarn in the bobbin having been 
exhausted. He merely refrained from saying any- 
thing beyond the falsity of the charge. The report 
of Shri Chari, Ext. D, clearly states that two of his 
looms were stopped and that is why he halted near 
the looms to see if they were out of order. He also 
says in the report that the other two looms which 
were working were also stopped by Gowkarn. It is 
therefore obvious that the explanation given for the 
first time by Gowkarn during the enquity that all the 
four looms had stopped as a result of the yarn 
in the bobbin having been exhausted 15 in 
all probability false. If as a matter of fact all the 
four looms had been stopped there is no reason why 
Shri Chari should state in his report that only two 
of the looms had stopped. No question on this point 
appears to have been put to Shri Chari either during 
his cross-examination here or during ×نا‎ cross- 
examination by Gowkarn himself during the enquiry. 
In the circumstances the story of Gowkarn that all 
the four looms stopped on account of the yarn 
having been exhausted in the bobbin must be held 
to be untrue and if that is held to be untrue or in 
other words if that part of the story of Gowkarn 
cannot be accepted as true the rest of his story also 
can hardly be accepted. It is also most unlikely 
that unless an incident like the one disclosed in 
Chari’s evidence actually took place between him 
and the workman, the workman concerned would 
have been a little later in a frame of mind in which 
he could have gone on abusing Shri Chari in his 
absence and in the presence of Hiralal and others. 
On the evidence, therefore, one is justified in the 
view that Gowkarn really behaved in a_ very 
disorderly manner in not merely refusing to offer an 
explanation for the stoppage of two of  the.-four 
looms but also in abusing Shri Chari in filthy 
language. The finding, therefore, arrived at by Shri 
Goel as a result of the enquiry ০011 hardly be 
legitimately assailed. The enquiry appears to have 
been conducted in a substantially fair manner. 
Gowkarn was present during the enquiry. He was 
allowed to cross-examine the witnesses he wanted 
to cross-examine and he made his own statement and 
was also questioned by the Enquiring Officer. 


Paragraph 1400)01)0৬111) and (xxiv) of the Standing 
Orders, Ext. J, makes wilful insubordination or 
disobedience to any lawful or reasonable order of a 
superior, disorderly behaviour during working hours 
and abusing any employee within the mill premises 
misconduct for which under paragraph 14(b) a work- 
man is liable to dismissal. On the materials, there- 
fore, the finding of the Enguiring Officer that 
Gowkarn was guilty of misconduct must be held to 
be correct. It is in accordance with the Standing 
Orders because paragraph 14(c)(i)(viit) and (xxiv) 
makes what Gowkarn was found guilty of 
misconduct for which the workman is liable to 
dismissal. The order of dismissal, therefore, must 
be held to be justified on the facts.

After service of notices on the parties, both the

Messrs. Indian Rubber Manufacturers Ltd. is an old

Production bonus scheme was introduced by the

Strenuous efforts on the part of the workmen bonus

administration. 


The Company, on the other hand, alleges as

or revised also. Of course, it is to be considered

From the concluding portion of the above para- 
graph, it appears that the parties incorporated a 
copy of the tentative production bonus scheme, 
appended the same with the compromise petition and 
marked same as Annexure “A”. But the award pub- 
lished does not show the Annexure “A” to the com- 
promise petition. From this agreement it will further 
appear that the Company agreed to introduce the 
production bonus scheme in one department only at 
first as an experimental measure. But it assured that 
the scheme would be progressively extended to other 
departments also, as soon as conditions were found 
favourable and preferably within three months from 
the date of agreement. But it is nobody's case that 
the Company has introduced or extended the pro- 
duction bonus scheme to all the departments up till 
now. Till the date of reference the Management 
introduced the production bonus scheme in 14/15 
departments only, though there were as many as 44 
different departments in the Company. It is also

permit the Union to raise an industrial dispute in 
respect of introduction or revision of a bonus 
scheme. The learned lawyer for the Company urges 
that the matter of production bonus scheme 15 
absolutely a Management function and is not within 
the purview of an Industrial Tribunal. But I am 
afraid, this is not the correct view of law as formu- 
lated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. Similar 
question was considered by Hon'ble Mr. Justice 
Sinha of the Calcutta High Court in a case between 
Philips India Ltd. vs. G. Kumar and others. The 
law on the point has been summarised by his lord- 
ship in the following words: 


“The legal position seems to me quite clear. It 
has been laid down in the case of Messrs. Burn & 
Co. vs. Their Employees-——A.1.R. (1960) S.C. p. 896 
as follows: 


‘Where an incentive bonus is in force in a 
concern for the majority of its workmen, the 
Tribunal can extend the same to the remainder 
of the workmen. The matter may, however, be 
different if the Tribunal is asked to impose an 
incentive bonus scheme for the first time in a 
concern.’ 


Reference was made to an earlier decision of the 
Supreme Court in Messrs. Titaghur Paper Mills Co. 
Ltd. v. Bengal Kagaz Kal Mazdoor Union ALR. 
(1959) S.C. p. 1095. That was a case of production 
bonus, which is almost the same as incentive bonus. 
It has been laid down there that the introduction of 
a production bonus or an incentive bonus was not 
compulsory on the employer and it was really a 
matter of policy or Managerial function whether it 
should be introduced or not, being in the nature of 
an extra payment. But once it is introduced and 
paid for some time, it may become a term of em- 
ployment and should be treated like any other kind 
of নি These two decisions of the Supreme Court 
taken together make the position quite clear. In a 
particular industrial unit, the introduction of an 
incentive bonus is not a matter of right. That is 
purely a discretion of the employer and is in the 
nature of a Managerial function. But once it is 
introduced, certain rights are created in the work- 
men and it may after some time become a term of 
employment. The next question as to whether this 
incentive bonus should also extend to other depart- 
ments under the same Management or to other facto- 
ries which are part of the same Management, depends 
on the fact as to whether these departments or 
factories are separate entities or part of the same 
industry or industrial unit. Whether several compo- 
nent units should be treated as one, for the purpose 
of payment of bonus or treated separately, has been 
the subject matter of a number of decisions of the 
Supreme Court See, Pratap Press v. Delhi Press 
Workers’ Union, A.I.R. (1960) S.C. 1213, Associated 
Cement Co. Ltd. v. Their workmen, A.I.R. (1960) 
S.C. 56 and the question depends on the facts of 
each case.” 


So, without further discussion, I may at once 
observe that in the instant case there is no question 
of validity or otherwise of the reference, in view of 
the fact that a scheme of production bonus or 
incentive bonus has actually been introduced in 
some of the departments at least on account of a 
previous award. It is also clear from the decision 
referred to above that under certain circumstances 
this scheme may be extended to other departments 


THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 12, 1962 1129 


Part 1ا1‎ 


ক্স سے‎ 


much is clear that the scheme is not there in the 
Boiler Department, Maintenance Department, Elec- 
tric Department and several other departments. 
Annexure “A” to the workmen’s written statement 
no doubt shows the departments in which the scheme 
was introduced and in which it was not. But I have 
already mentioned that the scheme has since been 
extended to certain other departments not specifi- 
cally mentioned in the Annexure “A”. So, as the 
matter Stands at present, the Tribunal is not in a 
position to find out the workmen who are yet 
deprived of the benefit of the scheme. Some of the 
wituiesses examined on behalf of the workmen allege 
that the scheme already introduced needs revision 
also on the ground that the norms and the target 
thereof are not proper or equitable. But I am afraid, 
unless the scheme as introduced in some of the 
departments 15 thoroughly scrutinised, it cannot be 
conveniently and properly revised. The materials 
on record are quite insufficient for the purpose. So, 
] am unable to revise the production bonus scheme 
of those departments for want of proper materials 
before me. ا‎ may also mention in this connection 
that formulation of proper incentive wage scheme is 
essentially an industrial engineer’s problem. In many 
respects, the administration of such a plan is 
engineering in nature. It goes without saying that 
there is no such thing as a_ umiversally applicable 
wage incentive plan, nor any general rule is invari- 
ably applicable to all. I have already pointed out 
that the scheme as introduced was so done with the 
consent of the departments concerned. So, it will 
not be proper for me to revise the scheme forthwith 
without a thorough scrutiny thereof. I may observe 
that there are few things that may lead to greater 
bitterness than *a_ badly conceived or imperfectly 
administered incentive plan. Of course, there may 
be considerable force in the argument that a properiy 
engineered incentive scheme is one of the best means 
not only to ensure efficient production but also to 
bring about job happiness. To tell a workman that 
his skill will be rewarded in accordance with his 
production is to ask him to feel his increased price, 
and this ultimately ensures benefit not only for the 
workmen but also for the Management. But in 
introducing such a scheme, it is the incumbent duty 
of the Management to make a scientific time and 
motion study. Mere past performance should not be 
relied upon for calculation of norms. In the face of 
these circumstances, | think, it will not be proper 
for me to revise the scheme as prayed for without 
thorough study of the existing scheme itself. Unfor- 
tunately, as I have pointed out, the materials are 
not sufficient to show what is exactly the existing 
scheme or what are the circumstances justifying a 
revision. 


Thus, in short, in accordance with the decision in 
the case of Titaghur Paper Mills Co. Ltd. vs. their 
workmen (1959 11 L.L.J. page 9), it may be held that 
a Tribunal is not entitled to impose an _ incentive 
bonus scheme for the first time in a concern. But in 
accordance with the decision of the Supreme Court 
in the case of Burn Co, Ltd. vs. Their employees 
(1960 1] L.L.J. page 261) it may be held that where 
incentive scheme has already been introduced by the 
Company for the major or a_ large section of its 
workmen, the benefit of the scheme may be extended 
to the remainder of the workmen. But in order to 
extend the scheme to the rest of the workmen, there 
must be sufficient materials before the Tribunal for 
formulating a scheme for them. It may also be held 


only. The Union's contention is that the Company 
is bound to introduce the production bonus scheme 
in all the departments of the Company, because these 
departments to which the scheme has not yet been 
extended are really parts of the same entity. The 
trend of the compromise also shows that the parties 
treated the entire establishment with all its depart- 
ments aS one industrial unit. Hence, all the depart- 
iments of the Company constitute one single unit 
und it was not the intention of either party to the 
ugreement that the workmen of a particular depart- 
ment 01 the Company should be deprived of the bene- 
nt of the scheme. As the different departments are 
not separate and independent units and as they are 
interrelated for the purpose of production as well, it 
will not be fit and proper to make invidious distinc- 
tion between different departments and exclude some 
departments from the benefit of the scheme. So, in 
all fairness, the scheme of production bonus should 
either be there for the entire establishment covering 
all the different departments or it should not be there 
at all, because partial execution of the scheme will 
create discontent in certain sections of the workers, 
and this may be considered as an_ unfair labour 
practice on the part of the Management. Of course, 
it may be contended that even according to the com- 
promise between the parties referred to above, this 
production bonus scheme was never intended to be a 
condition of service, and the Management was given 
liberty to withdraw the same at any time for trade 
or any other reason beyond:the control of the Com- 
pany. So, it will be consistent with the spirit of 
compromise also to retain the scheme in all the 
departments of the Company or to allow it to go from 
all the departments. As it is not the case of the 
Management that it has decided to withdraw the 
scheme altogether, I think, the workmen can legiti- 
mately claim for the extension of the scheme to the 
rest of the departments. But for revision of the 
scheme, there must be sufficient materials on record 
so that the Tribunal may consider what should be 
the proper way of revision. But unfortunately in the 
instant case, the materials on record are not sufficient 
for formulating a scheme for introduction of the 
same to the rest of the departments or revision of the 
scheme in respect of its coverage. Not only that, 
even the scheme as introduced has not been clearly 
proved before this Tribunal. It is sufficiently clear 
that the Management consulted the representatives 
of the departments concerned before extending the 
Same to those departments and that the agreed 
scheme was reduced to writing on cach occasion. I 
may also mention that certain papers were filed on 
behalf of the Management to show what were the 
terms of this bonus scheme as introduced. But as 
the Management failed to adduce any evidence, it 
failed to prove the connected papers. On the other 
hand, the workmen also refused to admit those 
papers as true copy of the scheme already introduced. 
In spite of my definite query on the point, the Union 
or the workmen concerned simply refused to admit 
those papers embodying the alleged agreement 
entered into in connection with the introduction of 
the production bonus scheme in the Company (vide 
Order No. 25, dated Ist February 1962). So, it is 
meaningless to ask me to revise the scheme, unless 
the scheme itself is placed before the Tribunal. | 
may also puint out that the oral evidences on behalf 
of the workmen are also not sufficient for any helpful 


revision of the scheme. Besides, the existing scheme 
itself is not sufficiently clear to this Tribunal. This 


(PART 1 


1130 THE CALOUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 12, 1962 


= re 


norm or: target has been fixed very high. However, 
this question may be conveniently considered while 
revising the scheme. It is also urged that 10 the 
departments where such scheme has been introduced, 
the workers either earn Re. 1 at least per diem or 
nothing at all, and that for earning Re. 1 as incentive 
bonus the quantum of production insisted 0001 is 
very big. Though I do not forthwith split up this 
minimum amount of Re. | into different bits for the 
purpose of earning proportional incentive bonus, I 
would very much appreciate if the Management can 
fix the minimum amount of incentive bonus at As. 4 
or As. 8 at least. Of course, I am not forgetful of 
the fact that the first or the minimum quantum of 
production on which production bonus will be avail- 
able to the workmen should be a bit bigger or larger 
in proportion to the subsequent slabs or stages of 
the scheme. For instance, if a workman now earns 
incentive bonus of Re. 1 per day by producing say 
40 pieces, and if this amount of Re. 1 is split up into 
four equal bits, with the required number of produc- 
tion for earning the different bits should be a bit 
different and graduated. This may be illustrated by 
the following example: 


As. 4 for production of 13 pieces. 
As. 8 for production of 24 pieces. 
As. 12 for production of 33 pieces. 
Re. 1 for production of 40 pieces. 

Subject to the above observations, I direct tkat 
the Management should introduce such bonus scheme 
as they consider fit and proper in consultation with 
the workmen or their representatives in the rest of 
the departments also within six months of the pub- 
lication of this award. Of course, I do not like to 
curtail the liberty of the Management to withdraw 
the scheme altogether if they so think fit, and this is 
in consonance with the spirit of the terms of agree- 


ment originally entered into and made part of the 
award already referred to. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
N. B. CHAUDHURI, Judge.

that under certain circumstances, the scheme sabes | 
introduced may be revised .also. But for suc 
revision, the materials and circumstances justifying 
such revision must be clearly proved. The learned 
lawyer for the Company urges that the departments 
like Boiler Department, Maintenance Department 
and Electric Department do not actually produce any 
marketable commodity for the Company, and _ their 
work also is not increased because of the increased 
production in other productive departments. But I 
have already pointed out that production is, in most 
cases, inter-related and one department has_ to 
depend on the other, and the final production is 
actually the cumulative result of the efforts of the 
different departments. It cannot be accepted that 
with the Increase ot production, the work of the 
Electric Department or the Maintenance Department 
or the Boiler Department does not increase at all. 
The workers of these departments may not produce 
goods like manual workers and their work may not 
increase in the same ratio or proportion with the 
work of manual workers of other departments pro- 
ducing goods, but there is no denying the fact that 
the work of their departments increases at least to 
some extent when there is voluminous increase of 
work in other departments. So, the Company should 
give such incentive bonus to the workmen of these 
non-producing departments also as is commensurate 
with the fatigue involved in their cases. Hence, the 
rates and conditions of the scheme applicable to 
these departments may be different, but they cannot 
be deprived altogether of the benefit of the scheme, 
because economically speaking they also take part in 
increasing production. In this view of the matter, J 
am unable to accept the contention of the learned 
lawyer for the Company and at the same time I 
cannot at once formulate any scheme for them here 
and now for reasons already explained. 


It is urged that the Management has fixed the 
norm and the target very high, and thus the work- 
men are unduly over-worked and sweated in earning 
the incentive bonus already introduced. This allega- 
tion of the workmen is also a bit vague. I have 
already pointed out that the scheme has actually 
been introduced in consultation and with the consent 
of the workmen concerned or their representatives. 
It is also clear from the evidence that in spite of the 
high norm or target, if any, the workmen are regularly 
earning incentive bonus almost every day. P.W. 7, 
Shri Purushuttam Das, admits that they are getting 
production bonus on every working day provided raw 
materials are available. So, it is difficult to accept 
forthwith the contention of the workmen that the

CALCUTTA POLICE NOTIFICATION 


Dated the 27th March 1962. 


In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (b) 
of sub-section (1), read with sub-section (2) of sec- 
tion 62 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act 
IV of 1866), and clause (b) of sub-section (1), read 
with sub-section (2) of section 39 of the Calcutta 
Suburban Police Act, 1866 (Bengal Act II of 1866), 
and with the previous sanction of the State Govern- 
ment, the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, makes 
the following amendments in the rules for the 
regulation of Traffic in the Streets and public places 
of Calcutta and its suburbs, published with Calcutta 
Police notification, dated the 13th January 1950, at 
pages 66-99 of Part I of the “Calcutta Gazette” of 
19th January 1950, as subsequently amended (here- 
inafter referred to as the said rules): — 


Amendments 


In Part II of the said rules, in section (A), after 
rule 4A, insert following heading and rule, namely: 


(3B) Portion of Belvedere Road covering 
the Zeerut Bridge and portion 
of Alipore Road. 


4B. Restrictions on cart traffic.—No bullock 
carts, buffalo carts or hand-carts shall proceed 
along Belvedere Road from its junction with 
Lower Circular Road up to its junction with 
Alipore Road covering with the Zeerut Bridge, 
and along Alipore Road from its junction with 
Judges Court Road up to its junction with 
Belvedere Road between the hours of 9 a.m. 
and 11 a.m. and 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. on all days.”

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Medical 
RESOLUTION 


No. Medl/3387/6A-9/62.—30th March 1962.— 
Whereas in the opinion of the Governor there have 
been circumstances which require that the functions 
of the General Council and State Faculty of Ayur- 
vedic Medicine, West Bengal, should continue to be 
performed by an Ad-hoc Committee in the interest 
of better and = efficient administration, after the 
expiry of the term of office of the Ad-hoc Committee 
appointed in resolution No. Medl/8916/6A-27/57, 
dated the 14th October 1957, read with resolution 
Nos. Medl/9745/6A-25/60 and Medl/9716/6A-37/ 
61, dated the 14th October 1960 and the 13th Octo- 
ber 1961, respectively; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred 
by the second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 9 
of the Statutes of the General Council and State 
Faculty of Ayurvedic Medicine, promulgated under 
Resolution No. 315Medl., dated 2nd February 1937 
and published in Part I, “Calcutta Gazette” of 11th 
February 1937, pages 243-249, as subsequently 


corrected by corrigendum No. 14905/L.S.-G.1A-4/61, 
dated the 2151 December 1961 and amended by noti- 
fication No. 904/L.S.-G.1A-4/61, dated the 8th Feb- 
ruary 1962, the Governor is pleased to extend the 
time for submission of the recommendations of the 
Town and Country Planning Legislation Commission 
to the 6th October 1962. 

By order of the Governor, 


J. C. TALUKDAR, Jt. Secy.

following draft of amendments which, in exercise of 
the power conferred by section 44 of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), the

Municipal Election Rules, 1960, published with

Gazette” of the 25th May 1960 (hereinafter referred 
to as the said rules), is hereby published, as required 
by sub-section (i) of section 505 of the said Act, for 
the information of persons likely to be affected 
thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on 
or after the 15th May 1962, and any objection or 
Suggestion with respect thereto which may be 
received by the undersigned before that date shall 
be considered. 


Draft Amendments 
In the said rules— 


1. for rule 3, substitute the 
namely:— 


“3, The District Magistrate shall issue an 
order in writing fixing the date— 


(a) (i) for a general election under sub- 
section (3) of section 24 of the Act, at 
least seven months before the expira- 
tion of the term of office of the com- 
missioner or commissioners under sub- 
section (1) or sub-section (5) of 
section 56, as the case may be; 


(ii) for a general election under clause (b) of 
sub-section (2) of section 554 of the 
Act, at least seven months before such 
election; and 


(b) for any other election (including a bye- 
election), not being an election referred 
to in section 24-A, as soon as possible 
on each occasion, but at least 50 days 
before any such election.”; 


2. after rule 3, incert the following new rule, 
namely:— 


“3A. The District Magistrate shall com- 
municate the date fixed for any election 
to the Chairman who shall forthwith 
publish the same in the manner 
prescribed by section 507 of the Act.’

“under rule 3”: 


4, in rule 6, in sub-rule (1), omit the words “of 
sub-rule (1); and

(b)”,

Kumar Banerjee, W.B.C.S., is hereby appointed to

as follows>— 


(a) up to the date of his superannuation from 
the West Bengal Civil Service, his grade 
pay in the West Bengal Civil Service, plus 
a special pay of Rs. 200 per month. 


(b) thereafter, the last pay including the special 
pay drawn by him before the said date of 
superannuation less pension and pension 
equivalent of retiring gratuity.

(111) Age for recruitment: Candidates shall be over 21 and

(iv) Qualifications: For direct recruitment, the qualifica- 
tions of a candidate shall be as follows :— 


(a) He shall be a native of or permanently domiciled in 
West Bengal fulfilling the conditions of (tizenship 
of India as defined in part IT of the Constitution of 
India. 


(b) He shall he of good moral character. 


(c) He shall have passed at least the degree examination 
in Arts or Science or an equivalent examination of 
any recognised University. He should have fluent 
knowledge of Bengali or Gurkhali and English. 


(d) He shall be free from. disease, constitutional affection 
or bodily infirmity making or likely to make him 
unfit for police duties. 


N.B.—Suttering or stammering is a defect which renders 
an applicant ineligible. 


(9) He shall not be less than 1.63 metres in height and 
8.74 centimetres round the chest with a minimum 
expansion of 5.08 centimetres. The following should 
be the corresponding weight according to height :—

Instructions for Filling in the Form 


I. Columns 1 to 14 of the form. should be filled in English by the 
applicant. 


II, Column 6: Age as noted in the Matriculation or school leaving 
certificate will be accepted. ও 


III. Column 7: Copies of Matriculation or other certificates should 
be attached to the application. The originals should 
be produced before the Superintendent of Police/the Central 
Board, when called for. 


IV. Column 13: Testimonials may he attached to the form. If 
copies and not the originals are attached, the latter must he 
produced hefore the Superintendent of Police/the Central Board, 
when required. The testimonials should include a certificate of 
moral character from some person who has known the applicant 
for at least 3 years and a certificate from the Principal of the 
school or college, in which the applicant has attended during 
the past 12 months. 


V. Column 14 should be verified by the Superintendent of Police and 
attested or discrepancy noted. 


VI. Column 15 should be filled in by the District Magistrate ond 
Superintendent. 


N.B.—Canvassing is forbidden and any attempt on the part of a 
candidate to enlist support for the application through relatives, 
friends, patrons or officials will disqualify him for appointment. 
Spontaneous recommendations from persons interested in the 
candidates or otherwise known to them will be disregarded. 


[A candidate who applies from more than one district should be 
automatically disqualified. ]

That Kulomoni was ill from the 16th to the 25th 
August 1961 is sought to be proved only by his own 
Statement and by the medical certificate Ext. 1. 
That he was ill is denied by the Company. It was, 
therefore, essential for him to prove his illness by 
proper evidence. It has been observed by the 
Supreme Court in the case between Petlad Turkey 
Red Dye Works Co. Ltd. and Dyes and Chemical 
Workers’ Union and others 1960—I, L.L.J. in 
connection with the proving of balance-sheets that 
if a person is to prove that he was ill on a 
particular day, the mere filing of a certificate of a 
medical man that he was ill on that date is not 
accepted as evidence to show that he was ill. The 
correctness of the statement made in the certificate 
has to be proved by an affidavit or oral testimony in 
Court by the doctor concerned or by some other 
evidence. The only evidence in this case about the 
workman’s illness is the evidence of the workman 
himself so that the medical certificate filed does not 
add anything more to that evidence. It is difficult 
to accept the uncorroborated testimony of the work- 
man that he was ill. It appears that the Company 
keeps two Mill doctors and the address of the 
doctor who certified the workman to be ill appears

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, filed by Shri Nand

against the said Company. (Case No. 93 of 1961

BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL,

Present:

AWARD 


This is an application under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act by Shri Nand Kishore, a 
Folder in the Folding Section, Ware House Depart- 
ment of Messrs. Kesoram Cotton Mills Ltd. 
Admittedly, he went home on leave for a month 
from the 10th of April 1961 to the 9th of May 1961 
as iS indicated by Ext. ,ا‎ the Gate Pass issued to 
him. On 6th May 1961 before the expiry of this 
leave, he asked for an extension of this leave for 
15 days from the 10th’ of May to the 24th of May 
1961 on the ground of his marriage. This application 
is Ext. A, Shri Pritendu Ghosh, S.P.W. 1, who dealt 
with the application, endorsed on the application the 
order “Not granted” on the 13th of May 196] and 


Part T] 


a= = 


from the certificate itself to be R/55 Garden Reach 
Road, Calcutta-24, while the address of the factory 
js 42 Garden Reach Road. If the workman could 
appear before this private doctor to whom he must 
have paid some fees it is difficult to understand why 
he could not appear before the Mill doctor who is 
bound to examine him free, when the Mills could 
not possibly be very far from the doctor who 
certified Kulomoni’s illness. This alone seems to 
me to make the whole story suspicious. Then, as 
regards the appearance of the man before a Mill 
doctor on the 26th of August, it is his case that he 
appeared before a fat doctor named Dhiren Babu 
but there is no such doctor in the Mill and Dr. Mohit 
Bhattacharjee has stated that the only other doctor 
employed in the Mill is Dr. Bhawani Bhattacharjee 
and Dr. Bhawani Bhattacharjee is not as fat as he 
himself is, so that Dr. Mohit Bhattacharyya is the 
fatter of the two doctors and he denies that Kulo- 
moni appeared before him on the 26th. There is 
no entry in either of the two registers maintained 
by Dr. Mohit Bhattacharyya and Dr. Bhawani 
Bhattacharyya that he appeared before them on the 
26th. In cross-examination the doctor ‘was asked 
whether there would be any entry if the medical 
certificate was a certificate of fitness and he answered 
the question in the negative. But then Ext. I, as 
I have already said, is not a certificate of fitness at 
all. It was a certificate of Kulomoni's illness between 
16th August 1961 and 25th August 1961. No 
question was put to this doctor whether in such a 
case there would be any entry in the register. Even 
apart from that question, there being nothing in the 
medical certificate to show that it was ever presented 
to any officer or doctor of the Company along with 
the original or Ext. 2 and there being nothing in the 
application under section 33A to suggest that either 
this medical certificate or the application with which 
it was submitted was returned to the workman, it is 
impossible to believe this story. On the merits, 
thercfore, it must be found not 00 be a case of 
refusal of employment by the Company to the work- 
man but a case of continucd absence of the work- 
man from 16th August 1961] to 25th August 1 
without leave. 

On this finding no question arises of any violation 
by the Company of any of the provisions of section 
33 and as a matter of fact there is nothing in the 
application to indicate that there was any such 
violation. Of course, had there been a_ refusal of 
employment and had this refusal amounted to a 
termination of the workman’s service, the fact that 
there were no payment of one month's wages and 
no application under section 33(2)(b) might constitute 
violations of the provisions of section 33. But this 
question does not arise in this case. 


My award therefore in this case is that there was 
-no refusal of employment by the Company to the 
workman on the 26th August 1961 or thereafter and 
it was really a case of the continued absence of the 
workman from the 16th August 1961 onwards and 
that the application is not maintainable.

before the expiry of his leave and in case the work- 
man loses his lien on his appointment, he shall be 
entitled to be kept on the 8911 list. It is clear from 
the evidence that the workman continued to be 
absent for months after his leave expired on the 9th 
of May 1961 and it further appears from his own 
application, Ext. D, that he had applied for leave on 
25th May 1961 and 22nd June 1961 but to his ill- 
luck he got the reply that the extension of leave 
could not be granted. In other words, this letter 
makes it clear that the refusal of the extension was 
duly intimated to him. Yet, he remained absent. 
Clearly, therefore, under the Standing Orders he had 
lost his lien on his appointment and the Company 
was entitled under the Standing Orders to direct him 
to join as a Badli worker although the status of a 
Badli must be inferior to that of a permanent work- 
man, for the simple reason that the Badli workman 
apart from any other disadvantages, is not 
entitled to work and wages for every work- 
ing day in the week like a permanent work- 
man. But it is clear that for this reduction' of 
his status, the workman’ was himself responsible. 
There was, therefore, no refusal of employment by 
the Company in this case. What happened was 
simply this that the workman continued to be absent 
on the expiry of his leave, even though he had 
received intimations that the extensions of leave he 
had prayed for were refused. By this continuous 
absence, he had lost his lien on his appointment and 
was liable to be treated as a Badli workman. 


In the cause title of the application order 
No. 4928-1.R. /IR;8L-2(D)/60, dated 17th September 
1960, obviously implying thereby that this industrial 
dispute between the partics was pending before the 
Tribunal. It appears that this industrial dispute 
was pending before the Tribunal at the date, viz., 
26th July 1962, of the alleged refusal of employment 
of the workman, so that if the facts amounted to a 
refusal of employment by the Company scction 33A 
would be attracted. As this was not a case of 


refusal of employment by the Company, section 33A 
has no application. 


My award accordingly is that the Company did 
not refuse employment to the workman Shri Nand 
Kishore in this case but what happened is that the 
workman by his continued absence on the expiry of 
his leave on the 9th May 1961 in spite of the 
rejection of his prayers for extensions of leave lost 
his lien on his appointment and so became liable 
under the Standing Orders of the Company to be 
treated as a Badli workman and he did not join as a 
Badli workman even though he was called upon to 
do so by the Company. The application is also not 
maintainable because there was no violation of the 
provisions of section 33 and there could not possibly 


be any violation of such provisions in view of the 
facts of the case.

thé earlier award it is stated that sick Icave shall be 
granted on a medical certificate and the Company 
shall have always the right to have any applicant for 
sick leave examined by its own doctor and at its 
own cost. In the later award it is stated that in the 
mills in this area, the existing practice of sick leave 
with pay shall continue and this sick leave shall be 
allowed on the basis of a medical certificate from 
the Medical Officer of the mill or from a qualified 
and registered medical practitioner. These provi- 
sions of the two awards are construed on ‘behalf of 
the workman as leaving no _ discretion to 006 
Management in estimating the value of the medical 
certificates and to that extent, in considering whether 
or not, leave should be granted. According to this 
line of argument, the grant of leave is automatic 
on the submission of a medical certificate, and in the 
last analysis this so-called grant of leave by the 
Management becomes a misnomer, because it is not 
the Management but the workman himself who by 
filing a medical certificate grants the leave himself. 
This construction appears to my mind to be totally 
unacceptable. The use of the word “shall” in both 
the awards means to my mind nothing more than 
this that when the Management decides on granting 
sick leave, the basis thereof must be the medical 
certificate of the qualified practitioner filed and not 
that on a medical certificate being filed, the Manage- 
ment has no option left to it but to grant the leave. 
The withdrawal of the Management’s discretion in 
this matter is such a serious limitation of its 
gencral powers of running the business _ efficiently 
and fairly that the Tribunals cannot be presumed 
in the absence of clear indications to that effect to 
have intended such a limitation. There is nothing 
in the two awards to suggest that before either of 
the two Tribunals, any such consideration was 
present at all. That no such serious limitation could 
be intended appears quite clear from the fact that 
the award of 1948 expressly gives the Company the 
right always to have any applicant for sick leave 
examined by its own doctor and at its own cost. 
The existence of such a right in the Company is 
inconsistent with the withdrawal of the Company's 
discretion in granting leave. What is spoken of as 
the existing practice in the award of 1958 is probably 
the practice of sick leave being granted, if at all, with 
pay and also the practice of the Company in having 
the workman concerned examined by its own doctor 
and at its own cost. It also follows from these 
awards that the Company not being physically in a 
position to have the applicant for an extension of 
leave ہہ‎ the ground of illness, examined by its own 
doctor when the applicant is away from the mill 
area, these provisions of the two awards were not 
meant to cover cases of extension of leave at all but 
was confined only to initial applications for leave. 
It must accordingly be held that the awards of 1948 
do not take away the Management’s inherent 
discretion in granting or refusing prayers for 
extension of leave when there are medical certificates 
in support of such prayers, though this discretion 
must be exercised fairly and reasonably.

The first question in this case is whether it has

the Badli list. Evidently, therefore, under the 
Standing Orders, the workman had lost his lien. 
The Company claims to have informed him _ that 
he should join his. duty as a Badli. This is the 
evidence of Shri Bijoy Bahadur Singh and this is 
borne out by Ext. 6, dated the 9th August 1961. 
In this it is distinctly stated that on the 26th June 
196] he was informed that according to the pro- 
visions of the Standing Orders he had lost his lien 
on his appointment and had been asked to join as 
a Badli but since then he has been absented himself 
without iniormation. Again he was asked to join

three days of the receipt of the letter but he aid 
not join as a Badli. Exhibit 6 admittedly reached 
the workman and though Shri Arun Sen alone 
stated that Shri Audhoo turned up in the factory 
thereafter on two occasions for work as a Badli, 
that story could not be accepted. It must in this 
state of the evidence be held that there was no 
refusal of employment by the Company and that the 
workman after having overstayed his leave by more 
than a month came to join on the 26th June 196! 
when he was told that as he had lost his lien on 
his service he should join as a Badli but he did not 
join as a Badli and on the 23rd October 1961 the 
Company informed the workman by Ext. A that in 
view of his continued unauthorised non-attendance 
as a Badli worker his name was removed from the 
list of Badli workers. The termination, therefore, 
of the services of the workman was the result of 
what he himself did. 


In the circumstances there is no question of any 
contravention by the Company of the provisions of 
section 33 nor is there any specific allegation that 
there was any such contravention but had the 
proved facts amounted to refusal of employment by 
the Company to the workman, there might have 
been contravention of the provisions of section 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act because there were 
no payment of a month's wages and no application 
as required by the proviso to section 33(2)(b). 


My award accordingly is that there was no refusal 
of employment by the Company to the workman 
Shri Audhoo but the workman himself overstayed 
his leave by more than a month and when he was 
told that he had lost his lien on his service and 
directed to join as a Badli worker he refused to join 
as a Badli and ultimately his continued ۹۰ 
attendance as a Badli worker led to the striking off 
of his name from the list of Badli workmen. The 
application is not also maintainable because there 
has been no contravention of the provisions of 
section 33.

that the workers are now suppressing the truth. The 
simple question here is whether the workers were 
guilty of gross misconduct which is of such a grave 
nature as arising from wrongful confinement of the 
proprietors for long six hours within the factory on 
the 27th July 1960. In order to come to a decision on 
the point, the entire evidence as recorded in the light 
of probablities of the case has got to be considered. 
It is clear from the evidence that the workers report- 
ed about the incident that happened on the 27th 
July to Shri Bimal Banerjee and the Management in 
spite of such situation wanted to discuss the matter 
with Shri Banerjee. What possibly could be the 
earthly reason to report to Shri Banerjee unless there 
was some incident on the 27th July. If everything 
passed off normally in the factorv on the 27th July 
as stated by the workmen, there could possibly be no 
reason for declaration of a closure of the factory by 
a proper notice issued to the workmen in early hours 
of the morning of 28th Julv. Besides in the notice 
the incident is fully described. It is abundantly 
clear from the evidence that right from the time this 
Union was formed, the workers broke discipline on 
many occasions on flimsy ground. The climax, 
however, was reached on the 27th July 1960. The 
whole incident as happened on the 27th July was 
clearly mentioned in the notice given by the Manage- 
ment on the 28th July. Upon consideration of the 
facts and circumstances of the case I have no hesita- 
tion in believing the version of the Management that 
the workers behaved in a most wicked manner and 
that thev had been guilty of gross misconduct. It is 
true that the Management did not hold any depart- 
mental enquirv upon the issue of charge-sheet to the 
workmen and giving ‘opsortunities to them to defend 
themselves. But obviously just because of the fact 
that no charge-sheet had been formally drawn up, 
that would not vitiate the order of dismissal when 
the workmen knew from the notice itself what were 
the charges against them and for that they had full 
Opportunity to give their explanation. Dismissal 
without giving opportunity to explain has been held 
to be in order if it anpears that there could possibly 
be no explanation. The offence was committed with 
respect to the proprietors of the Company and they 
were the proper persons to take a decision as to 
denartmental enquiry and arrive at finally as to the 
guilt of the workers. In this situation the proprietors 
themselves were the only witnesses who could speak 


7 
in. prévious‘wecks, I do not find any sharp fall in the 
earning of the worker. It further appears from the 
Wage Register that Asruf Khan did not take his 
wages for the next weék commencing from 25th 
June 1960. It is however clear from the Wage 
Register that. during that week the worker had 
worked for two days one hour: It also appears from 
the Attendance Register that he worked for only 
one hour on the 27th July 1960. The workers 
stopped work on the 27th July just because of the 
fact that they wanted to force the Management to 
increase the wages with respect to the work done by 
the newly introduced dice for preparation of section 
in which Asruf Khan alone was engaged at the 
relevent time. The rate of wages at 6 annas per 
gross is the highest piece-rate in this establishment. 
Clearly the move was to get the rate further 
increased. It appears from the evidence that on 27th 
July 1960 the workers after coming to the factory 
did not actually commence their work. Naturally 
they made preparation for the incident. At about 
9 am. about 20 or 25 workers entered into the room 
of the proprietor, Raj Paul Gambhir, and encircled 
him putting forward the demand for increase of the 
rates of wages with respect to the particular dice. 
Shri Gambhir stated that when he refused to increase 
thesrate of wages, they begun to abuse him in filthy 
language and even when he made _ entretics there 
was no response for the worker. The workers kept 
the proprictors confined in the room up to 3 or 
3-30 p.m. and it was only after the attendance card 
had been written that they allowed the proprietors 
to get out of the situation. The Attendance Cards, 
Ext. P series, show that the attendance had been 
noted. The evidence of Shri Gambhir is corroborated 
by O.P.W. 4, Shri Hem Chandra Sukla, a part-time 
worker of the concern, whose duty is to maintain 
the Attendance and Wage Registers for the purpose 
of affording benefit which the workers gct under 
the State Insurance Act. It further appears from the 
evidence that the workers forcibly compelled Shri 
Gambhir to remain seated in_his chair and that when 
he tries to get out of the situation, he was pushed 
under and prevented by the workers with respect to 
his movement. The evidence as adduced by the 
employer clearly indicates that the workers resorted 
not merely to a sit-down strike but they kept the 
Management wrongfully confined for long six hours. 
There was apparently a complete break of discipline 
when the workers there took the law in their own 
hand and went to the length of using force upon the 
proprietors and abuse them in most filthy language. 
Naturally, in the broad facts and circumstances as 
proved by evidence, there is no manner of doubt 
that the workers behaved in a most atrocious and 
‘wicked manner and that the acts committed by them 
constitute gross misconduct and insubordination. On 
the next date, i.e., 28th July 1960, the Company put 
up a notice at the factory gate at 6 a.m. wherebv 
the factory was closed for an indifinite period and 
the proprietors informed the workers that they had 
taken a decision to dismiss them from. service. A 
10009 was given in Urdu naturally because most of 
the workers are muslim and are acquainted with Urdu 
language. The Company furnishes a_ transliteration 
of the notice and it is marked as Ext. H. The Union 
filed a copy of the English translation of the notice 
which is marked as Ext. |. It aprears from Ext. 1 
that a copy of the said notice had been forwarded 
to a large number of authorities including some of 
the Ministers of the State. In this connection it is 
to be noted that the Union in paragraph 8 of the 


[Part I 


1202 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 19, 1962 


settled that when a departmental enquiry was not 
done by the Management, the Tribunal should give 
the parties full opportunities to give evidence on the 
point as to whether the charges of misconduct are 
established or not. So, apart from, the fact that there 
was no scope for holding the departmental enquiry 
in the circumstances of the case, I consider upon the 
evidence now adduced before me that the conclusion 
is irresistable that the workers barring Shri Bhupen 
Chandra Paul had been guilty of gross misconduct 
and that the decision of the Management to dismiss 
them can not be interferred with. From the facts 
and circumstances of the case I also take notice of 
the fact on that the Management could reopen the 
factory after long laps of time as during all 015 
period the workmen maintained a threatning attitude 
towards them. The Company lodged complaints at 
the police-station on various dates and the Police 
officers proved the G.D. entires which are marked as 
Ext. A to Ext. A(17). Shri Raj Paul Gambhir, a 
partner of the firm, stated before me that he 
apprehended personal safety as the factory is situated 
in a premises at Phears Lane which is blocked in one 
way and that any violent attitude taken by the 
workers might result in serious consequence on the 
pete and properties of the Company. The appre- 
ension of the proprietors is not unreasonable. : 


In the result I find that the dismissal of 12 work- 
men is justified and that they are not entitled to any 
relief whatsoever. So far as the worker Shri Bhupen 
Paul is concerned, I find his dismissal unjustified and 
direct that he should be reinstated within a month 
from the date of publication of this award. Consider- 
ing however the circumstances of the case, I do not 
consider it appropriate to give him wages for the 
period of his unemployment which should be treated 
as leave without pay. 


This is my award. 
K. K. MITRA, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
22-3-1962.

have been completely redundant in such a situation 
to expect that the proprietor would act as an enquir-

It has been urged by the Union that the employer 
took the decision to dismiss these 13 workmen as 
they were active members of the Trade Union. It 
appears from the evidence that Munif Khan was the 
Secretary of the Union. There is no other evidence 
to show that the other dismissed workers were 
members of the Executive Committee of the Union 
or otherwise acting as active members of the Union. 
Even assuming that some of them were connected 
with the Union Executive Committee, they cannot 
claim any privilage to be execused for such acts of 
gross misconduct.
