No. 984L.—-2nd February 1962.—Whereas I am 
of opinion, as the result of an enquiry held into the 
constitution, working and financial condition of the 
Contai Co-operative, Industrial and Agricultural 
Marketing Society, Ltd. (Registered No. 59 of 
1954), in the Contai subdivision of the district of 
Midnapore, under sub-section (1) of section 84 of 
the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940, that the 
Society ought to be wound up;

by sub-section (1) of section 89 of the Bengal Co- 
operative Societies Act, 1940 (Bengal Act XXI of 
1940), I hereby order the winding-up of the said 
Society.

by section 90 of the said Act, I hereby appoint the 
Inspector of Co-operative Societies, Contai, to be 
Liquidator of the said Society.

charge-sheet to him. So the Union contends that

witness has not been cross-examined on behalf of the 
emplover. S othe evidence of this witness remains

also difficult to understand why the Company follow- 
ed this practice of leaving certain matters unrecorded 
although other matters in that connection are placed 
on the record. It is likely that in any concern of 
this nature, paper work is sought to be reduced to 
the bare minimum but when there is paper work at 
all, there is no reason why it should not be made 
perfectly clear what was being actually done. It is 
thus highly desirable that the officers should be 
trained in expressing themselves concisely but 
clearly.

It is certainly true that the Standing Orders of the 
Company do not provide for any warning notice. 
But then the Industrial Employment Standing Orders 
Act does not provide that the Standing Orders must 
be exhaustive of all the powers which the Manage- 
ment has in the maintenance of discipline in the 
factory. The preamble of the Act provides that 
whereas it 1s expedient to require employers in 
industrial establishments to define with sufficient 
precision the conditions of employment under them 
and to make the said conditions known to workmen 
employed by them. While “Conditions of employ- 
ment” certainly include the terms and conditions on 
which the workmen may be employed in the 
industrial concern, they cannot certainly exhaust 
all the powers of the Management, especially in the 
matter of maintaining discipline in عط‎ establish- 
ment. In this connection reliance was placed by 
both the parties on two awards, one was the award 
of 1933 in the industrial dispute of Cotton Textile 
Industry in West Bengal, Ext. 4, and the other was 
the award in a similar dispute in 1948, Ext. 8. In 
Ext. 4, page 2119, there is a summary of the award 
of 1948 on leave, holidays, working hours and in 
Ext. 4, paragraph 11(6) at page 2669 provides for 
sick leave. This paragraph 1s as follows: 


“As regards sick leave, all employees are eititled 
under the First Award to sick leave with full pay for 
15 days in the year..... In the Mill in this area, 
the exisintg practice of sick leave with pay shall 
continue. This sick leave shall be allowed on the 
basis of a medical certificate from the Medical 
Officer of the Mill or from a qualified and registered 
medical practitioner”. There is nothing in_ the 
award of 1948 which would go to show that when 
a man falls sick and absents himself without 
previous leave, the employer will be entitled to 
require the workman to have a warning recorded in 
the warning register before he should be permitted 
to resume his duties. As a matter of fact, neither of 
the two awards, either expressly or by implication,

On behalf of the Company reliance was placed 
on the Supreme Court decision in the case of Central 
Bank of India Ltd. and Meenakshisundaram, 1959 
L.L.J. Vol 1, page 446 in support of the contention 
that what the Company did in this case did not 
amount to এ tefusal of employment. The Supreme 
Court decision was in respect of a case where a 
Bank employee was transferred and he was directed 
to resume his work from a particulur date. On his 
refusal to so report he was finally warned that failure 
on his part to do so would be treated as voluntary 
ubandonment of service on his part. The employee 
failed to obey such directions. This was pending 
adjudication proceedings before the Sastri Tribunal. 
Sabseaentle the request of the concerned 
employee to allow him to resume his work was 
refused by the Bank. Thereupon the employee 

referred an application under section 23 of the 
ndustrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act com- 
plaining against the refusal of the Bank to give him 
work. The Supieme Court observed that the 
Tribunal! erred in holding that the appellant's action 
amounted to refusal to give work to the_respondent 
and that it would be altogether wrong to suppose 
that this was a case where an emplover had con- 
tinuously refused to give work to his employce 
There was, therefore, no question of any violation 
of any of the provisions of section 33 of the Act by 
the Company I do not see how this case really 
helps the Company.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act filed by Shri Raghu 
Nandan Singh, Durwan, c/o Hind Motors 
Employees’ Union, Uttarpara, Hooghly, against 
Messrs. Hindustan Motors Ltd., Uttarpara, 
Hooghly. (Case No. 56/61 /33A.) 


BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, 
WEST BENGAL 


Present: 


Shri N. B. CHAUDHURI, Judge, Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal. 


AWARD 


This is an application purported to be under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act and the 
complaint is that the applicant, though a permanent 
workman of the opposite party Company, the latter 
has dismissed the former during the pendency of a 
dispute referred to this Tribunal under section 10 
of the Act (vide G.O. No. 6117-1.R., dated 25th 
November 1960) without any proper enquiry and in 
gross violation of rules of natural justice, simply on 
the allegation of a misconduct, though in fact the 
applicant never committed any misconduct. 


The Company files a written statement opposing 
the application on the ground that the provisions 
of section 33(2)(b) were not violated as alleged, and 
that the applicant has rightly been dismissed after a 
proper and bona fide enquiry. It is also urged that 
the Company has already 11190 an application under 
section 33(2)(b) of the Act on 26th April 1961 and 
hence this application is not at all maintainable, 


It may be mentioned here that this application 
has been filed on 4th September 1961, whereas the 
Company filed an application under section 33(2)(b) 
of the Act on 26th April 1961 seeking approval of 
this Tribunal for dismissal of the present applicant. 
It is also not in dispute that the Company's 
application under section 33(2)(b) has already been 
disposed of on contest, and the punishment of the 
applicant by dismissal has already been approved by 
this Tribunal on 20th February 1962. As the law 
stands, where an employer contravenes the provisions 
of section 33 during the pendency of a proceeding 
before a Tribunal, the employee aggrieved by the 


1244 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 26, 1962 


مسجم 4‫ بے 


makes provisions for any such thing. While the 
award of 1948 refers to the existing practice in the 
matter of granting sick leave, it seems to me_ to 
mean no more and_ ono less than what it actually 
says, namely that the existing practice of granting 
sick leave with pay shall continue. It does not seem 
to me to carry any implication about any practice 
as to the methods how this leave should be granted 
or refused or how after a man has absented himself 
on account of alleged sickness, he should be dealt 
with before being permitted to resume his duties. 
The silence of the Awards or the Standing Orders in 
this respect can only mean that the residual discre- 
tionary powers of the Management are left 
untouched. Although, therefore, the Standing 
Orders or the Awards referred to do not provide 
either expressly or by implication for a warning 
being recorded in the warning register when a man 
has turned up for work after having absented 
himself from duty without leave, there is nothing 
in the Standing Orders or in the Awards even to 
Suggest that such a practice was in any way wrong 
or unjustified. As I have already said, these matters 
must be left to the discretion of the Management 
who have to maintain discipline and as long as they 
do not contravene any provisions of the Standing 
Orders or the Awards governing them, it is not open 
to Tribunals to interfere with the discretion exercised 
by the Management in such matters. 


My award therefore is that it was not a case of 
refusal of employment to Shri Gopi alias Gopibandhu 
Jena by the Company but a case of the workman 
having absented himself without leave from the 2nd 
of October 196] and that the application is not main- 
tainable, because there was no question of a viola- 
tion of any of the provisions of section 33 in such 
Case. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

ybjection with which we are concerned in the present 
case. The case in 64 C.W.N., 191, has also been 
cited. This case has nothing in common with the 


present case. In this case, there was a dispute 
between an Education Society and an Employees’ 
Union and it was held on the facts relating to the 
nature of the Education Society that under no 
stretch of circumstances could such an institution 
called an industry. This case cannot be accepted as 
an authority for allowing the preliminary objection 
in the present case which relates to a Company 
which, as I have already indicated above, really, 
carries on the business of letting out an immovable 
property to tenants for the purpose of making 
income. In the case reported in A.LR. 1960, nage 
610 (S.C.) some tests for deciding whether an 
activity amounted to an industry within section 2(}) 
were laid down, but the tests were never Said to be 
exhaustive or conclusive. The present case also 
may be said to satisfy some of the working principles 
laid down in that case, because the facts admitted 
and proved show that the business of house letting 
in the present case has been organised or arranged 
in a manner in which trade or business is generally 
organised or arranged and it is not casual. nor for 
oneself, nor for pleasure and for the purpose of the 
business of the Company, co-operation between the 
employer and the employees for the purpose of 
rendering service to the tenants is essential and the 
workers concerned are mostly employed for the 
purpose of rendering such service, e.g., Liftmen, 
Pumpmen, Sweepers, etc. So. there is no conflict 
between the principles laid down in this Supreme 
Court case and the facts of the present case. The, 
case reported in ۸ھ‎ 60 (S.C.), page 675, las 
hardly any application to the present case because 
it related to a Municipal Corporation. Moreover, 
the present case also satisfies to some extent the 
principles laid down in that case. It was laid down 
in that case that the basic concept of an industry is 
that the activity shall be an organised one and not 
that which pertains to private or personal employ- 
ment. In the present case. the concerned workers 
are employed not for any private or personal ٠٠۰ 
pose but for the purpose of the organised business 
of the Company consisting of letting out the house 
to tenants for income. In the above view of the 
facts of the case and the law applicable thereto, | 
hold that it is a case of industrial dispute hetween 
the Company and its workmen and _ accordingly, I 
reject the preliminary objection against the ۰+ 
tainability of the present reference and the juris- 
diction of the Government to make it and of this 
Tribunal to entertain and adjudicate upon it.

In fixing the above scales of wages and D.A., I 
have taken into consideration the fact that all the 
employees are provided with free quarters in the 
building. This is certainly an amenity which may 
be counted towards special cmoluments of the 
workers. The system of providing free quarters 
shall continue. 


Before parting with these issues, I consider it 
necessirv to specify the time from which the new 
scales of wages and D.A. fixed under issues Nos | 
and 2 shall come into force. It is claimed on behaif 
of the Union that these new scales should be made 


the consolidated wage paid to the workers, I prefer 
to accept the evidence of the Company's Sarkar as 
more competent and reliable. The evidence in 
these respects is practically oath versus oath and in 
the circumstances of the 0850) the oath of the 
Company's Sarkar has impressed me as more 
competent and reliable. It is also to be noticed 
that there is not very much difference between the 
evidence of the two aforesaid witnesses regarding 
the matters discussed above. 


The Union in its charter of demands claimed the 
following scale of pay and dearness allowance for 
Durwans, Liftmen and Jamadar: 


Scales of Pay: Rs. 35—2—47; 
80—4—100; 100—-5—120. 


Dearness Allowance: 
On salary up to Rs. 50—Rs. 50. 
On salary from Rs. 51 to Rs. 100-—Rs. 55. 
On salary above Rs. 101 to Rs. 120-—Rs. 60. 


There is_ no satisfactory evidence to prove the 
actual rent income of the Company from this house 
and the profit which goes to the Company after 
defraying the necessary expenses. On the Company's 
side, there is absolutely no evidence on this point. 
No account book or other document has been pro- 
duced and its only witness, Shri Jyotish Chandra 
Guha (O.P.W. 1), has not said a word about the 
rent-income or the profit. It is at the same time 
significant to note that the Companv has not 
clearly and specifically pleaded in its written state- 
ment, nor has it adduced any evidence at the hear- 
ing to show that the Company is incapable of 
taking any further liability on it by way of increase 
of the wages of the workers and its financial condi- 
tion is such that it would not be in a position to 
bear the burden of higher scales of pay and D.A. 
for the workers. On the Union's side, the Secre- 
tary, Shri Munish Chandra Roy, has stated that the 
monthly rent-income of the Company from this 
building alone is Rs. 37,000. In  cross-examination 
on this point, he has stated that his knowledge in 
this respect is based upon his acquaintance with 
many of the companies which have rented rooms in 
this building and also personal acquaintance with 
Shri Anadi Nown, one of the Directors of the Com- 
pany. His evidence in this respect is not also very 
reliable and it is, in the final analysis, practicallv 
hearsay evidence. Nevertheless, from the fact that 
the Company has not disclosed its income and 
profit from the building, nor has pleaded that its 
financial condition is such that it is unable to pav 
higher scale of wages and D.A. to the workers, it 
may be 5861 inferred that reasonable increases of 
the wages of the employees by fixation of reason- 
able scales of pay and D.A. for the workers will not 
be an unbearable financial burden on the Company. 
Moreover, it is well-settled that where it is found 
that the actual wages paid to the workers are below 
the reasonable minimum standard, it is open to the 
Tribunal to fix a reasonable scale of wages and D.A. 
in order to ensure to the workers at least a reason- 
able standard of living according to their status and 
nature of employment. Company which employs 
workmen must pav reasonable scales of wages and 
D.A. to them so that thev can at least maintain 
ressonable living standard. There is no evidence on 
either side to show the scales of wages and D.A.

I award accordingly under this issue. 


Issues Nos. 5, 6 and 7: Retirement age, Provident 
Fund and Gratuity 


All these issues really arise out of claims relating 
to retirement benefits. After having regard to the 
overall facts and circumstances of the case, I do not 
consider it fair and proper to grant any of these 
claims. In making this decision, ] have followed 
the principles laid down in the case reported in 
1952 L.A.C., page 418, already referred to and dis- 
cussed above in connection with the preliminary 
objection raised by the Company. In that case, the 
only source of income of the Company was from the 
rents from shops and other immovable properties. 
The income was inelastic owing to rent control by 
legislation and the Company gave accommodation 
to the workmen. Upon these facts, it was held that 
as the Company did not carry on any business or 
industry in the “ordinary sense”, the Adjudicator. 
was right in not granting separate schemes of 
Provident Fund and Gratuity. The facts of the 
present case are very similar to the facts of that 
case. Here also the only source of income of the 
Company is from rents of accommodation let out to 
different mercantile firms in the building and the 
tenancies are governed by the West Bengal Premises 
Rent Control Act, which puts a severe check on 
elasticity of rent and this Company also grants free 
quarters to the employees. The principles laid down 
In 1952 L.A.C. case, referred to above in regard to 
the grant of retirement benefits, should apply in the 
present case and accordingly, all the claims for 
retirement benefits must be dismissed. Accordingly, 
1 hold and award that the claims for retirement age, 
provident fund and gratuity are not maintainable and 
these are, therefore, dismissed. 


Issue No. 8: Conditions of permanency 


The evidence discloses that all the concerned 
workmen are employed on permanent basis and 
there is no system of making appointments initially 
on a temporary basis. It is, however, claimed on 
behalf of the Union that some provision should be 
made for conditions of permanency so _ that the 
Company may not introduce the system of tempo- 
rary appointments to the prejudice of the workmen. 
After considering all the facts and circumstances of 
the case, 1 consider it fair and proper to award under 
this Issue that upon completion of satisfactory 
service for six months, every worker must be made 
permanent and ] award accordingly.

Issue No. 3: Working hours 


According to the Union, all these workmen are 
yenerally required to work from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. 
daily and it is claimed that the working hours 
should be limited to eight hours per day with 45 
minutes’ recess. This appears from the evidence of 
P.W. 1 Shri Munish Chandra Roy, the Union Secre- 
tary. According to the evidence adduced on behalf 
of the Company through its Sarkar, Shri Jyotish 
Chandra Guha (O.P.W. 1), the working hours for 
Sweepers and Farashes are from 7 a.m. to 8 a.m. 
in the morning and after 5 p.m. in the evening and 
for Durwans and Liftmen from 8-30 a.m. to 6 p.m. 
with one hour's recess. Having regard 10 the 
undisputed fact that the tenants in the building are 
commercial establishments who have their working 
hours generally from 10 am. to 5 p.m. and 2190 
having regard to the nature of the work required to 
be done by these workmen, I fix the following hours 
for them: 


Sweepers and Farashes:

and 5-00 p.m. to 6-30 p.m. 


For Saturdays: 7-30 am. to 9 am. and 
2-00 p.m. to 3-30 p.m. 
Liftmen and Durwans: 
For full working days: 
For Saturdays: 


9 am. to 6 p.m. 
9 am. to 3 p.m. 


Each of these workers is to be allowed rest for 
one hour on full working days and half-an-hour on 
Saturdays. The rest hours are to be so staggered as 
not to cause any break in the general services 
required of these workmen. 


Pumpmen: Same working 
Durwans and Liftmen 
Pumpman is appointed. 


Issue No. 4: Leave—Casual and Sick 


It is an admitted position that all the employees 
now get 15 days’ leave with full pay in 3 year. 
Besides this leave, the Union claims some casual and 
sick leave. 


After carefully considering the facts and circum- 
stances of the case, | award that besides the leave 
now available to the workers, they shall get casual 
leave for seven days in a year and no further leave. 
I disallow the claim for sick leave.

G.S.R. 1134.—In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) 
of section 4 and sub-section (1) of section 23 of the Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Act, 1954 (37 of 1954), the Central Grovernment after con- 
sultation with the Central Committee for Food Standards, hereby makes the 
following rules further to amend the Prevention of Food Adulteration 
Rules, 1955, the same having been previously published as required by sub- 
section (1) of section 23 of the said Act, namely :— 


1. (1) These rules may be called the Prevention of Food Adulteration 
(Second Amendment) Rules, 1961. 


(2) They shall come into force on the first day of October, 1961.

referred to as the said rules), after rule 44-A, the following rule shall be 
inserted, namely :—

‘AGMARR’ sealed container, in quantities not exceeding 2 kilograms at a 
time and (ii) used in the preparation of confectionery (including sweet- 
meats) 3

rule (1) and (ii) confectionery (including sweetmeats) in the preparation 
of which such ghee is used, shall give a declaration in Form VI-B, to the 
Food Inapector when a sample thereof is taken by him for analysis under 
section 10 of the Act and also to a purchaser desiring to have the sample

stundards of quality prescribed for the aren where it is alleged to have

GOVERNMENT OF ASSAM 
Political (A) Department 


NOTIFICATION 


No. PLA.15/60/Pt.VII/21.—18th December 1961. 
—Whereas the Governor of Assam is Satisfied that 
the pamphlet entitled “Assam Desher Bengali Hatyar 
Kabita” (Poem on Killing of Bengalis in Assam) in 
Bengali, written by Shri Satyendra Chandra Deb 
Nath of Odaypur, post office Bogram, district West 
Dinajpur, West Bengal, and printed at Jatin Press, 
Raygonj (West Bengal), contains matters which 
promote or are intended to promote feelings of 
enmity and hatred between different classes of 
citizens of India, viz., between the Assamese and the 
Bengalees; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred 
by section 99A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1898 (Act V of 1898), the Governor of Assam is 
pleased to declare every copy of the aforesaid 
pamphlet to be forfeited to Government. 


By order of the Governor, 
A. N. KIDWAI, Chief Secy. 


GOVERNMENT OF KERALA 
Home (D) Department 


NOTIFICATION 


G.O. (MS) No. 740.—30th December 1961.-- 
Whereas the Government of Kerala are of opinion, 
after consultation with the Advocate-General, that 
the Malayalam book entitled “Oru Pidi Choaru” poy 
Padiyath, published by Sree Narasimhavilasam Book 
Depot, Thuravoor, Kerala, is a harmful _ publica- 
tion within the meaning of section 2 of the Young 
Persons (Harmful Publications) Act, 1956 (Central 
Act 93 of 1956), as it portrays certain incidents of a 
repulsive nature which would tend to corrupt young 
persons into whose hands it might fall; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers 
conferred by section 4 of the said Act the Govern- 
ment of Kerala hereby declare that every copy of 
the said book shall be forfeited to the Government. 


By order of the Governor, 
P. I. JACOB, Secy.

ciigible to receive the medal of the same class, such 
further act of humane service shall be recognised by 
a Bar to be attached to the riband by which the medal 
is suspended and, for every subsequent act of humane 
service, an additional Bar shall be added and such 
Bar or Bars may also be awarded posthumously. 
For every such Bar, a replica of the medal in minia- 
ture shall be added to the riband when worn alone. 


Tenthly.—-If a recipient of the medal of any of the 
three classes shall again perform such an act of 
humane service as would have made him or her 
eligible for the award of a medal of a class different 
from the one already received, such further act of 
humane service shall be recognised by the award of 
another medal of the appropriate class. On those 
occasions, when only the riband is worn, an additional 
riband pertaining to the appropriate class shall also 
be worn. 


Eleventhly.—The miniature medal which may be 
worn on certain occasions by recipients shall be half 
the size of the medal, and a sealed pattern of the 
Said miniature medal shall be deposited and kept. 


Twelfthly.—The President may cancel and annul 
the award of the medal to any person and thereupon 
the name of such recipient in the Register shall be 
erased and the recipient shall be required to surrender 
the insignia; but it shall be competent for the 
President to restore the decoration when 5101) 
cancellation and annulment has been withdrawn.

of the said Act, by Shri Sudhir Kumar Mandal, Purapara, police-station

Election Petition No. 71 of 1962 
BEFORE THE ELECTION COMMISSION, NEW DELHI 


In the Matter of an_ election petition under the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951 


And 


In the Matter of purported election for KAhargram 
Legislative Assembly Constituency, Murshidabad, 
West Bengal, held on the 18th February 1962 


And 
In the Matter of 


Sudhir Kumar Mandal, residing at Purapara,

daha, in the district of Murshidabad, Petitioner 


versus 


Abhay Pada Saha, residing at Bharatpore, 
police-station and post office Bharatpore in the 
district of Murshidabad, Respondent. 


The humble petition of the abovenamed petitioner most respectfully 
Sheweth : 


1. At all material times your petitioner was, and is a citizen of India, 
and a person whose age was more than 25 years. Your petitioner is an 
elector as defined in section 2(e) of the Representation of the People Act, 
1951 (hereinafter referred to as the ‘‘said Act’’), and neither is nor was 


54 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, APRIL 26, 1962 [Part IA 
eee on 


subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in section 16 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1950. Your petitioner’s name is entered 
as Serial No. 512 in Part 152 of the electoral roll of the 49—Khargram 
Legislative Assembly Constituency in West Bengal. 


2. Your petitioner possesses all qualifications necessary for membership 
of the State Legislatures as prescribed by or under the Constitution of any 
law made by the Parliament. 


3. Your petitioner being a member of Konai caste is a member of the 
Scheduled Castes specified in the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 
1950, in relation to West Bengal Legislative Assembly in the First and 
Second General Elections held in the years 1952 and 1957 from the Kandi 
Legislative Assembly Constituency seat reserved for Scheduled Castes. 


4. On the 18th day of February 1962 the General Election of a member 
of West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khuargram Legislative 
Assembly Constituency, reserved for members of the Scheduled Castes of 
West Bengal was held; and your petitioner and the respondent were candi- 
dates for election from the seat of the said Constituency reserved for members 
of Scheduled Castes. The symbols chosen by and allotted to your petitioner 
and the respondent under the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961, were as 
stated hereunder: — 


Your petitioner—Two bullocks with yoke on. 
Respondent—Spade and stoker. 


9, On the 26th day of February 1962 the Returning Officer of the 
said Constituency declared the result of the said election and returned the 
respondent as duly elected. In the return of election and the final result- 
sheet 16,739 valid votes were shown to have been polled in favour of the 
respondent and 15,523 in favour of your petitioner. The respondent 
purported to secure 1,216 votes more than those cast in your petitioner’s 
favour. 


_ 6. Your petitioner states that the purported election of the respondent 
is void and liable to be set aside inter ulia on the following grounds: — 


(a) That the result of the said election in so far as it concerns the 
respondent has been materially affected by the improper rejec- 
tion of many valid votes cast in your petitioner's favour. 
Particulars of such improper rejections will ie given after dis- 
covery and inspection of the rejected ballot papers numbering 
1,216. 

(b) That the result of the said election in so far as it concerns the 
respondent has been materially affected by the improper 
reception of a large number of votes, as many ballot papers 
purporting to bear the mark on the respondent’s symbol did not 
appear to have been marked with the instrument supplied by the 
polling authorities. 


(c) That on the date of his election the respondent was not qualified 
and/or was disqualified to be chosen to fill the seat (reserved 
for a member of the Scheduled Castes in West Bengal), under 
the Constitution and the Representation of the People Act. 


Particulars 


(i) The Respondent is a member of the Saha caste and not a member 
of any of Scheduled Castes specified in Vart XIII of the 
Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950. The respondent 
was not mentioned or described in the nomination papers filed 
before the Returning Officer to be a member of the Sunri 
caste, which 1s a Scheduled Caste specified in the Constitution 
(Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, but was described as a ‘‘Saha’’; 
and the objections taken by your petitioner in this behalf as to 
the eligibility of the respondent for nomination as a candidate 
for election from the said Constituency on the ground that 
he was not member of the ‘‘Sunri’’ caste was summarily 
rejected on January 22, 1962, without making any enquiry or 
taking any evidence, on the basis of the declaration purported 
to have been made by the respondent in the hody of the 
nomination paper in the prescribed form. 


(11) That the respondent is also disqualified to be chosen to fill the 
seat under the provisions of Article 191 of the Constitution of 


India read with sections 6 and 7 of the Representation of the 
People Act, 1951.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
BENGAL ENGINEERING COLLEGE 
P.O. Botanic Garden, Howrah 


THE Bengal Engineering College will open next 
session on July 2, 1962. The College 15 a residential 
one and offers courses for the B.E. Degree Examina- 
tion of the Calcutta University in Civil, Mechanical, 
Electrical, Metallurgical, Mining and Tele-communi- 
cation Engineering and also for the Degree in 
Architecture. Admission will be granted on the 
results of an admission test consisting of a written 
examination for all candidates to be conducted by 
the “West Bengal Board of Examination for ۰ی‎ 
sion to Engineering Colleges” as per dates given 
below which will be followed by a medical [23 and 
viva-voce test. Applications must be made in the 
prescribed form with a crossed Indian Postal Order 
showing deposit of Rs. 12 (Rs. 6 being the registra- 
tion fee payable to the Board plus Rs. 6 payable to 
each College to which admission is sought) payable 
to the “West Bengal Board of Examination for admis- 
sion to Engineering Colleges” and should seach the 
Office of the Board, c/o Bengal Engineering College, 
P.O. Botanic Garden, Howrah, on or before April 
18, 1962. The College prospectus and _ requisite 
application forms may be obtained from the college 
Office either personally or by sending an unstamped 
self-addressed envelope of 10”X4}” size on and 
from 26th March 1962. A number of scholarships 
and stipends will be awarded to meritorious 
students on the results of the Admission Test. 
Applications for the Five-year intcgrated degree 
course under the new regulations of the Calcutta 
University will be entertained from candidates who 
have either passed or will appear this year in the

Stores Committee.

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 


NOTICE 


Dated the 2nd March 1962 


NOTICE is hereby given for the information of the 
public that the Corporation of Calcutta under powers 
vested unto it, has by its resolution, dated the 29th 
December 1961, prescribed the alignments of two 
30 ft. projected streets, i.e., (a) one running north to 
South connecting Fern Road with a 30 ft. road con- 
structed by industhan Corporation Insurance 
Society Ltd. (now Ekdalia Place) and (b) the other 
running east to west connecting Ballygunge Station 
Road with aforesaid 30 ft. road under section 356 
read with section 363 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 
1951, as shown in the plan prepared for the purpose 
in Ward No. 61 (old No. 27), 


A copy of plan prepared in this behalf may be 
seen in the office of the Chief Valuer and Surveyor on 
any working day during the hours of 11 a.m. and 
2 p.m. on payment of usual fees. 


P. C. MAJUMDAR, Commissioner.

NOTICE 
Calcutta, the 5th March 1962. 


Notice is hereby given under section 47(3) of the 
Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911, that the Board of 
Trustees for the Improvement of Calcutta have 
applied to the State Government for sanction to the 
Improvement Scheme No. LXXXII (Shyam Bose 
Road, Chetla) which was first published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette” and in local newspapers on the 
6th Julv 1961.

CALCUTTA IMPROVEMENT TRUST 


THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES FOR THE IMPROVE- 
MENT OF CALCUTTA 


Notice under section 43 of the Calcutta Improvi ment 
Act, 1911 (Bengal Act V of 1911) 


SCHEME NO. LXXIII (AREA BETWEEN PARK 
CIRCUS AND LINTON STREET) 


IT is hereby notified under section 43 of the Calcutta 
Improvement Act, 1911, that a General Improvement 
Scheme (to be known as Scheme No. LXXIII) for the 
purpose of developing the area between Park Circus 
and Linton Street by providing building sites, 
remedying defective ventilation, creating mew or 
improving existing means of communication and 
facilities for traffic, affording better facilities for con- 
Servancy and rehousing bustee-dwellers likely to be 
displaced, has becn framed by the Board of Trustees 
for the Improvement of Calcutta in the above area

Short recital of the case 


A dispute arose between Raymon’ Engineering 
Works Ltd. (hereafter to be mentioned 25 the 
Company) and their workmen on the Company’s 
terminating the services of three workmen, namely, 
(1) Biswanath Das, (2) Pannalal Bhattacharjee, and 
(3) Shyamal Bose on the charges mentioned in the 
Company's written statement submitted 00 the 
Tribunal. The matter was referred to the Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal for adjudication by West Bengal 
Government order No. 4208-IR/IR/10L-159(A)/61, 
dated 3rd July 1961. 


In the meantime, the parties have had long dis- 
cussions among themselves and ultimately an amic- 
able settlement was arrived at on the following 
terms: 


(1) That out of the three workmen mentioned 
above, the Company will take back (rein- 
State) Shri Biswanath Das and he will be 
paid compensation equivalent to 84 davs’ 
wages, including dearness allowance, for the 
entire period of his unemployment after 
dismissal till the date of his reinstatement. 
Continuity of his service, however, will be 
maintained and the period will be treated as 
leave without pay. 


The issues framed ہ۱۸‎ this caSe are as under: 


(1) Whether the termination of services of Shri 
Pannalal Bhattacharvya and Shri Shama! 
Bose is justified? To what relief, if any, ar- 
they entitled? 


(2) Whether the 5051৮551011 and refusal of employ- 
ment to Shri Biswanath Das is justified? To 
what ۱٥۱٥١٢١ if any, is he entitled? 


AWARD 


It may be mentioned that the issue 1 
framed by the Government was worded in a different 
form. However, by a corrigendum, dated the 3151 
October 1962, as referred to above, the issue was 
recast and given the above form. There has been 
however, no substantial change in the matter of 
reference. After the receipt of the original order of 
reference, notices were issued as usual to both the 
parties, and both the parties entered appearance and 
filed their respective written statements also. After 
receipt of the corrigendum mentioned above, both 
parties were given fresh option to file additional state- 
shents, if any, but neither party did actually file any 
additional statement. On 8th February 1960, how- 
ever, the parties filed a joint petition of compromise 
after settling their dispute out of Court. I have 

efully gone through the terms of settlement, and 

ink that the terms are nof only lawful but fair 
and reasonable also. So, the petition of compromise 
is recorded, and the award is passed in terms thereof. 
The joint petition of compromise inclusive of 19 
Annexure A (bipartite agreement) will form part of 
this award, and it is marked as Annexure (F) to this 
award. f think, Both the parties deserve apprecia- 
Hon fot stiowing this commendable spirit of con- 
Giliation and making an amicable settlement of the 
dispute.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS, 


The West Benga) Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 (West 
Bengal Act IJ of 1948) will cease to be in force after the 19 March, 1962. 


2. The Act provides for an expeditious way of acquiring land for 
certain public purposes after going through requisition at the initial stage. 
For getting quick possession of lands required for various urgent develop- 
ment projects already undertaken und to be undertaken under the Five 
Year Plans, it is necessary to retain the Act. The life of the Act was 
accordingly extended for a further period of five years from the Ist April, 
1 promulgation of the West Bengal Land (Requisition and 
রে (Amendment) Ordinance, 1962 (West Benyal Ordinance No. I 
of 1962). 


3. The Bill seeks to enact the provisions of the aforesaid Ordinance.

1262 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, MARCH 15, 1962 


AWARD 


This is an application by Shri Sheo Nandan Singh 
against his employet Messrs. Hindusthan Motors 
Ltd., purported to be under section 33A of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act. The petitioner's case is that he 
had been working as a darwan with a clean record 
of service. On 25th March 1961 he was wrongly 
charge-sheeted by the management on a frivolous 
ground and dismissed him with effect from 26th 
April 1961 without any proper enquiry and without 
giving him any reasonable opportunity to defend 
himself. Thus, it is alleged his dismissal was in con- 
travention of the provisions of section 33 of the Act. 


The Company on the other hand inter aiia alleges 
that in fact and law there was no contravention of 
the provisions of section 33 of the Act and hence 
this present application is not maintainable. The 
petitioner failed or negiected to attend his usual 
parade from 27th February 1961 although he was 
cautioned in that connection on different dates. He 
was charge-sheeted for this major misdemeanour and 
after proper enquiry and due compliance of all rules 
of natural justice, he was dismissed for disobedience 
of a Jawful and reasonable order of a superior. 


Points for decision are— 


Issues 


(1) whether the application is maintainable as 
such? 


(2) what relief, if any, is the applicant entitled 
to? 


Decision 


*It will be clear from the written statement of the 
Company that it actually filed an application under 
section 33 of the Act on 1188 May 1961 for approval 
of the punlshment by dismissal of Shri Singh. It is 
also not in dispute that the application under section 
33 of the Act has been allowed on contest and the 
approval sought by the employer has been actually 
granted on 13th October 1961. It may be mentioned 
in this connection that the Company filed its petition 
under section 33 of the Act on 11th May 196] and 
the workman entered appearance in that case on 
15th June 1961 and filed its written statement also 
on 6th July 1961. The hearing of the application 
was taken up on 7th September 1961 and concluded 
on 8th September 1961. Yet the workman filed the 
present application under section 33A on 4th Sep- 
tember 1961, knowing fully well that the other 
application was pending from long before. From the 
annexure 1) of the present application it appears that 
this petitioner darwan was dismissed with effect from 
۱1:١ May 1961 and not 26th April 1961, as alleged 
by him in his application. Thus the application 
under section 33 of the Act was filed simultaneously 
with the dismissal of the workman. Be that as it 
may, the fact remains that the approval under section 
33 of the Act has already been given by this Tribunal 
and so there is no scope for a complaint under 
section 33A of the Act. It is not open to the 
Tribunal any longer to treat its previous order as a 
nullity on an application under section 33A and pass 
an Award on such an application. So no relief is 
open to the petitioner under section 33A of the Act. 
The remedy, if any. of the workman lies under some 
other provisions of law and he may also raise an 
industrial dispute according to law. So I find that 


12621) 


personal malice. The fact, which according to his 
statement before me is responsible for this personal 
malice, was Shri Singha’s complaint against Shri 
Mukherjee before the Assistant Registrar but as that 
complaint was made, as is clear from Ext. C, only 
after the dismissal of Shri Singha, it is at once 
obvious that there is no truth whatever in the allega- 
tion of Shri Singha, that Shri Aswini Kumar 
Mukherjee made a false complaint against him ‘out 
of enmity, resulting from Shri Singha’s complaint 
against Shri Mukherjee before the Assistaat Registrar 
of Co-operative Societies. As this turns out clearly 
to be false, the ground for disbelieving the statement 
of Shri Mukherjee before the enquiring officer 
disappears. 


As regards the incident itself, there is on the 
record of the enquiry a good deal of evidence on 
which on both the charges, the conclusions arrived 
at by the enquiring officer, appear to be amply 
justified. The Standing Orders of the Company are 
Ext. 7. Under section 13(i) of the Standing Orders 
and under section }3(xi), wilful insubordination or 
disobedience of any lawful and reasonable order of 
a superior and disorderly behaviour, threatening a 
superior or.a person in authority are major mis- 
demeanours for which a workman is liable to 
demotion or dismissal without notice. Thus, under 
the Standing Orders, the dismissal of Shri Mukunda 
Murari Singha would be justified even if there was 
nothing else against him, but Ext. 10 shown there 
was a Similar charge against him on the 3rd_ of 
November 1960 also and that in this letter (Ext. 10), 
Shri Singha stated amongst other things that he was 
expressing his regret for the whole affair and would 
request the Management to view his offence leniently 
and excuse him from the charge served on him and 
for this, he would remain grateful. He concluded by 
Saying that mercy should be shown to him. In his 
cross-examination, Shri Singha admits before me 
Ext. 10 to have been signed by him, but he says that 
the word ‘mercy’ was not there and the word that 
was actually there was ‘pardon’. There was no trace 
of the word ‘mercy’ having been over-written on any 
other word, nor is there any mark of any erasure to 
confirm this statement of Shri Singha. But even if 
this evidence of Shri Singha could be taken at its 
face value, the replacement of the word ‘pardon’ by 
the word ‘mercy’ does not make any difference to 
the contents of the letter and on the evidence of 
Shri Singha himself, Ext. 10 which bears his genuine 
Signature is a letter of apology for an incident of a 
similar nature. Quite clearly then, Shri Singha was 
guilty on a similar charge on one other occasion, so 
as to justify the Management in ordering his 
dismissal. 2 


My award accordingly is that the dismissal of Shri 
Mukunda Murari Singha is justified and that he is 
not entitled to any relief. 

Dictated and corrected by me.

Karmachari Sangha, the only issue is whether the 
dismissal of Shri Mukunda Murari Singha is justified 
and to what relief, if any,-he is entitled. 


Admittedly, in consequence of an incident between 
Shri Aswinit Kumar Mukherjee, the assistant head 
clerk of the Company and Shri Mukunda Murari 
Singha, the workman concerned in this dispute, 
there was a complaint against the latter by the 
former. This was followed up by a charge-sheet 
against him by the Company. There was an enquiry 
into this charge-sheet and a number of witnesses was 
examined for the Company and for Shri Singha. As 
a result of the enquiry, the two charges against Shri 
Singha were found to be proved and Shri Singha was 
served with a notice (Ext. 6), dated the 17th of May 
1961, dismissing him from the Company’s _ service 
with immediate effect. The complaint of Shri Aswini 
Kumar Mukherjee is Ext. 1, dated the 17th of April 
1961. The charge-sheet is Ext. 2, dated the 10th of 
April 1961. Exhibit 3 is Shri Singha’s explanation and 
Ext. 4 is the record of enquiry and Ext. 5 the report 
of the enquiring officer. 


Before me were examined only two witnesses, one 
for the Company, namely, Shri P. K. Sur, the 
Assistant Manager of the Company, who held the 
enquiry and submitted the report, and one for the 
Union. namely, Shri Mukunda Murari Singha 
himself, 


The officer holding the enquiry, has no personal 
knowledge of the incident that led to the charge- 
Shect against Shri Singha and the enquiry. He 
merely proves the record of the proceedings. Shri 
Singha denies the allegations made against him by 
Shri Aswini Kumar Mukhcriee and says that he had 
quarrels with Shri Mukheriee because Shri Mukherjee 
as the Secretary of the Badminton and Recreation 
Club and also of the Co-operative Society had 
refused to pay him his salary as a part-time employee 
of the Co-operative Society, although this salary was 
shown in the cash-book as having been paid to him. 
He also claims in his examination-in-chief to have 
reported this to the Assistant Registrar of Co-opera- 
tive Societies against Shri Aswini Kumar Mukherjee. 
But he admits in his cross-examination that he stated 
during the enquiry that he had great friendship with 
Shri Mukherjee and a very long-standing friendship. 
[1 further appears from his own application (Ext. C), 
dated the 26th of June 1961. that he applied to the 
Acsistant Registrar after he had been already served 
with the notice of dismissal by Ext. 6, dated the 17th 
of Mav 1961. As a matter of fact, in Eyt. C he 
mentioned the fact of his discharge. It is thus 
Qbvious that the impression which Shri Singha 
wanted to produce on the Tribunal that there was 
an enmity between him and Shri Aswini Kumar 
Mukherjee and that in consequence of this enmity, 
Shri Aswini Kumar Mukherjee made a false com- 
plaint against him, is entirely incorrect. On the other 
hand. his clear statement before the enquiring 
officer which he admits in his cross-examination 
before me, was that he and Shri Mukherjee were 
Sreat friends for a long time and that he was very 
much aggrieved when he found that Shri Mukherjee 
had complained against him. He appears there to 
have ascribed Shri Mukherjee’s complaint against 
him to the instigations of Dhiren Babu and De Babu. 
Clearly then, during the enquirv there was not any 
Suggestion trom Shri Singha that Shri Mukherjee 
was actuated in filing a complaint against him by

the valve testing and against the unusual heat of 
450° F., and that there were many accidents and 
cases of burn injury to the workmen who were

whether the workmen while engaged in the operation

The case made by the Union in its written state-

tection against the steam that might be escaping at

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act filed by Shri Nani 
Gopal Chakrabarty, c/o Secretary, Howrah 
Jela Bus Karmi Parishad of 4/1 Muktaram 
Babu Debnath Lane, post office Santragachi, 
Howrah, against Shri Ashutosh Kundu, owner 
of bus No. W.B.U. 73 of 20 Nilmani Mullick 
Lane, Howrah (Case No. 95 u,s 33A of 1961). 


BEFORE THE SEVENTH INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Present: 
Shri S. K. RAY, Judge, Seventh Industrial Tribunal. 


AWARD 


This is an application under section 33A, Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, by Shri Nani Gopal Chakrabarty 
against Shri Ashutosh Kundu, the Opposite Party. 


The complaint made in the application is sub- 
Stantially that the applicant was a permanent 
employee in a public bus bearing No. W.B.U. 73, 
owned and operated by the opposite party on a 
certain route in Howrah, but the applicant was 
illegally dismissed from service by the opposite 
party in the circumstances alleged in the applica- 
tion without complying with the provisions of 
section 33, Industrial Disputes Act, during the 
pendency of the adjudication proceedings of another 
dispute between the opposite party and his work- 
men, which was referred for adjudication to this 
Tribunal by the Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department order No. 4083-I.R./1IR/4L- 
34/59, dated the 2nd August 1960. The applicant 
claims reinstatement to his service under the 


Opposite party with continuity of service and all 
back wages. 


After service of notice of the present application 
upon the opposite party, he entered appearance 
through a_ representative, but no written state- 
ment was finally filed on his behalf though several 
adjournments were taken for the purpose. The 
applicant too defaulted in appearance on_ several 
dates up to 15th January 1962. On 15th January 
1962 the Tribunal suo moto adjourned the case to 
30th January 1962, directing that the case would be 
disposed of according to law if no written statement 
was filed within 12 am. on that date, On 


In four years, according to Shri Shastri, safety valves 
were lifted on 250 occasions. That works roughly 
at 62 or 63 occasions a year. Actually there are 16 
boilers in this generating station, and each boiler 
has four valves. Every boiler is surveyed once a 
year under the Boilers Act. After surveying, the 
safety valves are floated once a year, so that four 
boiler suits only would be necessary for the purpose. 
The cost of these four boiler suits, according to the 
estimate given by the Secretary of the Union, is only 
Rs. 43 and these boiler suits would last for about 
2/3 years according to the evidence of the Secretary. 
That the Company would be resisting a claim which 
would cost it only Rs. 43 once in two or three years 
if it were really needed, seems to me to be incredible 
and on the evidence, I think, it must be held that 
there is really no necessity for boiler suits for the 
workmen when they are engaged in the floating of 
safety valves in boilers. As to the contention of the 
Union that this work was suddenly transferred to 
the workmen of the Boiler House Maintenance 
Department as a measure of harassment in July 1960 
when this particular Union was formed, I may sav 
at once that as the Union has led no evidence what- 
ever to show that any workman of this department 
took any part in the formation of the Union to the 
knowledge of the Company, even the Secretary to 
the Union having been admittedly attached to some 
other department, it is impossible to find that therc 
is any truth in this allegation. 


My award accordingly is that the workmen while 
engaged in the operation of floating safety valves in 
boilers need not be furnished by the Company with 
boiler suits. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


S. N. GUHA ROY, 
Judge.

Judge, First Industrial Tribunal.

dated 215 ؟‎ March 1958, for adjudication which has 
been replaced by the Sixth Industrial Tribunal

Issue

রে SE OST Se রি‏ ہے 


K. K. Maitra হা the Company. None 
turned up from the side of the workmen. I heard 
the matter ex parte. 


It appears that the Company raises a preliminary 
objection regarding the maintainability of this case 
on the ground that not a single workmen engaged in 
this concern is a member of the New Allenberry 
Works Employees’ Union, which is shown as the 
particular Trade Union representing the workmen 
in the order of reference. It is accordingly alleged 
that the Union has no locus standi to raise anv 
industrial dispute as contemplated under the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act. Prima facie the onus is upon 
the Union to show that the workers of the industry 


are connected by membership with the Trade Union, 


organisation representing the workmen. Apparently, 
when the Union is not coming forward to proceed 
with the case and lead evidence challenging the con- 
tention of the employer, I take it that this Union 
does not represent the workmen of the Industry and, 
as such, it has no locus standi to proceed with the 
dispute. Besides, the fact that the Union is not 
eager to rroceed with the case, lends sunport to the 
employers’ version that there is no existence of anv 
dispute. The Tribunal cannot obviously proceed to 
adjudicate upon a dispute which is not being sup- 
ported by the workers or by any Trade Union in 
which the workers are alleged to be connected as 
being members of the same. In the circumstances, I 
pass a ‘no dispute’ award. 


K. K. MITRA, Judge, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 19th February 1962.

Decisions 


For proper appreciation of the present case, J 
shall incidentally mention certain other facts. The 
matter in dispute in the present case has rather a 
chequered career. 1 have already mentioned that a 
charge-shect was issued against the workman, Shri 
Pandey, in respect of an incident, dated 2nd Julv 
1955. The charge-sheect was actually issued against 
him on 4th July 1955. But from before this Jate, 


a reference under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act was pending before a_ Tribunal in 
respect of certain other disputes between the 
Company and its workmen. After issue of this 


charge-sheet, the Management purported to hold 
some sort of enquiry against Shri Pandey and 
decided to dismiss him. Accordingly, on 18th July 
1955 or so the Management filed an application 
under section 33 of the Act before the said Tribunal. 
On or about the same date, Shri Pandey also filed 
a complaint under section 33A of the Act before the 
same Tribunal on the allegation that the Manage- 
ment had violated the provisions of section 33 of the 
Act. During the pendency of these two applications 
on 6th October 1955, the Tribunal concerned passed 
an award in respect of the original dispute under 
section 10 of the Act. Thus the Tribunal became 
functus officio in respect of the application under 
section 33 of the Act by 6th November 1955. 
Nevertheless, the application under section 33A of 
the Act remained pending. Sometime  thercafter, 
appeals were preferred before the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal against the award passed by the said 
Tribunal. On Ist December 1955 the Company 
informed Shri Pandev that it would seck permission 
of the Labour Appellate Tribunal under section 22 
of the Act for dismissing him as previously decided. 
After this intimation, on 13th February 1956 Shri 
Pandey filed an application under section 23 of the 
Act before the Labour Appellate Tribunal. On 16th 
February 1956 the Company actually filed an 
application under section 22 of the Act before 
the Labour Appellate Tribunal seeking approval 
for dismissal of Shri Pandey. The Company 
filed another application also under section 22 of 
the Act before the Labour Appellate Tribunal 
seeking approval for action taken against another 
durwan named Keshoram Dubey charge-sheeted in 
connection with the same incident. On 30th April 
1956 Shri Pandey withdrew his application under 
section 33A of the Act pending before the Industrial 
Tribunal. On 3rd May 1956 all the three applications 
under sections 22 and 23 of the Act pending before 
the Labour Appellate Tribunal were heard together. 
The Labour Appellate Tribunal in its judgment not 
only directed the Management to hold fresh enquirv 
into the charge levelled against Shri Pandey, but 
fave certain other directions also regarding his 
Suspension, subsistence allowance and_ interim

Pandey on the results of the thorough enquiry, and 
nothing more. Neither Mr. Jacks nor the Assistant 
Manager has been examined before this Tribunal, 
and so this Tribunal is not in a position to know 
what were the materials or reasons, if any, on which 
the Management based its own conclusion. As the 
bona fides and justification of the Management 
decision is challenged by the workmen concerned, 
I am required to consider whether the Management 
has been guilty of a basic error or whether on the 
materials the finding of the Management 5أ‎ 
completely baseless or perverse. The principle in 
this connection has been enunciated by their lord- 
ships of the Supreme Court while deciding the case 
of Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. and another vs. 
Their workmen (1958 S.C. 130), and I may quote 
below the observations of their lordships on the 
point: 

“Undoubtedly the Management of a concern 
has power to direct its own internal administra- 
tion and discipline; but the power 15 not unlimited 
and when a dispute arises, Industrial Tribunals 
have been given the power to see whether the 
termination of service of a workman 19 justified 
and to give appropriate relief. In case of 
dismissal on misconduct, the Tribunal does not, 
however, act as a court of appeal and substitute 
its own judgment for that of the Management. 
It will interfere— 


(i) when there is want of good faith, 


(ii) when there is victimisation or unfair 
labour practice, 


(111) when the Management has been guilty 
of a basic error or violation of a principle of 
natural justice, and 


(iv) when on the matcrials, the finding is 
completely bascless or perverse.” 


In a case reported in 1952 L.A.C. 490 (Buckingham 
& Carnatic Co. Ltd.) it has 0০61) held that in all 
these cases the requirement of bona fides is essential. 
The termination of service in colourable exercise of 
the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair 
labour practice or caprice should be prevented. 
Arbitrary conduct or unnecessary harshness on the 
part of the employer judged by the normal standard 
of a reasonable man may be cogent evidence of 
victimisation or unfair labour practice. Where no

After service ot notice of tiie present application 
upon the opposite party, he entered appearance 
through a represeutative, but no written statement 
was finally filed on his behalf though several adjourn- 
ments were taken for the purpose. The applicant 
too defaulted in appearance on several dates up to

Tribunal suo moto adjourned the case to 30th 
January 1962, directing that the case would be 
disposed of according to law if no written state- 
ment was filed within 12 am. on that date. On 
30th January 1962 Shri M. Saha, Advocate, appeared 
for the applicant, but on an application for adjourn- 
ment made on behalf of the opposite party, the 
case was adjourned to 16th February 1962 with the 
same directions as on the 15th January 1962. There 
was no appearance for the opposite party on 16th 
February 1962, but an application for adjournment 
was again made on behalf of the applicant and 
upon this application, the case was adjourned to 
23rd February 1962 for peremptory hearing with 
the direction that no further time would be allow- 
ed. On 23rd February 1962 none appeared for 
either side and no step was taken. It is clear from 
the non-appearance of the parties on the final 0400 
of hearing, 23rd February 1962, that the complaint 
under section 33A, Industrial Disputes Act, is not 
pressed and pursued by the applicant and the dis- 
pute arising out of the alleged dismissal of the 
concerned worker in contravention of section 33, 
Industrial Disputes Act, has ceased to exist. In 
view of this position, the complaint under section 
33A, Industrial Disputes Act, is to be dismissed as 
not pressed and an award is to be made that the 
dispute referred to in the application has ceased to 
exist. 


In the result, I dismiss the complaint under 
section 33A, Industrial Disputes Act, as not pressed 
and also award that the dispute referred to in 0০ 
application under section 33A has ceased to exist.

PART V—Acts of the Parliament of India assented to by the President and 
Ordinances promulgated by the President 


COVERNMENT OF INDIA 
Ministry of Law 
(Legislative Department) 


_The following Ordinance was promulgated by the 
President on the Sth March, 1962, and is hereby published 
for general information :— 


THE GOA, DAMAN AND DIU (ADMINISTRATION) 
ORDINANCE, 1962 


No. 2 OF 1962 
[Sth March, 1962. | 


Promulgated by the President in the Thirteenth Year of the 
Republic of India. 


An Ordinance to provide for the administration of the Union 
territory of Goa, Daman and Diu and for matters 
connected therewith. 


Whereas the territories comprised in Goa, Daman and 
Diu have been acquired with effect from the twentieth 
day of December, 1961, and have, by virtue of sub-clause (c) 
ot clause (3) of article 1 of the Constitution, been comprised 
within the territory of India; 


AND WHERFAS it is expedient to make provision for the 
administration of the said territories; 


AND WHEREAS Parliament is not in session and the 
President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render 
it necessary for him to take immediate action; 


Now, THEREFORE, in exercise of the powers conferred by 
clause (1) of article 123 of the Constitution, the President is 
pleased to promulgate the following Ordinance :— 


1. (Z) This Ordinance may be called the Goa, Daman Short title 
and I)iu (Administration) Ordinance, 1962. and com- 


(2) It shall come into force at once. ee 


ment, 
1305a 


)0 ৬ 


1962 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, MARCH 19, 


1305b 


পি স্টল ক 


2. In this Ordinance, unless the context othorwise 
requires, — 


(a) ‘‘Administrator” means the Administrator of Goa, 
Daman and Jieu; 


(9) “appointed day’’ means the twentieth day of 
December, 1961; 


(c) ‘Goa, Daman and Diu’’ means the Union territory 
ot Goa, Daman and Diu. 


3. Without prejudice to the powers of the Central 
Government to appoint from time to time such 
officers and authorities as may be necessary for the 
administration of Goa, Daman and Diu, all judges, magis- 
trates and other officers and authorities who, immediately 
before the commencement of this Ordinance, were exercising 
lawful functions in connection with the administration of 
Goa, Damani and Diu or any part thereof shall, unless 
otherwise directed at any time by the Central Government in 
relation to any such judge, magistrate or other officer or 
authority, or until other provision is made by law, continue 
to exercise in connection with such administration their 
respective functions in the same manner and to the same 
extent as before such commencement ‘with such altered 
designation, if any, as that Government may determine. 


4. (/) All laws in force immediately before the appointed 
day in Goa, Daman and Diu or any part thereof shall 
continue to be in force therein until amended or repealed 
by a competent Legislature or other competent authority. 


(2) For the purpose of facilitating the application of any 
such law in relation to the administration of Goa, Daman 
and Diu as a Union territory and for the purpose of bringing 
the provisions of any such law into accord with the provisions 
of the Constitution, the Central Government may within 
two years from the appointed day, by order, make such 
adaptations and modifications, whether by way of repeal or 
aniendment, as may be necessary or expedient and thereupon 
every such law shall have effect subject to the adaptations 
and modifications so made. 


5. The Central Government may, by notification in the 
Official Gazette, extend with such restrictions or modifica- 
tions as it thinks fit, to Goa, Daman and Diu any enactment 
which is in force in a State at the date of the notification. 


6. For the purpose of facilitating the application of any 
jaw in relation to Goa, Daman and Diu, any court or other 
authority may construe any such law in such manner not 
affecting the substance, as may be necessary or proper to 
adapt it to the matter before the court or other authority. 


7. (4) All things done and all action taken (including 
any acts of executive authority, proceedings, decrees and 
sentences) in or with respect to Goa, Daman and 1018 on or 
after the appointed day and hefore the commencement of 
this Ordinance, by the Administrator or any other officer of 
(xovernment, whether civil or military, or by any other 
peraon acting under the orders of the Administrator or such 
officer, which have been done or taken in good faith and in 
reasonable belief that they were necessary for the peer 
and good government of Goa, Daman and Diu, shall be aus 
valid and operative as if they had been done or taken in 
accordance with law.

Company. The management after due consideration 
of his finding and recommendations dismissed the 
workman from 10th May 1960. There was nothing 
mala fide in the charge-sheet and the enquiry that 
followed. It was not a case of victimisation for 
unfair labour practice. The (Company was not at 
all aware if the concerned workman was an active 
member of the Union. There was nothing mala fide 
in the action of the Company taken against the 
concerned workman and as such he is not entitled 
to get any relief. 


Decision 


The Union examined two witnesses only and the 
Company examined four witnesses and tendered 
into evidence a number of documents. 


Admittedly Seu Narayan Singh was in the employ 
of the Company in the Galvanising Department. He 
was drawing a monthly salary of Rs. 55 before his 
dismissal was effected on the 10th May 1960 as a 
result of a domestic enquiry in respect of charges 
of misconduct levelled against him by the Company. 
P.W. 1 Shri Seu Narayan Singh admits the domestic 
enquiry which was held by D.W. 3 Shri Madhabendu 
Nath Gupta. The workman was first charge-sheeted 
on 16th December 1959. Exhibit B is the copy of 
the charge-sheet. The evidence shows that the 
workrhan having refused to accept the charge-sheet 
it was sent to him by registered post with 
acknowledgment due (vide Ext. B/1). By 0115 
document the workman was charged for instigating 
other workmen to remain idle while on duty. The 
workman was asked to explain his conduct within 
two days. But according to the Company the work- 
man did not care to submit any explanation. On 
the contrary, he went on creating further trouble 
and on the 23rd December 1959 he brought into 
the factory one Chandradeo Shaw who was an 
ex-employee and was previously dismissed from 
service, in spite of the durwan’s protest and at the 
Same time instigated an illegal strike and resorted 
to indiscipline and physical violence, in consequence 
of which the factory had to be locked out. Exhibit D 
is the charge-sheet, dated 24th December 1959. This 
document shows that the Company wanted dismissal 
of the workman with immediate effect. This letter, 
as I have stated, is dated 24th December 1959 and 
the workman having refused to accept, it was sent 
to his residence by registered post with acknowledge- 
ment due. But before it reached the destination 
the Company amended the order on the very next 
day, ie, on 25th December 1959 (vide Ext. D/1) 
and thereby the workman was called upon to submit 
an explanation within 48 hours from the receipt of 
this letter. He was also informed that he would 
remain under suspension pending an enquiry into 
the charges levelled against him. The workman Shri 
Seu Narayan Singh refused to accept both the charve- 
Sheets (Exts. B and D), dated 16th December 1959 
and 24th December 1959. Therefore, they were sent 
to his same residential address by registered post 
with acknowledgment due as will appear from the 
posting receipts (Ext. B/1 and another one appended 
to Ext. D). The workman admits to have submitted 
explanation to the second charge-sheet but he did 
not offer any explanation to the first one. He has 
stated before the enquiring officer that he does not

Issue 
Whether the termination of employment of Seu

The reference relates to an industrial dispute 
existing between Messrs. Shree Viswakarma 
Industries of 14/1 Krishna Dayal Jalan Road, 


Howrah (hereinafter be referred to as the Company), 
and their workmen represented by Howrah Zilla 
Balti Sramik Union (hereinafter be referred to as the 
Union). 


It was received in December 1960 and immediately 
thereafter notices were issued for service upon both 
the parties who duly entered appearance on receipt 
of the notice. They also filed their respective 
written statements. The case of the Union as 
Stated in the written statement is as follows:— 


That the ‘Company is an old and prosperous 
concern carrying on bucket manufacturing business. 
It earns huge profit every year, but does not pay 
proper remuneration to its workmen who having 
failed to impress upon the Company about their 
individual grievances, have organised themselves und 
formed their Union. 


That Shri Seu Narayan Singh, who was a 
permanent workman of the Company, was an active 
member of the Union and because of his activities 
as such he incurred the displeasure of the 
Company. 


On 16th December 1959 the Company, therefore, 
wrongfully charge-sheeted him on the allegation that 
he had instigated people to an illegal strike. The 
workman submitted an explanation. He was again 
charge-sheeted for having violated factory discipline 
and causing disturbance inside the factory and also 
for instigating other workmen to an illegal strike. 
There was a show of enquiry in April and May 
1960. The concerned workman was not given proper 
Opportunity to defend himself but he was arbitrarily 
dismissed from service with effect from 10th May 
1960. 


There was no justification for the order of 
dismissal. Hence the dispute. 


The Company has resisted the Union’s claims by 
denying the alleged arbitrary dismissal of the 
concerned workman without holding proper enquiry 
on account of his trade union  uctivities. The 
Union’s case, on the contrary, is that the concerned 
workman Shri Seu Narayan Singh was charge- 
sheeted on 16th December 1959 for idling away 
while on duty and at the same time instigating 
other workmen to remain idle. He having refused 
to accept the charge-sheet, it was sent to him by 
registered post with acknowledgment due. He failed 
to submit an explanation called for from him. Then 
again, on the 23rd December 1959, he made a 
forcible entry into the factory premises along with 
an outsider and instigated the workmen to resort 
to an illegal strike, in consequence of which the 
management had to close the factory after declaring 
a lock-out. Shri Seu Narayan Singh was again 
charge-sheeted on the 24th December 1959 for the 
aforesaid misconduct of his. Thereafter in pursuance 
of a tripartite agreement the lock-out was lifted and

Findings 


The Association has raised a preliminary objection 
that the workmen of the Association are not members 
of the Union in question; but the Association has 
adduced no evidence in support of that contention. 
On the other hand, P.W. 1, Shri Satkori Roy 
Choudhury, says in his evidence that all the 
employees of the Association except one are members 
of the Union. The Association has not been able 
to show anything to discredit this statement of 
P.W. 1. So it must be held that almost all the 
employees of the Association are members of the 
Union. Hence I decide that this is an industrial 
dispute and reject the preliminary objection of the 
Association. 


As to the merits, it is the common case of both 
Sides that Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury was 
suspended pending permission of this Court. Neither 
side says that he was subsequently dismissed. So 
the issue in the order of reference as to whether the 
dismissal of Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury is justified 
is not literally correct. But since he has been under 
Suspension uptil now, this suspension 15 virtually 
dismissal. So the issue in the order of reference, 
though not literally correct, is materially apposite. 
Hence I am passing this award on the issuc as 
framed in the order of reference. 


The Union has stated in its written statement 
that no proper enquiry about the charge-sheet was 
held. P.W. 1 says that an enquiry was held on 10th 
April 1959 in his absence; but O.P.W. 1 Shri Sunil 
Kumar Roy, the then Secretary of the Association 
5895 in his evidence that the enquiry to be held on

Both sides admit that an enquiry was held on 23rd

hot cross-examine two of the three witnesses of the

The case of the Serampore-Chinsurah-Boinchee 
Bus Workers’ Union, the Union mentioned in the 
order of reference briefly stated, is as follows: 


Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury, the workman 
mentioned in the issue of the order of reference, 
was a Starter under Messrs. Serampore-Bandel Bus 
Association (Route No. 2), for about 8/9 years. He 
is an important office-bearer of the Union and 
contributed a lot to the formation of the Union. 
The Association did not take his Union activities 
in good grace and started harassing him in various 
ways. On 15th March 1959 the Association issued 
a charge-sheet to him without any justification 
making some baseless allegations against him. He 
gave his explanation in time denying the charges as 
baseless. Thereafter the Association decided to 
dismiss him without holding any proper enquiry and 
suspended him. An adjudication proceeding between 
the Association and the Union was pending before 
this Court (Second Labour Court) then. So the 
Association applied to this Court for permission to 
dismiss Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury. This Court 
became functus officio before it could dispose of the 
above application. So the Union contends that the 
action of the Association in keeping Shri Satkori 
Roy Choudhury under suspension with the inten- 
tion to dismiss him is unjustified. 


The Association has raised a preliminary objection 
to the effect that this is not an industrial dispute 
on the ground that the workmen of the Association 
are not members of the Union in question. As to 
the merits of the issue, the Association states that 
Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury was charge-sheeted for 
his gross misconducts of remaining absent from duty 
during hours of duty and of making back entries in 
the way bills. He submitted his explanation to the 
charge-sheet. After receipt of the Jexplanation he 
was informed by a letter, dated 4th April 1959, 
that an enquiry about the charge-sheet would be 
held on 10th April 1959. On that date, i.e., on 10th 
April 1959 he informed the Association by a letter 
that his wife was suffering from illness and that as 
such it would not be possible for him to attend the 
enquiry fixed for that date. Accordingly the 
Association adjourned the enquiry to 230 April 
1959 and informed him accordingly. On that date 
he attended the enquiry and participated in it by 
making his own statement and by cross-examining 
some witnesses of the Association. The result of the 
enquiry clearly established that Shri Satkori Roy 
Choudhury was guilty of the charges mentioned in 
the charge-shect. The report of the enquiring officer 
and all connected papers were placed before a 
meeting of the executive committee of the Associa- 
tion on 2150 May 1959; the executive committee 
after going through all the relevant papers 
unanimously recommended that Shri Satkori Roy 
Choudhury should be dismissed and forwarded the 
matter to the general meeting of the Association for

Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury. So the fact that the 
statement of O.P.W. 1 was written beforehand and 
that the papers in support of his statement were not 
actually handed over to Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury 
does not prove that the enquiry was not properly held. 
Shri N. হি. Roy, Advocate appearing for the Union, 
has made a grievance that the signatories of the 
papers produced in support of the statement of 
O.P.W. ۱ were not examined at the enquiry, and that 
as such Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury got no 
opportunity to cross-examine them. So he contends 
that the enquiry has been vitiated on account of the 
violation of the principles of natural justice. In 
support of his contention he has referred to a 
decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of 
Choudhury reported at page 494 of L.L.J. 1957, 
Volume I. But in that case certain witnesses 
examined behind the back of the charge-sheeted 
workman, were not tendered for cross-examination.

AWARD 


The above dispute over the issue given in the 
order of reference and _ re-produced below was 
referred for adjudication to this Tribunal by the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, 
order No. 7483-1.R./IR/11L-481(A)/61, dated the 
Ist December 1961. 


The issue referred for decision is as foliows:— 


Issue 


Whether the refusal of employment to Shri 
Nandalal Ram is justified? To what relief, 
if any, is he entitled? 


After receipt of the reference, usual notices were 
issued to the parties and the notices were served. 
Both parties appeared on the first date. Then the 
Union took several adjournments for filing written 
statement and there were also some defaults in the 
appearance by the parties on some dates. Finally, 
12th March 1962 was fixed for filing written state- 
ment by the Union. On that date, instead of filing 
any written statement, the Union, together with the 
Company and the concerned worker himself, filed 
a joint petition of compromise setting out the terms 
upon which the dispute under reference had been 
amicably settled between them and praying for a 
compromise award on the basis of those terms. I 
heard the representatives of the partics on that day 
and I was satisfied that there had been a bona fide 
settlement of the dispute between the parties in 
terms of the joint petition. I have also considered 
the terms of compromise and they appear to me to 
he quite lawful and fair. So, the case is to be 
disposed of by a compromise award. 


In the result, I make a compromise award in terms 


of the joint petition of the parties filed on 12th 
March 1962, a copy whereof is made a part of the 
award as an Annexure. 


S. K. RAY, 
Judge, Seventh Industrial Tribunal. 
The 13th March 1962. 


case that Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury was on duty 
at Taldanga, which is a sub-station. The exhibits 
produced and the evidence adduced on behalf of the 
Association also prove that Shri Satkori Roy 
Choudhury made some back entried in the way bills. 
They also prove that O.P.W. 1 found Shri Satkori 
Roy Choudhury absent on Ist March 1959 and 6th 
March 1959. As to absence on Ist March 1959, Shri 
Satkori Roy Choudhury has explained that he went 
to answer call of nature. Even if this explanation 
he accepted as satisfactory, there is no answer to 
other charges mentioned in the charge-sheet. Hence 
I hold that the evidence adduced before me proves 
the other charges in the charge-sheet beyond any 
shadow of doubt. These charges are so serious in 
consideration of the nature of work of a starter 
that dismissal is the proper punishment for them. 


In view of the above considerations, I hold that 
the dismissal of Shri Satkori Roy Choudhury is 
justificd. Hence he is not entitled to any relief. 


Taken at my dictation and corrected by me. 


H. R. DEB, 
Presiding Officer.
